title: Water Supply, Sanitation and Environment — practice questions
$comment: Answer positions were distributed while authoring, per the discipline recorded after the chapter 1 bank was found to key 55% of its questions to option (b). Numerical items were recomputed independently before keying.

questions.stem: The total PER CAPITA DEMAND used in designing a town water supply is made up of:
options: The domestic demand alone
Domestic and industrial demand only
Domestic demand plus a fixed allowance of 20 per cent for everything else
Domestic, industrial, institutional and commercial, and public (civic) demands, together with an allowance for losses and wastage
questions.solution:
**DOMESTIC, INDUSTRIAL, INSTITUTIONAL and COMMERCIAL, and PUBLIC demands, together with an allowance for LOSSES and WASTAGE** — the losses commonly being the largest single item after domestic use.

**The components, with typical figures for an Indian or Nepali town:**

| Component | Typical allowance (litres per capita per day) |
|---|---|
| **DOMESTIC — drinking, cooking, bathing, washing, flushing** ← | **135 for a piped supply with sewerage; 70 to 100 without** ← |
| **INDUSTRIAL** ← | **20 to 25, or computed separately for a major industry** ← |
| **INSTITUTIONAL and COMMERCIAL — schools, offices, hospitals, hotels, markets** ← | **20 to 25** ← |
| **PUBLIC (civic) — street washing, gardens, public fountains, public toilets** ← | **10 to 15** ← |
| **FIRE fighting** ← | **1 to 5, though the demand is instantaneous rather than continuous** ← |
| **LOSSES and WASTAGE — leakage, theft, unmetered use, meter error** ← | **15 to 25 per cent of the total — often the largest item after domestic use** ← |
| **TOTAL** | **About 200 to 270 lpcd for a fully served town** ← |

> **THE LOSSES IN THE SIXTH ROW ARE THE ITEM MOST WORTH THINKING ABOUT AND THEY ARE ROUTINELY UNDER-ESTIMATED IN DESIGN AND UNDER-ATTENDED IN OPERATION:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The design allowance of 15 to 25 per cent is a DESIGN target, not a description of reality** ← | ← |
| **Actual NON-REVENUE WATER in many South Asian systems is 30 to 50 per cent** ← | **And in some Nepali towns higher still** ← |
| **So a system designed for 20 per cent losses and operating at 45 per cent is short of water from the day it opens** ← | **The shortfall being invisible in the design and unmistakable at the tap** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW DESCRIBES A REAL AND COMMON OUTCOME AND IT LEADS TO AN IMPORTANT CONCLUSION ABOUT PRIORITIES: reducing losses is almost always cheaper than augmenting supply.**

> **A town losing 40 per cent of its water can recover more supply by leak detection and repair than by building a new intake, at a fraction of the cost and without any new source, land acquisition or treatment capacity.**

> **Yet augmentation is politically visible and leak repair is not, so the harder and cheaper option is regularly deferred in favour of the easier and dearer one.**

> **This is one of the clearest instances in public infrastructure where the engineering judgment and the political incentive point in opposite directions, and it is worth being able to state the case plainly.**

**HOW THE DOMESTIC FIGURE DIVIDES, WHICH IS USEFUL FOR JUDGING WHETHER AN ALLOWANCE IS REASONABLE:**

| Use | Litres per capita per day |
|---|---|
| **Drinking** ← | **About 5 — a tiny fraction of the total** ← |
| **Cooking** | **5** |
| **Bathing** ← | **55 — the largest single domestic use** ← |
| **WC flushing** ← | **30 — and this is why sewered towns need much more water than unsewered ones** ← |
| **Washing clothes** | **20** |
| **Washing utensils** | **10** |
| **House cleaning** | **10** |
| **TOTAL domestic** | **135** ← |

> **THE DRINKING FIGURE IN THE FIRST ROW IS WORTH NOTING FOR THE PERSPECTIVE IT GIVES: only about 4 per cent of a domestic supply is actually drunk.**

> **Everything else is used for washing, flushing and cleaning, for which drinking-quality water is not strictly necessary.**

> **That observation is the basis of DUAL SUPPLY proposals — a treated supply for drinking and cooking and an untreated or reclaimed supply for flushing and irrigation — which are attractive in principle and rarely built, because two pipe networks cost far more than one and the risk of cross-connection is serious.**

> **It is nevertheless the reason RAINWATER HARVESTING and greywater reuse are worth pursuing for the non-potable uses, since those uses account for the overwhelming majority of the demand and have no quality requirement to speak of.**

examTip.trick: **Domestic + industrial + institutional/commercial + public + fire + LOSSES.** About 135 lpcd domestic for a sewered town, 200-270 total.
examTip.trap: **Design allows 15-25 % losses; reality is often 30-50 %** — so the system is short of water from the day it opens, and the shortfall is invisible in the design.
examTip.mnemonic: **Only about 5 lpcd is actually DRUNK** — bathing is 55 and flushing 30. Which is why sewered towns need more water, and why non-potable reuse has such scope.

questions.stem: Among the methods of forecasting a town's future population, the GEOMETRIC INCREASE method:
options: Assumes a constant percentage rate of growth, so the population grows exponentially
Assumes a constant absolute increase in each decade
Assumes the rate of increase itself changes by a constant amount each decade
Fits an S-shaped curve approaching a saturation population
questions.solution:
**It assumes a constant PERCENTAGE rate of growth, so the population grows exponentially** — appropriate for a young, rapidly expanding town but liable to give absurdly high figures over a long forecast.

**The methods compared:**

| Method | Assumption | Suited to |
|---|---|---|
| **ARITHMETIC increase** ← | **A constant ABSOLUTE increase per decade: P_n = P₀ + n·x̄** ← (option b) | **Large, OLD, established cities whose growth has settled** ← |
| **GEOMETRIC increase** ← | **A constant PERCENTAGE rate: P_n = P₀(1 + r)ⁿ** ← | **YOUNG, rapidly growing towns — this question** ← |
| **INCREMENTAL INCREASE** ← | **A constant increase in the increase — the average increment plus the average of the increments' increments** ← (option c) | **A compromise between the two above, and generally the most reliable of the three** ← |
| **DECREASING RATE of growth** ← | **The percentage rate itself declines, as the town approaches saturation** ← | **Towns whose growth is slowing** ← |
| **LOGISTIC curve** ← | **An S-shaped curve rising to a SATURATION population** ← (option d) | **The most realistic long-term model, and the hardest to fit** ← |
| **GRAPHICAL comparison** ← | **Extrapolating by analogy with similar towns that are further along the same path** ← | **Where local data is poor** ← |

> **THE ARITHMETIC-GEOMETRIC CONTRAST IN THE FIRST TWO ROWS IS THE ESSENTIAL DISTINCTION AND IT IS EASY TO REMEMBER FROM WHAT EACH IMPLIES:**

> **Arithmetic growth means the town adds the same NUMBER of people each decade regardless of its size — which is what happens when growth is driven by a fixed inflow into a large established city.**

> **Geometric growth means the town adds the same PROPORTION each decade — which is what happens when growth is driven by natural increase and by the town's own attractiveness, both of which scale with its size.**

> **The two diverge dramatically over a long forecast: a town of 50,000 growing arithmetically at 10,000 a decade reaches 80,000 in thirty years, while the same town growing geometrically at 20 per cent a decade reaches 86,400 — and over sixty years the gap widens to 110,000 against 149,000.**

> **So the choice of method matters more the longer the design period, which is why it must be made from the town's actual growth PATTERN rather than by preference.**

**THE PRACTICAL APPROACH, WHICH IS WORTH STATING BECAUSE IT IS WHAT COMPETENT PRACTICE ACTUALLY DOES:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. Obtain the CENSUS series — as many decades as exist** ← | **In Nepal, the decennial census back to 1952** ← |
| **2. Compute the increments and the rates, and LOOK at them** ← | **Is the absolute increase steady, or the percentage?** ← |
| **3. Apply two or three methods and compare** ← | **The spread between them is a measure of the forecast's real uncertainty** ← |
| **4. Check against any MASTER PLAN or land-use limit** ← | **A town cannot grow beyond the land available to it** ← |
| **5. Consider migration, administrative changes and specific developments** ← | **A new highway, a new industry, a municipality boundary change, or a district headquarters designation can dominate the demographic trend entirely** ← |

> **THE FIFTH STEP IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST IN NEPAL AND IT DEFEATS EVERY MATHEMATICAL METHOD: the country's urban population has grown largely by MIGRATION and by ADMINISTRATIVE RECLASSIFICATION rather than by natural increase.**

> **When a cluster of villages is declared a municipality, its 'urban population' rises by tens of thousands overnight with no demographic event whatever.**

> **When a new road reaches a town, its growth rate can change permanently within a few years.**

> **And the Kathmandu valley's growth over recent decades has been driven by internal migration on a scale that no extrapolation of its earlier census figures would have predicted.**

> **So a forecast in this context is a judgment informed by arithmetic rather than a result produced by it, and a designer who presents a geometric extrapolation as a prediction has mistaken the tool for the answer.**

> **The honest practice is to state the forecast as a range, to say which assumptions drive it, and to design for staged augmentation so that being wrong is recoverable.**

examTip.trick: **Constant PERCENTAGE rate: P_n = P₀(1 + r)ⁿ.** Option (b) is arithmetic, (c) incremental increase, (d) the logistic curve.
examTip.trap: **Arithmetic suits OLD large cities, geometric suits YOUNG growing towns** — and the two diverge sharply over a long design period, so the method must match the observed pattern.
examTip.mnemonic: **In Nepal, migration and municipal RECLASSIFICATION dominate any demographic trend** — a village cluster declared a municipality gains 'urban population' overnight. Design for staged augmentation.

questions.stem: The DESIGN PERIOD adopted for the various components of a water supply scheme differs from one component to another. The reason a PUMPING PLANT is given a shorter design period than a STORAGE DAM or a transmission main is that:
options: Pumps are more likely to be stolen
The pump has a short physical life
Pumping plant is not essential to the scheme
Dams do not deteriorate
questions.solution:
**Because the PUMP has a short physical LIFE and can be REPLACED or ADDED TO cheaply and without disturbing anything else** — whereas a dam or a buried main cannot be enlarged later without enormous cost and disruption.

**Typical design periods:**

| Component | Design period (years) |
|---|---|
| **STORAGE and impounding reservoirs, DAMS** ← | **50, and often longer** ← |
| **INTAKE structures** ← | **30** ← |
| **Water TREATMENT plant** ← | **15, in modular units that can be added to** ← |
| **PUMP SETS** ← | **10, or less — the shortest of all** ← |
| **Pump HOUSE (the civil structure)** ← | **30 — much longer than the pumps inside it** ← |
| **Transmission and distribution MAINS** ← | **30 to 40** ← |
| **Service RESERVOIRS (overhead and ground)** ← | **15 to 30** ← |
| **WELLS and tube wells** ← | **25** ← |

> **THE CONTRAST BETWEEN THE PUMP SETS AND THE PUMP HOUSE IN THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS ILLUSTRATES THE WHOLE PRINCIPLE AND IS WORTH DWELLING ON: the building is designed for thirty years and the machines inside it for ten.**

> **The reason is that the pumps will be replaced two or three times during the building's life, and each replacement is a straightforward operation provided the building has ROOM for the larger set that may be needed.**

> **So the civil works are built for the ultimate capacity and the mechanical plant for the immediate need — which is exactly the right allocation, since concrete is cheap to build once and expensive to extend, while machinery is the reverse.**

> **A pump house built to fit only today's pumps is a false economy that will be paid for at every future augmentation.**

**THE PRINCIPLE BEHIND ALL OF THESE FIGURES, WHICH MAKES THEM REASONABLE RATHER THAN ARBITRARY:**

| Factor | Effect on the design period |
|---|---|
| **How EASILY the component can be extended later** ← | **Hard to extend means a LONG design period; easy means a short one** ← |
| **The component's physical LIFE** ← | **No point designing a pump for fifty years when it will wear out in fifteen** ← |
| **The RATE of interest, and the cost of capital** ← | **A high interest rate discourages building capacity years ahead of need, since the money is idle** ← |
| **The certainty of the DEMAND forecast** ← | **A doubtful forecast argues for shorter periods and staged construction** ← |
| **ECONOMY of scale in construction** ← | **Where a larger unit costs little more than a smaller one, build the larger** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FIFTH ROWS PULL IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS AND THE BALANCE BETWEEN THEM IS THE WHOLE ECONOMICS OF STAGING:**

> **Economy of scale says build big now — a 600 mm main costs little more than a 450 mm main, since most of the cost is trenching and laying.**

> **The cost of capital says build small now and enlarge later — money spent early is money tied up for years before it earns anything.**

> **The resolution depends on which effect is larger, and it differs by component: for a BURIED MAIN the trenching dominates and staging is uneconomic, so the main is laid at its ultimate size; for a TREATMENT PLANT the units are modular and staging is cheap, so it is built in stages.**

> **That is precisely why the table gives 30 to 40 years for mains and 15 for treatment works, and it means the design periods are not conventions to be recalled but conclusions that can be reasoned out from the nature of each component.**

> **The general rule that follows is worth carrying: design for a LONG period whatever is hard to change, and a SHORT period whatever is easy — which applies well beyond water supply, to roads, to buildings and to any staged infrastructure.**

examTip.trick: **Design for a LONG period whatever is hard to extend, and a SHORT period whatever is easy.** Dams 50 years, mains 30-40, treatment 15, pumps 10.
examTip.trap: **Pump sets 10 years but the pump HOUSE 30** — build the civil works for the ultimate capacity and the machinery for today's need. Concrete is dear to extend; machines are not.
examTip.mnemonic: **Economy of scale versus cost of capital** — trenching dominates a main's cost so lay it full size; treatment units are modular so stage them. The figures follow from the reasoning.

questions.stem: A town's average daily water demand is 4.0 million litres per day. Taking the maximum daily demand as 1.8 times the average and the maximum hourly demand as 1.5 times the maximum daily rate, the PEAK HOURLY demand for which the distribution system must be designed is:
options: 6.0 MLD
7.2 MLD
10.8 MLD
12.0 MLD
questions.solution:
**10.8 MLD.**

**The calculation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Average daily demand** | **4.0 MLD** ← |
| **Maximum DAILY demand** | **= 1.8 × 4.0 = 7.2 MLD** ← |
| **Maximum HOURLY demand** ← | **= 1.5 × 7.2 = 10.8 MLD** ← |
| **So the overall peak factor is** | **1.8 × 1.5 = 2.7 times the average** ← |

> **The distribution system must therefore be designed for a rate of 10.8 MLD, that is 2.7 times the average.**

**WHY THE FACTORS COMPOUND RATHER THAN BEING TAKEN SEPARATELY IS THE POINT OF THE QUESTION, and option (b) is what a candidate gets by stopping one step early:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The maximum daily factor accounts for variation between DAYS of the year** ← | **The hottest day, a festival, a dry spell** ← |
| **The maximum hourly factor accounts for variation between HOURS of that day** ← | **The morning and evening peaks** ← |
| **Both occur TOGETHER — the peak hour of the peak day** ← | **So the factors multiply** ← |
| **Giving an overall peak of 2.7 times the average** ← | **Which is the figure the distribution network must carry** ← |

**WHICH FACTOR APPLIES TO WHICH COMPONENT IS THE PRACTICALLY IMPORTANT DISTINCTION:**

| Component | Design flow |
|---|---|
| **SOURCE, INTAKE and raw water main** ← | **MAXIMUM DAILY demand — the source must supply the peak day's total** ← |
| **TREATMENT plant** ← | **Maximum daily demand** ← |
| **Pumping main to the service reservoir** ← | **Maximum daily demand, adjusted for the hours of pumping** ← |
| **SERVICE RESERVOIR** ← | **Sized to absorb the difference between the steady inflow and the varying outflow** ← |
| **DISTRIBUTION system downstream of the reservoir** ← | **MAXIMUM HOURLY demand — this question** ← |
| **Or, where there is no reservoir, the whole system to the peak hourly rate** ← | ← |

> **THE SERVICE RESERVOIR IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE ELEMENT THAT MAKES THE WHOLE ARRANGEMENT ECONOMIC AND ITS FUNCTION IS WORTH STATING CLEARLY: it DECOUPLES the upstream works from the hourly variation.**

> **Upstream of the reservoir, everything runs at a steady rate — the intake, the treatment plant and the pumping main all deliver the day's total spread over the pumping hours.**

> **Downstream of it, the distribution network experiences the full hourly peak.**

> **The reservoir absorbs the difference, filling when demand is low and emptying when it is high.**

> **Without it, the treatment plant and the raw water main would have to be sized for 2.7 times the average instead of 1.8 — which for the plant in this example means 10.8 MLD of capacity instead of 7.2, a 50 per cent increase in the most expensive part of the scheme.**

> **So a service reservoir pays for itself several times over in the upstream capacity it saves, quite apart from the reserve it provides against a breakdown and for fire fighting — and that is the reason virtually every gravity or pumped scheme has one.**

> **A further consequence worth noting is that the reservoir also fixes the PRESSURE in the distribution system, since the head available is set by the reservoir's water level rather than by a pump's characteristic — which makes the network's hydraulics stable and predictable in a way that direct pumping into a network never is.**

verification.notes: 4.0 x 1.8 = 7.2 MLD max daily; 7.2 x 1.5 = 10.8 MLD peak hourly; overall factor 2.7.

examTip.trick: **The factors MULTIPLY: 4.0 × 1.8 × 1.5 = 10.8 MLD**, an overall peak of 2.7 × average. Option (b) is stopping at the max daily figure.
examTip.trap: **Source, intake and treatment take MAX DAILY; the distribution network takes MAX HOURLY.** Getting these the wrong way round oversizes or undersizes by 50 %.
examTip.mnemonic: **The service reservoir DECOUPLES the two** — steady flow upstream, peaky flow downstream. Without it the treatment plant would need 50 % more capacity.

questions.stem: The TEMPORARY (carbonate) hardness of water differs from PERMANENT (non-carbonate) hardness in that temporary hardness:
options: Is caused by sodium and potassium salts
Cannot be removed by any treatment
Is measured in different units
Is caused by the bicarbonates of calcium and magnesium
questions.solution:
**It is caused by the BICARBONATES of calcium and magnesium and can be removed by simple BOILING** — whereas permanent hardness, from the sulphates and chlorides of those metals, cannot.

**The two kinds:**

| Type | Caused by | Removed by |
|---|---|---|
| **TEMPORARY (carbonate) hardness** ← | **Ca(HCO₃)₂ and Mg(HCO₃)₂ — the BICARBONATES** ← | **BOILING, which drives off CO₂ and precipitates the carbonate; or lime softening** ← |
| **PERMANENT (non-carbonate) hardness** ← | **CaSO₄, MgSO₄, CaCl₂, MgCl₂ — sulphates and chlorides** ← | **Lime-SODA softening, or ion exchange (zeolite) — boiling has no effect** ← |

> **THE MECHANISM BY WHICH BOILING WORKS IS WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE IT EXPLAINS BOTH THE NAME AND A FAMILIAR NUISANCE:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Bicarbonate is only stable in the presence of dissolved CO₂** ← | ← |
| **Boiling drives the CO₂ out of solution** ← | ← |
| **The bicarbonate then decomposes: Ca(HCO₃)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O + CO₂** ← | ← |
| **Calcium carbonate is INSOLUBLE, so it precipitates** ← | **As the white SCALE in a kettle, a boiler or a hot water pipe** ← |
| **The hardness has therefore been removed from the water — onto the vessel** ← | **Which is the problem: the same reaction that softens the water fouls the equipment** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE PRACTICAL SIGNIFICANCE OF CARBONATE HARDNESS IN INDUSTRY AND IT IS WHY BOILER FEED WATER IS SOFTENED: scale in a boiler is a thermal insulator, so the tube metal overheats while the water on the other side stays cool.**

> **A scale layer of a few millimetres can raise tube temperatures enough to cause failure, and it also wastes a substantial amount of fuel by impeding heat transfer.**

> **So boiler water must be softened before use, and the softening must remove permanent hardness too — which is why lime-soda or ion exchange, and not merely deaeration, is used.**

**THE UNITS AND CLASSIFICATION, WHICH ARE WORTH HAVING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Hardness is expressed as mg/l of CaCO₃ EQUIVALENT** ← | **So that calcium and magnesium salts of different molecular weights can be added together** ← |
| **Soft** | **Below 75 mg/l** ← |
| **Moderately hard** | **75 to 150 mg/l** ← |
| **Hard** | **150 to 300 mg/l** ← |
| **Very hard** | **Above 300 mg/l** ← |
| **NDWQS limit for drinking water in Nepal** ← | **500 mg/l as CaCO₃ — a generous limit, hardness being an aesthetic and economic nuisance rather than a health hazard** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE POINT THAT PUTS HARDNESS IN PERSPECTIVE AND IS OFTEN MISUNDERSTOOD: hard water is not unhealthy.**

> **There is no established health harm from hardness at ordinary levels, and some epidemiological evidence suggests a modest cardiovascular benefit from calcium and magnesium in drinking water.**

> **What hardness does is waste SOAP — reacting with it to form an insoluble scum instead of a lather — deposit scale in pipes, kettles and heaters, stain fittings, and spoil laundry.**

> **So softening a public supply is an economic and amenity decision rather than a public health one, and it is justified by the soap and the scale it saves rather than by any disease it prevents.**

> **That is quite different from the treatment of turbidity or bacteriological contamination, which are health matters, and it explains why the drinking water standard for hardness is set so much more loosely than for those parameters.**

> **A useful corollary: in a scheme with limited resources, hardness removal is the item to defer, and disinfection is the item that cannot be.**
tags: hardness is not a health hazard

examTip.trick: **Temporary = BICARBONATES, removed by boiling. Permanent = sulphates and chlorides, needs lime-soda or ion exchange.**
examTip.trap: **Boiling removes the hardness FROM the water and puts it ON the vessel** — as kettle and boiler scale, which insulates tubes and wastes fuel.
examTip.mnemonic: **Hardness is an economic and amenity problem, not a health one** — it wastes soap and deposits scale. NDWQS allows 500 mg/l. Defer softening; never defer disinfection.

questions.stem: The ALKALINITY of water is important in water treatment principally because it:
options: Measures the water's capacity to neutralise acid
Is a direct measure of the water's hardness
Indicates the concentration of dissolved oxygen
Determines the water's turbidity
questions.solution:
**It measures the water's capacity to NEUTRALISE ACID** — that is, its BUFFERING capacity — so it determines how much the pH will fall when an acidic coagulant such as alum is added.

**What alkalinity is:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Alkalinity is the concentration of BASES able to neutralise acid** ← | **Principally BICARBONATE, with carbonate and hydroxide at higher pH** ← |
| **It is expressed as mg/l of CaCO₃ equivalent** ← | **The same convention as hardness** ← |
| **It is NOT the same as pH** ← | **pH measures the intensity of acidity; alkalinity measures the CAPACITY to resist a change in it** ← |
| **Two waters of the same pH can have very different alkalinities** ← | **And will behave quite differently when a coagulant is added** ← |

> **THE pH-AGAINST-ALKALINITY DISTINCTION IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE ONE MOST WORTH GETTING RIGHT AND AN ANALOGY MAKES IT PLAIN: pH is like TEMPERATURE and alkalinity is like HEAT CAPACITY.**

> **A cup of water and a bathtub of water at the same temperature are equally hot, but the bathtub takes vastly more cooling to change.**

> **In the same way, two waters at pH 7.5 are equally acidic, but the one with high alkalinity will barely shift when acid is added while the other will drop sharply.**

> **Which is why a treatment plant needs to know both, and why alkalinity rather than pH is the parameter that governs coagulant dosing.**

**WHY IT MATTERS FOR COAGULATION, WHICH IS THE PRACTICAL POINT:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **ALUM (aluminium sulphate) is an acidic salt** ← | **When it dissolves, it releases acid** ← |
| **It REACTS WITH the water's alkalinity to form the aluminium hydroxide floc** ← | **The alkalinity is a REACTANT, not merely a bystander** ← |
| **Each mg/l of alum consumes about 0.5 mg/l of alkalinity as CaCO₃** ← | ← |
| **If the water's alkalinity is INSUFFICIENT, the pH falls sharply** ← | **Out of the optimum range for floc formation, which is about 6.5 to 7.5 for alum** ← |
| **And the floc then does not form properly** ← | **So the coagulation fails, and adding MORE alum makes it worse rather than better** ← |
| **The remedy is to ADD alkalinity — lime, soda ash or sodium bicarbonate** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW DESCRIBES A GENUINELY COUNTER-INTUITIVE OPERATIONAL SITUATION AND IT IS WORTH RECOGNISING: when coagulation is poor, the instinctive response is to increase the alum dose.**

> **If the problem is insufficient alkalinity, that response depresses the pH further and makes the floc worse — so the operator sees the water deteriorating as he adds more chemical, and may add more still.**

> **The correct response is to check the pH and, if it has fallen below the optimum range, to add lime rather than alum.**

> **This is why a jar test — dosing several samples at different alum doses and pH values and observing the floc — is the standard means of setting the dose, and why a plant treating a soft, low-alkalinity water needs a lime dosing facility as well as an alum one.**

> **SOFT WATERS ARE THE ONES AT RISK, WHICH HAS A DIRECT NEPALI APPLICATION: the country's hill and mountain surface waters, draining hard crystalline rock, are frequently very soft and low in alkalinity.**

> **A plant designed on the assumption of an alkaline water — as many Indian plains sources are — will find its coagulation failing on such a source, particularly in the monsoon when the turbidity is highest and the coagulant demand greatest.**

> **So the source's alkalinity is a design parameter to be measured, and provision for pH correction is not an optional refinement in a soft-water catchment but a necessary part of the plant.**

examTip.trick: **Alkalinity is the CAPACITY to neutralise acid — the buffer.** pH is like temperature; alkalinity is like heat capacity.
examTip.trap: **Alum CONSUMES alkalinity (about 0.5 mg/l per mg/l of alum)** — if there is not enough, the pH crashes out of the 6.5-7.5 optimum and the floc fails.
examTip.mnemonic: **When coagulation is poor, check the pH before adding more alum** — more alum on a low-alkalinity water makes it worse. Add LIME. Nepal's soft hill waters are exactly this case.

questions.stem: Under the National Drinking Water Quality Standards of Nepal, the maximum permissible concentration of ARSENIC in drinking water is:
options: 0.5 mg/l
questions.solution:
**0.05 mg/l.**

**The standards, and the important comparison:**

| Standard | Arsenic limit |
|---|---|
| **WHO guideline value** ← | **0.01 mg/l** ← (option b) |
| **NDWQS of Nepal** ← | **0.05 mg/l — five times the WHO value** ← |
| **Indian standard IS 10500** | **0.01 mg/l, with 0.05 permitted where no alternative source exists** ← |

> **THE GAP BETWEEN THE FIRST TWO ROWS IS DELIBERATE AND ITS REASONING IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING RATHER THAN CRITICISING, since it illustrates how a standard is actually set:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **The WHO value of 0.01 mg/l is a HEALTH-BASED guideline** ← | **The concentration at which the lifetime cancer risk is considered acceptable** ← |
| **A national STANDARD must also be ACHIEVABLE and ENFORCEABLE** ← | **A limit that most of the country's water fails, with no means of remedy, protects nobody** ← |
| **In the Terai, a large number of tube wells exceed 0.01 but fall below 0.05** ← | **Condemning them all at once would leave communities with no source at all, and they would return to unsafe surface water** ← |
| **So an INTERIM standard of 0.05 was adopted, with a programme of testing, marking and mitigation** ← | **Prioritising the worst wells** ← |
| **The intention is progressive tightening as alternatives become available** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW STATES THE REAL DILEMMA AND IT IS A GENUINE ONE RATHER THAN AN EXCUSE: a community whose only well is condemned does not thereby obtain a safe supply.**

> **It returns to a river or a pond, and the resulting diarrhoeal disease may kill more people, and kill them sooner, than the arsenic would have.**

> **So the choice is not between arsenic and safety but between arsenic and pathogens — and arsenic, whose effects appear after years of exposure, is the lesser immediate hazard.**

> **That is an uncomfortable calculation and it is the correct one, provided it is accompanied by an actual programme to provide alternatives rather than used as a reason for inaction.**

**THE ARSENIC PROBLEM IN THE TERAI, IN OUTLINE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The arsenic is NATURAL, not industrial** ← | **Released from the alluvial sediments of the Ganges basin under reducing conditions in the aquifer** ← |
| **It affects shallow tube wells in particular** ← | **The problem arose as tube wells replaced surface water, which was itself a public health measure** ← |
| **It is TASTELESS, ODOURLESS and COLOURLESS** ← | **So it cannot be detected without testing, and the water looks and tastes excellent** ← |
| **Chronic exposure causes ARSENICOSIS** ← | **Skin lesions, keratosis, pigmentation changes, and eventually cancers of the skin, bladder and lung** ← |
| **The effects take 5 to 20 years to appear** ← | **So a community can be exposed for a generation before anyone falls ill** ← |
| **Wells are tested and painted RED (unsafe) or GREEN (safe)** ← | **A simple, effective and widely used communication measure** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FIFTH ROWS TOGETHER EXPLAIN WHY THIS BECAME A CATASTROPHE RATHER THAN A MANAGEABLE PROBLEM, and the lesson generalises well beyond arsenic.**

> **A hazard that is imperceptible and slow-acting produces no feedback: nobody notices anything wrong, so nothing is done, and the exposure continues for decades.**

> **A hazard that is perceptible and fast-acting — turbid water that causes diarrhoea within days — produces immediate feedback and immediate action.**

> **So the most dangerous water quality problems are precisely the ones that cannot be seen or tasted, and the whole apparatus of routine sampling and testing exists because human senses are not merely imperfect detectors of water quality but systematically biased ones — reassuring exactly where reassurance is least warranted.**

> **The other parameters worth knowing from the NDWQS: turbidity 5 NTU (10 permitted where no alternative), pH 6.5 to 8.5, iron 0.3 mg/l, total coliform and E. coli both ZERO per 100 ml, and residual chlorine 0.1 to 0.2 mg/l at the point of use.**

examTip.trick: **NDWQS allows 0.05 mg/l — five times the WHO guideline of 0.01.** An interim standard, adopted because condemning every well between the two values would leave people with nothing.
examTip.trap: **The choice is arsenic against PATHOGENS, not arsenic against safety** — a community whose only well is condemned returns to surface water, and diarrhoeal disease kills sooner.
examTip.mnemonic: **Tasteless, odourless, colourless, and 5-20 years to show** — a hazard with no feedback. Which is exactly why routine testing exists. Also know: turbidity 5 NTU, coliforms ZERO.

questions.stem: In the classification of water-related diseases, CHOLERA and TYPHOID are WATER-BORNE, whereas TRACHOMA and SCABIES are classified as WATER-WASHED. The distinction is that a water-washed disease is prevented principally by:
options: Boiling the drinking water
Increasing the quantity of water available for personal and domestic hygiene
Chlorinating the supply
Filtering the water to remove the pathogen
questions.solution:
**Increasing the QUANTITY of water available for personal and domestic HYGIENE** — the pathogen being transmitted by contact rather than by ingestion.

**The classification, which organises the whole subject:**

| Category | Transmission | Examples | Control |
|---|---|---|---|
| **WATER-BORNE** ← | **The pathogen is INGESTED in the water** ← | **Cholera, typhoid, paratyphoid, bacillary and amoebic dysentery, hepatitis A and E, polio, giardiasis** ← | **Improve water QUALITY — treat and disinfect** ← |
| **WATER-WASHED (water-scarce)** ← | **Transmitted by CONTACT, and prevented by washing** ← | **Trachoma, scabies, skin and eye infections, typhus, and much diarrhoeal disease** ← | **Improve water QUANTITY and ACCESS, and promote hygiene** ← |
| **WATER-BASED** ← | **Part of the pathogen's life cycle occurs IN WATER, in an intermediate host** ← | **Schistosomiasis (bilharzia), guinea worm** ← | **Avoid contact with the water; control the snail or copepod host** ← |
| **WATER-RELATED INSECT VECTOR** ← | **Transmitted by insects that BREED in or near water** ← | **Malaria, dengue, filariasis, Japanese encephalitis, onchocerciasis** ← | **Control the breeding sites; drainage; nets** ← |

> **THE FIRST TWO CATEGORIES ARE THE ONES A WATER ENGINEER CAN ACT ON DIRECTLY AND THE CONTRAST BETWEEN THEM IS THE MOST USEFUL DISTINCTION IN PUBLIC HEALTH ENGINEERING:**

> **A WATER-BORNE disease is controlled by making the water CLEANER.**

> **A WATER-WASHED disease is controlled by making the water MORE PLENTIFUL and more accessible — its cleanliness being almost irrelevant.**

> **These lead to opposite investment priorities, and getting the diagnosis wrong wastes the money entirely.**

> **A community with a distant, meagre but clean source suffers water-washed disease, and a treatment plant will not help it — a nearer, larger supply will.**

> **A community with an abundant but contaminated source suffers water-borne disease, and more of the same water will not help it — treatment will.**

**THE QUANTITY THRESHOLD IS WORTH KNOWING, SINCE IT QUANTIFIES THE SECOND CATEGORY:**

| Availability | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Below about 20 lpcd, or a source more than 1 km or 30 minutes away** ← | **Only drinking and cooking are served; personal hygiene is essentially abandoned, and water-washed disease is prevalent** ← |
| **20 to 50 lpcd, source within reasonable reach** ← | **Basic hygiene becomes possible** ← |
| **Above about 50 lpcd with a household connection** ← | **Hygiene is no longer constrained by water availability** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW CONTAINS THE OBSERVATION THAT SHAPED MODERN RURAL WATER POLICY AND IT IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY: when water must be CARRIED, the quantity used collapses.**

> **A household fetching water from a source 30 minutes away will use it for drinking and cooking and very little else, because every additional litre is another journey.**

> **Hand washing, bathing, washing clothes and cleaning the house all give way to the effort of collection — and those are precisely the activities that prevent water-washed disease.**

> **So bringing the source CLOSER can improve health more than treating the water, because it changes the quantity used rather than its quality.**

> **This is why the standard for a rural water supply is expressed in terms of both quantity and DISTANCE or time, and why a scheme that provides a treated supply at a single distant standpost may achieve less health benefit than an untreated supply at every household.**

> **It is also the reason HAND WASHING promotion — which requires only water, soap and habit — is among the most cost-effective public health interventions known, and why a water scheme without a hygiene promotion component leaves much of its potential benefit unrealised.**

examTip.trick: **Water-borne = ingested, cured by QUALITY. Water-washed = contact, cured by QUANTITY and access.** Water-based = life cycle in water. Vector = breeds near water.
examTip.trap: **The two lead to OPPOSITE investment priorities** — a clean but distant source causes water-washed disease, and a treatment plant will not help it. Bringing it closer will.
examTip.mnemonic: **When water must be CARRIED, quantity collapses to drinking and cooking** — and hygiene is abandoned. Below 20 lpcd or 30 minutes away, water-washed disease is inevitable.

questions.stem: Excessive FLUORIDE in drinking water is of concern because it causes:
options: Immediate gastrointestinal illness
Blue baby syndrome in infants
Skin lesions and keratosis
Dental fluorosis (mottling of the teeth) and
questions.solution:
**DENTAL FLUOROSIS (mottling of the teeth) and, at higher concentrations and longer exposure, SKELETAL FLUOROSIS** — while a DEFICIENCY of fluoride causes dental caries, so the acceptable range is narrow.

**The dose-response relationship, which is unusual among water quality parameters:**

| Fluoride concentration | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Below about 0.5 mg/l** ← | **Increased incidence of DENTAL CARIES (tooth decay) — a deficiency** ← |
| **0.5 to 1.0 mg/l** ← | **The OPTIMUM — maximum protection against caries with no visible fluorosis** ← |
| **1.0 to 1.5 mg/l** ← | **The permissible upper range; mild dental mottling may appear** ← |
| **1.5 to 4 mg/l** ← | **DENTAL FLUOROSIS — brown mottling and pitting of the enamel; permanent and cosmetic** ← |
| **Above about 4 to 10 mg/l, over years** ← | **SKELETAL FLUOROSIS — the fluoride is deposited in bone, causing stiffness, pain, calcification of ligaments and eventually crippling deformity** ← |

> **THE FACT THAT BOTH TOO LITTLE AND TOO MUCH ARE HARMFUL MAKES FLUORIDE UNIQUE AMONG THE COMMON WATER QUALITY PARAMETERS AND IT IS THE POINT OF THE QUESTION:**

> **For turbidity, arsenic, coliforms and nearly everything else, less is better and zero is ideal.**

> **For fluoride there is an OPTIMUM, and the standard therefore has a lower bound in effect as well as an upper one.**

> **This is why some countries deliberately ADD fluoride to supplies that are deficient — fluoridation — while others must remove it from supplies that have too much: DEFLUORIDATION.**

> **The same element, the same public health objective, and opposite treatment processes, depending only on the source's natural concentration.**

**THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE ALL REAL CONDITIONS AND WORTH DISTINGUISHING:**

| Condition | Cause |
|---|---|
| **BLUE BABY SYNDROME (methaemoglobinaemia)** ← | **NITRATE, above about 45 to 50 mg/l — the nitrate is reduced to nitrite in an infant's gut, which converts haemoglobin to methaemoglobin and impairs oxygen transport** ← (option b) |
| **SKIN LESIONS and KERATOSIS** ← | **ARSENIC — arsenicosis** ← (option c) |
| **Immediate gastrointestinal illness** ← | **Bacteriological contamination, or an acute chemical dose** ← (option a) |
| **Discolouration and staining of fittings and laundry** | **IRON and MANGANESE, above 0.3 and 0.1 mg/l** ← |
| **Dental and skeletal fluorosis** ← | **FLUORIDE — this question** ← |

> **THE NITRATE CONDITION IN THE FIRST ROW DESERVES A NOTE BECAUSE IT SPECIFICALLY THREATENS INFANTS AND NOT ADULTS, which is unusual: an adult's stomach is acidic enough to prevent the bacterial reduction of nitrate to nitrite, and an adult's enzyme system reconverts any methaemoglobin formed.**

> **A young infant's stomach is less acidic and its enzyme system immature, so the reduction proceeds and the methaemoglobin accumulates.**

> **Hence a nitrate concentration entirely harmless to the rest of the household can be dangerous to a bottle-fed baby — and the danger is greatest where the formula is MADE UP with the water, since that is the infant's whole fluid intake.**

> **Nitrate in groundwater usually indicates contamination from sewage, latrines or fertiliser, so a high nitrate reading is also a warning that the well may be bacteriologically contaminated — which makes it doubly significant as an indicator.**

> **THE DEFLUORIDATION METHODS, FOR COMPLETENESS: the NALGONDA technique — coagulation with alum and lime followed by settling — is the cheapest and most widely used in South Asia; activated alumina adsorption, bone char and reverse osmosis are the alternatives.**

> **All of them are more troublesome than the alternative of BLENDING with a low-fluoride source or switching source entirely, which is why the first response to a fluoride problem is always to look for another well rather than to build a treatment plant.**

examTip.trick: **Too little causes caries, too much causes fluorosis** — optimum 0.5-1.0 mg/l, permissible to 1.5, dental fluorosis above that, skeletal above about 4.
examTip.trap: **Fluoride is the one parameter with a LOWER bound as well as an upper one** — hence fluoridation in some places and defluoridation in others, for the same public health objective.
examTip.mnemonic: **Blue baby = NITRATE (infants only, immature gut chemistry); keratosis = ARSENIC.** High nitrate also warns of sewage contamination, so it is doubly significant.

questions.stem: Compared with a surface water source, GROUNDWATER is generally characterised by:
options: Lower turbidity and bacteriological contamination but higher dissolved mineral content
Higher turbidity and lower dissolved solids
Greater seasonal variation in both quality and quantity
A higher dissolved oxygen content
questions.solution:
**LOWER turbidity and bacteriological contamination but HIGHER dissolved mineral content** — so it usually needs little treatment beyond disinfection, while its hardness, iron or arsenic may be problematic.

**The two source types compared:**

| Property | SURFACE water | GROUNDWATER |
|---|---|---|
| **TURBIDITY** | **HIGH and highly variable — very high in the monsoon** ← | **LOW and steady; the aquifer has filtered it** ← |
| **Bacteriological quality** | **POOR — always assumed contaminated** ← | **GOOD, if the well is properly constructed and protected** ← |
| **DISSOLVED solids and hardness** | **LOW** ← | **HIGH — the water has been in contact with rock and soil for a long time** ← |
| **DISSOLVED OXYGEN** ← | **HIGH — in contact with the air** ← | **LOW or nil — which is why iron and manganese remain dissolved, and why arsenic is mobilised** ← (so option d is inverted) |
| **TEMPERATURE** | **Varies with the season** ← | **Nearly CONSTANT through the year** ← |
| **Seasonal variation in quality and quantity** | **LARGE** ← | **SMALL — a major practical advantage** ← (option c is inverted) |
| **Treatment usually needed** | **Coagulation, sedimentation, filtration, disinfection — the full works** ← | **Disinfection; sometimes iron removal, softening or arsenic removal** ← |
| **Cost of development** | **Intake and a full treatment plant** ← | **Wells and pumps; usually cheaper in total** ← |

> **THE DISSOLVED OXYGEN ROW IS THE KEY TO SEVERAL OF GROUNDWATER'S CHARACTERISTIC PROBLEMS AND IT IS WORTH FOLLOWING THROUGH, because it explains what would otherwise be a list of unrelated nuisances:**

| Consequence | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **IRON and MANGANESE stay in solution** ← | **In the reduced (ferrous and manganous) state they are soluble; on exposure to air they OXIDISE and precipitate as rust-coloured and black deposits** ← |
| **Which is why the water is clear at the pump and turns brown in the bucket** ← | **A characteristic and instantly recognisable symptom** ← |
| **ARSENIC is mobilised** ← | **Reducing conditions release arsenic from the iron oxide coatings on the sediment grains** ← |
| **HYDROGEN SULPHIDE may be present** ← | **The rotten-egg smell, from sulphate reduction** ← |
| **And the water is CORROSIVE to some metals** ← | **Being oxygen-free and often carrying dissolved CO₂** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW DESCRIBES THE MOST FAMILIAR DIAGNOSTIC IN GROUNDWATER SUPPLY AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING AS SUCH: water that is perfectly clear when drawn and discolours within minutes has dissolved iron, not turbidity.**

> **A turbidity measurement made at the wellhead will read low and a measurement made an hour later will read high, from the same sample — so the sampling procedure matters, and an iron problem can be missed entirely by prompt testing.**

> **The treatment is straightforward and follows directly from the mechanism: AERATE the water to oxidise the iron, then SETTLE and FILTER the precipitate out.**

> **A cascade aerator followed by a sand filter is often all that is needed, and it is one of the simplest and most reliable treatment processes there is.**

**THE SELECTION OF A SOURCE, WHICH IS THE PRACTICAL QUESTION BEHIND ALL THIS:**

| Criterion | Note |
|---|---|
| **QUANTITY — adequate and dependable in the DRIEST season** ← | **The dry-weather yield governs, not the average** ← |
| **QUALITY — and hence the treatment needed** ← | ← |
| **Elevation relative to the town** ← | **A source above the town permits GRAVITY supply, with no pumping cost for ever — which frequently outweighs every other consideration** ← |
| **Distance, and hence the transmission cost** ← | ← |
| **Legal and social rights over the source** ← | **Existing users, downstream users, and any customary rights** ← |
| **Vulnerability to CONTAMINATION and to landslide, flood or earthquake** ← | ← |

> **THE GRAVITY CONSIDERATION IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE ONE THAT DOMINATES SOURCE SELECTION IN NEPAL'S HILLS, and it is worth being explicit about why: a gravity scheme has no pumps, no electricity supply, no fuel, no standby generator and no operator to run them.**

> **Its running cost is nearly nil and it works during a power cut, which in much of the country is a substantial part of the year.**

> **A pumped scheme of the same capacity may be far cheaper to build and dearer to run for ever, and it stops entirely when the power fails or the fuel is not paid for — which is the commonest reason rural schemes fall out of use.**

> **So a spring or a stream ABOVE the settlement, even if smaller and further away, is frequently preferred to an abundant river below it — and the hill topography that makes so much else difficult in Nepal makes this one thing easy.**

examTip.trick: **Groundwater: low turbidity and bacteria, high dissolved solids.** Needs disinfection, and perhaps iron removal, softening or arsenic treatment.
examTip.trap: **Groundwater has LOW dissolved oxygen, not high** — which is exactly why iron, manganese and arsenic are in solution, and why H₂S may be present.
examTip.mnemonic: **Clear at the pump, brown in the bucket = dissolved IRON.** Aerate, settle, filter. And in the hills, a GRAVITY source above the town beats an abundant river below it.

questions.stem: In developing a SPRING as a water source, the essential protective measure is to:
options: Line the spring's outlet channel with concrete
Chlorinate the spring water at its point of emergence
Construct a spring box enclosing the point of emergence
Deepen the spring by excavation until the flow increases
questions.solution:
**Construct a SPRING BOX enclosing the point of emergence, with a cut-off wall, a surface water diversion drain uphill, and a fenced protection area** — so that the water is collected before it can be contaminated at the surface.

**The elements of a properly developed spring source:**

| Element | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **The SPRING BOX (intake chamber), built INTO the hillside at the eye of the spring** ← | **Collects the water where it emerges from the ground, before it flows over the surface** ← |
| **A CUT-OFF WALL keyed into the impervious stratum** ← | **Forces all the flow into the box rather than allowing it to seep past** ← |
| **A permeable collection zone of graded gravel behind the wall** ← | **Admitting water while retaining the soil — the filter criteria again** ← |
| **A DIVERSION DRAIN uphill of the works** ← | **Intercepting surface runoff before it reaches the spring area** ← |
| **A watertight COVER and a lockable access** ← | **Excluding light (which grows algae), animals, debris and people** ← |
| **A FENCED protection zone, typically 15 to 50 m uphill** ← | **Excluding grazing, latrines, cultivation and washing** ← |
| **An OVERFLOW and a washout** ← | **So the box does not back up, and can be cleaned** ← |
| **A screened, raised air VENT** | **Preventing a vacuum, excluding insects** ← |

> **THE PRINCIPLE UNDERLYING ALL OF THIS IS A SINGLE ONE AND IT IS WORTH STATING BEFORE THE DETAILS: spring water is generally SAFE AT THE MOMENT IT EMERGES and becomes unsafe immediately afterwards.**

> **It has been filtered by its passage through the ground, and if the aquifer is deep and the recharge area is uncontaminated the water reaching the eye of the spring may be excellent.**

> **The instant it flows across the surface it is exposed to animal droppings, human contact, washing, runoff and debris.**

> **So spring protection is entirely a matter of CAPTURING the water before that exposure occurs — which is why the box must be built AT the eye of the spring and into the hillside, and not as a tank a few metres downstream collecting water that has already run over the ground.**

> **A collection tank fed by an open channel from a spring is a very common arrangement in practice and it forfeits the whole benefit of the source.**

**THE PROTECTION ZONE IN THE SIXTH ROW IS THE MEASURE MOST OFTEN OMITTED AND THE HARDEST TO SUSTAIN:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Contamination can enter the ground UPHILL of the spring and travel to it** ← | **So protecting the emergence point alone is insufficient** ← |
| **A latrine, a cattle shed or a grave uphill of a spring can contaminate it** ← | **Particularly in fissured or karst ground, where travel is rapid and unfiltered** ← |
| **The zone must be legally secured and physically fenced** ← | **A line on a drawing does not exclude a goat** ← |
| **And it must be MAINTAINED — fences fall, and land uses change** ← | **A spring protected at construction and unprotected ten years later is an unprotected spring** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE POINT THAT MAKES SPRING PROTECTION GEOLOGICALLY DEPENDENT AND IT DESERVES CARE: in a fine-grained soil, water travels slowly and pathogens die off before they reach the spring, so a modest protection zone suffices.**

> **In FISSURED rock or limestone, water can travel hundreds of metres in a day through open channels with no filtration whatever — so a spring emerging from such ground may be drawing water from a contaminated source far away, and no local protection zone will help.**

> **This is why a spring's protection requires the RECHARGE AREA to be identified and not merely the emergence point, and why a spring in karst terrain should be treated with the same suspicion as a surface source however clear it runs.**

> **The tell-tale sign is RESPONSIVENESS: a spring whose flow and turbidity change within hours of rainfall is connected to the surface by open pathways and is not truly a groundwater source at all, whatever it looks like — while one whose flow varies slowly over months is genuinely filtered by a substantial aquifer.**

> **Observing that response over a wet season is therefore worth more than a single water quality test, and it is a cheap investigation that is regularly skipped.**

examTip.trick: **Capture the water AT the eye of the spring, before it runs over the surface** — box, cut-off wall, uphill diversion drain, cover, and a fenced protection zone.
examTip.trap: **A tank fed by an open channel from a spring forfeits the whole benefit** — the water is contaminated in those few metres. Very common in practice.
examTip.mnemonic: **A spring whose flow or turbidity changes within HOURS of rain is not really groundwater** — it is connected to the surface. Watch the response over a wet season; it beats one water test.

questions.stem: COLLOIDAL impurities in water are distinguished from suspended and dissolved impurities in that colloids:
options: Can be removed by plain sedimentation within a few hours
Are too fine to settle out in any practicable time and carry a surface electrical charge that keeps them mutually repelling
Are removed by boiling
Consist entirely of dissolved salts
questions.solution:
**They are too FINE to settle out in any practicable time and carry a surface ELECTRICAL CHARGE that keeps them mutually repelling** — so they must be COAGULATED before they can be removed.

**The three classes of impurity by size:**

| Class | Size | Behaviour | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SUSPENDED** ← | **Above about 1 micron — silt, sand, clay flocs, algae** ← | **SETTLE under gravity in a reasonable time** ← | **Plain SEDIMENTATION, then filtration** ← |
| **COLLOIDAL** ← | **About 1 nanometre to 1 micron — fine clay, colour, some bacteria and viruses** ← | **Do NOT settle; kept in suspension indefinitely by Brownian motion and mutual repulsion** ← | **COAGULATION and flocculation, then sedimentation and filtration — this question** ← |
| **DISSOLVED** ← | **Below about 1 nanometre — salts, gases, some organics** ← | **In true solution; not removable by any physical separation of particles** ← | **Ion exchange, membranes, adsorption, aeration, chemical precipitation** ← |

> **THE MIDDLE CLASS IS THE ONE THAT DEFINES CONVENTIONAL WATER TREATMENT AND THE MECHANISM BY WHICH IT IS DEALT WITH IS WORTH SETTING OUT PROPERLY:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Colloidal clay particles carry a NEGATIVE surface charge** ← | **From the mineral structure and from adsorbed ions** ← |
| **Like charges REPEL, so the particles cannot approach one another** ← | **The repulsion is measured as the ZETA POTENTIAL** ← |
| **They therefore remain dispersed indefinitely** ← | **A colloidal suspension is stable for months** ← |
| **A COAGULANT supplies highly charged POSITIVE ions — Al³⁺ or Fe³⁺** ← | **Which compress the repulsive double layer and NEUTRALISE the charge** ← |
| **The particles can then collide and stick — DESTABILISATION** ← | **Which is the coagulation step, and it is essentially instantaneous** ← |
| **FLOCCULATION then follows: gentle stirring brings the destabilised particles together into large flocs** ← | **A slow process taking 20 to 40 minutes** ← |
| **The flocs are large enough to SETTLE, and are removed by sedimentation and filtration** ← | ← |

> **THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN THE FIFTH AND SIXTH STEPS IS THE ONE MOST WORTH GETTING RIGHT AND IT DICTATES THE PHYSICAL DESIGN OF THE PLANT:**

> **COAGULATION is a CHEMICAL process — charge neutralisation — and it requires RAPID, VIOLENT mixing so that the coagulant is dispersed throughout the water within a second or two, before it hydrolyses locally.**

> **FLOCCULATION is a PHYSICAL process — particle collision and growth — and it requires SLOW, GENTLE stirring for many minutes, because vigorous stirring would tear the fragile flocs apart as fast as they formed.**
> **So the plant has a FLASH MIXER of a few seconds' detention with high energy input, followed by a FLOCCULATOR of half an hour with very low energy input — two units with opposite requirements in immediate succession.**

> **Confusing the two, or attempting both in one tank, is a design error that produces either poorly dispersed coagulant or broken flocs, and either way the sedimentation tank downstream cannot recover from it.**

**AND THE PARTICLE SIZE RANGE EXPLAINS WHY FILTRATION ALONE IS NOT ENOUGH, WHICH IS WORTH NOTING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A rapid sand filter's pores are far LARGER than a colloidal particle** ← | **Perhaps 100 microns against 0.1 micron — a thousandfold difference** ← |
| **So a filter does not STRAIN colloids out** ← | **They pass straight through, which is why raw water cannot simply be filtered** ← |
| **What a filter removes is FLOCS, and it removes them by adhesion within the bed depth** ← | **Not by straining at the surface** ← |
| **Which is why coagulation must PRECEDE filtration and cannot be replaced by it** ← | ← |

> **The third row is worth emphasising because the mental picture of a filter as a sieve is misleading: a rapid sand filter works chiefly by particles ADHERING to the grains as the water threads its way through, not by being caught on the surface.**

> **That is why the filter's DEPTH matters, why its removal efficiency depends on the water's chemistry as much as on its grain size, and why a filter receiving poorly coagulated water fails to clarify it however fine the sand.**

examTip.trick: **Too fine to settle and mutually repelling** because of their surface charge — so they need a coagulant to neutralise it before anything can remove them.
examTip.trap: **Coagulation is CHEMICAL and needs RAPID violent mixing; flocculation is PHYSICAL and needs SLOW gentle stirring.** Two units, opposite requirements, in succession.
examTip.mnemonic: **A sand filter's pores are a thousand times bigger than a colloid** — it removes FLOCS by adhesion within its depth, not by straining. So coagulation cannot be replaced by filtration.

questions.stem: EUTROPHICATION of a lake or reservoir used as a water source is a problem for the water supply engineer because it:
options: Increases the reservoir's storage capacity
Reduces the water's hardness
Has no effect on treatment, being purely an ecological matter
Produces algal blooms that cause taste and odour
questions.solution:
**It produces ALGAL BLOOMS that cause TASTE and ODOUR, CLOG the filters, consume chlorine, may release TOXINS, and on dying deplete the DISSOLVED OXYGEN** — which in turn releases iron, manganese and phosphorus from the bed sediments.

**The process:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **NUTRIENTS — chiefly PHOSPHORUS, and also nitrogen — enter the water body** ← | **From sewage, detergents, fertiliser runoff and animal waste** ← |
| **Algae and aquatic plants multiply explosively** ← | **A BLOOM, often visible as a green scum** ← |
| **The bloom shades the deeper water, and eventually the algae DIE** ← | ← |
| **Their decomposition CONSUMES dissolved oxygen** ← | **Which can drive the lower layers ANOXIC** ← |
| **Anoxic conditions at the bed RELEASE iron, manganese and more PHOSPHORUS from the sediment** ← | **Which feeds the next bloom — a self-sustaining cycle** ← |
| **Fish and other aerobic life die** ← | ← |

> **THE FEEDBACK IN THE FIFTH ROW IS WHAT MAKES EUTROPHICATION SO DIFFICULT TO REVERSE AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING: once a lake has become eutrophic, its OWN SEDIMENTS become a nutrient source.**

> **Phosphorus accumulated in the bed over years is bound to iron oxides while the water above is oxygenated.**

> **When the bed goes anoxic, that iron is reduced and the phosphorus is released back into the water — so the lake fertilises itself.**

> **This is called INTERNAL LOADING, and it means that cutting off the external nutrient supply may not restore the lake for many years, because the accumulated store must be exhausted first.**

> **The practical consequence is that eutrophication is far cheaper to PREVENT than to cure, and that the time to act is before the bloom rather than after it.**

**THE TREATMENT PROBLEMS ALGAE CAUSE, WHICH IS THE ENGINEER'S IMMEDIATE CONCERN:**

| Problem | Note |
|---|---|
| **TASTE and ODOUR** ← | **Geosmin and MIB, produced by blue-green algae, are detectable at nanogram concentrations and are the commonest cause of consumer complaint** ← |
| **Filter CLOGGING** ← | **Algal cells and filaments blind a rapid sand filter quickly, shortening the run between backwashes drastically** ← |
| **High CHLORINE demand** ← | **The organic matter consumes disinfectant, so more must be added to leave a residual** ← |
| **DISINFECTION BY-PRODUCTS** ← | **The organic matter reacts with chlorine to form trihalomethanes, which are themselves a health concern** ← |
| **CYANOTOXINS** ← | **Some blue-green algae release toxins (microcystin) that conventional treatment does not remove** ← |
| **pH rise during the day** ← | **Photosynthesis strips CO₂, raising the pH and upsetting the coagulation** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW CONTAINS A GENUINELY AWKWARD DILEMMA AND IT IS WORTH STATING BECAUSE IT IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE: treating an organically rich water with more chlorine creates a different health risk.**

> **Chlorine reacting with natural organic matter forms trihalomethanes and other by-products which are suspected carcinogens on long exposure.**

> **So the operator faces a trade between microbiological risk, which is immediate and certain, and by-product risk, which is remote and statistical.**

> **The resolution is not to reduce disinfection — the immediate risk always dominates — but to REMOVE THE ORGANIC MATTER BEFORE chlorinating, by good coagulation, by activated carbon, or by using an alternative disinfectant.**

> **THE PREVENTIVE MEASURES ARE ALL IN THE CATCHMENT RATHER THAN THE PLANT, WHICH IS THE CLOSING POINT: intercept sewage before it reaches the reservoir, control fertiliser and animal waste in the catchment, maintain a vegetated buffer strip around the water body, and where possible draw water from a DEPTH below the algal zone by means of a multi-level intake.**

> **The multi-level intake is the one measure available to the engineer after the fact, and it is a valuable one: it allows the operator to select the best water available at any season — avoiding the surface bloom in summer and the anoxic bottom layer when the lake is stratified — which is why any reservoir intake worth building has more than one draw-off level.**

examTip.trick: **Taste and odour, filter clogging, chlorine demand, toxins, and oxygen depletion** — which then releases iron, manganese and more phosphorus from the sediment.
examTip.trap: **INTERNAL LOADING makes it self-sustaining** — anoxic sediment releases its accumulated phosphorus, so cutting off the external supply may not restore the lake for years.
examTip.mnemonic: **Remove the organics BEFORE chlorinating** — more chlorine on organic-rich water makes trihalomethanes. And build a MULTI-LEVEL intake: it is the only fix available after the fact.

questions.stem: The removal of dissolved IRON from groundwater is normally achieved by:
options: Aeration to oxidise the soluble ferrous iron to insoluble ferric hydroxide
Ion exchange with a sodium zeolite
Adding lime to raise the pH above 11
Reverse osmosis
questions.solution:
**AERATION to oxidise the soluble ferrous iron to insoluble ferric hydroxide, followed by SEDIMENTATION and FILTRATION to remove the precipitate.**

**The process:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Groundwater holds iron in the reduced FERROUS (Fe²⁺) state, which is SOLUBLE** ← | **Because the water is oxygen-free** ← |
| **AERATION introduces oxygen** ← | **By a cascade, a spray, a tray aerator, or a diffused air system** ← |
| **The ferrous iron oxidises to FERRIC (Fe³⁺), which is INSOLUBLE** ← | **Precipitating as reddish-brown ferric hydroxide** ← |
| **The precipitate is allowed to SETTLE and then FILTERED out** ← | **Usually on a rapid gravity or pressure sand filter** ← |
| **Aeration also strips CO₂, raising the pH, which accelerates the oxidation** ← | **A useful side effect, since the reaction is faster at higher pH** ← |
| **And it strips hydrogen sulphide, removing the rotten-egg smell** ← | **Another useful side effect** ← |

> **THE ELEGANCE OF THIS PROCESS IS THAT IT ADDS NO CHEMICAL AT ALL AND IS WORTH APPRECIATING FOR THAT: the treatment agent is atmospheric oxygen, which is free, and the process needs no dosing equipment, no chemical store and no operator judgment about doses.**

> **A cascade aerator is a set of steps down which the water falls, and it has no moving parts.**

> **This makes iron removal one of the very few treatment processes genuinely suited to a small rural installation with no chemical supply chain and minimal operator training — which matters a great deal in a Nepali context, where most water supplies are small and remote.**

**MANGANESE IS REMOVED BY THE SAME PRINCIPLE BUT IS MORE DIFFICULT, AND THE DIFFERENCE IS WORTH KNOWING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Manganese oxidises much more SLOWLY than iron at neutral pH** ← | **So simple aeration is often insufficient** ← |
| **It needs a higher pH — above about 9 — or a stronger oxidant** ← | **Potassium permanganate or chlorine** ← |
| **Or a CATALYTIC filter medium** ← | **Manganese-coated sand or greensand, on which the oxidation proceeds far faster** ← |
| **So a plant designed for iron alone may pass manganese straight through** ← | **And the manganese then oxidises in the distribution main, producing black water complaints weeks later** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW DESCRIBES A PARTICULARLY FRUSTRATING FIELD PROBLEM AND IT IS WORTH RECOGNISING: the plant's outlet water is clear and meets its iron standard, and consumers at the far end of the network report black water.**

> **The manganese passed through the plant in solution, oxidised slowly in the main over hours or days, and precipitated as black manganese dioxide in the pipe — from where it is dislodged by any change in flow.**

> **The symptom therefore appears far from its cause, both in space and in time, and testing at the plant reveals nothing.**

> **The diagnosis requires a manganese test on the raw water, and the remedy is to treat for manganese specifically rather than assuming that an iron process covers it.**

**AND THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE ALL REAL PROCESSES FOR OTHER PURPOSES, WHICH IS WORTH SORTING OUT:**

| Process | What it is for |
|---|---|
| **Sodium ZEOLITE ion exchange** ← | **SOFTENING — exchanging calcium and magnesium for sodium** ← (option b) |
| **LIME to pH above 11** ← | **Excess-lime softening, for magnesium hardness removal** ← (option c) |
| **REVERSE OSMOSIS** ← | **Desalination and the removal of dissolved solids generally — it would remove iron, at many times the cost and with a brine to dispose of** ← (option d) |
| **AERATION** ← | **Iron and manganese removal, CO₂ and H₂S stripping, taste and odour control — this question** ← |

> **The reverse osmosis option is worth a comment because it illustrates a general error in treatment selection: a powerful process will indeed solve a simple problem, at a wholly disproportionate cost.**

> **Choosing the SIMPLEST process that achieves the objective is the mark of good treatment design, and reaching for membranes to remove an iron that a flight of concrete steps would precipitate is the opposite of it.**

examTip.trick: **Aerate, settle, filter** — oxygen converts soluble ferrous to insoluble ferric hydroxide. No chemical needed, which makes it ideal for small rural plants.
examTip.trap: **MANGANESE oxidises far more slowly** — an iron plant passes it through, and it then precipitates as black deposits in the mains, appearing days later and far away.
examTip.mnemonic: **Choose the SIMPLEST adequate process** — reverse osmosis would remove the iron too, at many times the cost and with a brine to dispose of. A flight of concrete steps does it.

questions.stem: TURBIDITY of water is measured in NTU (nephelometric turbidity units) by an instrument that:
options: Weighs the residue after evaporating a known volume
Measures the depth at which a standard printed target ceases to be legible
Measures the intensity of light scattered at 90 degrees to an incident beam
Measures the electrical conductivity of the sample
questions.solution:
**It measures the intensity of light SCATTERED at 90 degrees to an incident beam** — the scattering being proportional to the concentration of suspended particles.

**The instrument and what it measures:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A beam of light passes through the sample** ← | ← |
| **Suspended particles SCATTER some of it in all directions** ← | ← |
| **A detector at 90 degrees to the beam measures the scattered intensity** ← | **The 90-degree position being chosen because it sees scattered light and not the direct beam** ← |
| **The reading is compared with a standard suspension — FORMAZIN** ← | **Hence 'nephelometric turbidity units', calibrated against formazin standards** ← |
| **Turbidity is therefore an OPTICAL property, not a measurement of mass** ← | **Two waters of equal suspended solids can have very different turbidities** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE POINT MOST WORTH UNDERSTANDING AND IT IS OFTEN GLOSSED OVER: turbidity is not suspended solids.**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **Scattering depends on particle SIZE, SHAPE, COLOUR and refractive index as well as on concentration** ← | ← |
| **FINE particles scatter far more per unit mass than coarse ones** ← | **A gram of clay gives a much higher turbidity than a gram of sand** ← |
| **DARK particles ABSORB light rather than scattering it, so they read LOW** ← | **Which is why a black organic sludge can look opaque and measure a modest turbidity** ← |
| **So there is no universal conversion between NTU and mg/l of suspended solids** ← | **A site-specific correlation can be established, and it applies only to that water** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW HAS A USEFUL PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE FOR TREATMENT: turbidity is most sensitive to precisely the particles that are hardest to remove.**

> **Coarse silt settles readily and contributes little to the reading; fine colloidal clay does not settle at all and dominates it.**

> **So a high turbidity is a warning that the water contains material requiring coagulation, and a falling turbidity through a plant is a direct measure of how well the coagulation is working.**

> **This is why turbidity is the primary operational control parameter in a treatment plant — it responds quickly, it is cheap to measure continuously, and it tracks the thing that actually matters.**

**THE FILTERED WATER TURBIDITY TARGET IS THE MOST IMPORTANT NUMBER IN THE SUBJECT AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING WHY:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The drinking water standard is 5 NTU (NDWQS), and WHO recommends below 1 NTU** ← | ← |
| **But good practice aims at below 0.5 or even 0.1 NTU from a filter** ← | **Far below the standard** ← |
| **The reason is that turbidity SHIELDS pathogens from disinfection** ← | **A particle can harbour bacteria and protozoa within it, where chlorine does not reach** ← |
| **And CRYPTOSPORIDIUM and GIARDIA cysts are essentially resistant to chlorine at practical doses** ← | **So they must be removed PHYSICALLY, by filtration, and the only routine indicator that the filter is achieving that is its turbidity** ← |
| **Hence low filtered turbidity is a SURROGATE for cyst removal** ← | **A 0.1 NTU filtrate implies effective physical removal; a 1 NTU filtrate does not** ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS CONTAIN THE MODERN JUSTIFICATION FOR TIGHT TURBIDITY CONTROL AND IT IS A DIFFERENT ARGUMENT FROM THE TRADITIONAL AESTHETIC ONE: turbidity used to be controlled because cloudy water is unappealing.**

> **It is now controlled because it is the only continuously measurable indicator that the filters are removing chlorine-resistant parasites.**

> **A plant whose filtered water rises from 0.1 to 0.5 NTU has not become aesthetically worse — it may still look perfectly clear — but it has lost a substantial part of its barrier against cryptosporidiosis, and there is no other on-line measurement that would reveal it.**

> **That is why individual filter turbidity monitoring, rather than a single combined reading, is now regarded as best practice: one failing filter among six can be masked entirely in the combined figure while passing cysts continuously into the supply.**

examTip.trick: **Light scattered at 90° to the beam**, calibrated against formazin standards. An OPTICAL property, not a mass measurement.
examTip.trap: **There is no universal NTU to mg/l conversion** — fine particles scatter far more per unit mass, and dark particles absorb rather than scatter, reading low.
examTip.mnemonic: **Low filtered turbidity is a SURROGATE for cyst removal** — cryptosporidium resists chlorine, so filtration is the only barrier and turbidity the only on-line indicator that it is working.

questions.stem: A RESIDUAL CHLORINE of 0.1 to 0.2 mg/l is required at the consumer's tap principally to:
options: Improve the taste of the water
Demonstrate that the water was disinfected AND provide a continuing safeguard against any contamination entering the distribution system between the plant and the tap
Prevent scale forming in the pipes
Reduce the water's hardness
questions.solution:
**To demonstrate that the water was disinfected AND provide a continuing safeguard against any CONTAMINATION entering the distribution system between the plant and the tap.**

**The two functions:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **EVIDENCE that disinfection took place and that the chlorine demand was satisfied** ← | **A residual means the chlorine was not all consumed, so the demand was met with something to spare** ← |
| **A CONTINUING BARRIER through the distribution system** ← | **Any small ingress of contamination downstream of the plant meets a residual disinfectant** ← |
| **A rapid INDICATOR of a problem** ← | **A residual that has disappeared at a particular point is evidence of contamination or of excessive age, and it can be measured on the spot in seconds** ← |

> **THE SECOND FUNCTION IS THE MORE VALUABLE AND IT ADDRESSES A REAL AND UNDERAPPRECIATED RISK, which is worth setting out:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A distribution system is not sealed** ← | **It has thousands of joints, valves, connections and repairs** ← |
| **When the pressure FAILS or the supply is intermittent, the pipes DRAIN** ← | ← |
| **Groundwater, sewage and surface water around the pipe are then drawn IN through the same defects** ← | **Because the pressure gradient has reversed** ← |
| **On refilling, that contamination is delivered to the consumers** ← | ← |
| **A residual disinfectant is the only barrier against it** ← | **The treatment plant, however good, is upstream of the problem** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW DESCRIBES THE SINGLE GREATEST WATER QUALITY RISK IN AN INTERMITTENT SUPPLY AND IT IS WORTH BEING BLUNT ABOUT IT: a system that is not continuously pressurised is a system that sucks in contamination every time it empties.**

> **This is the fundamental objection to intermittent supply, and it is a water QUALITY objection rather than a convenience one.**

> **A town supplied for two hours a day has its mains empty for twenty-two hours, sitting in ground that frequently contains leaking sewers and latrine seepage — and every one of those hours is an opportunity for ingress.**

> **No amount of treatment at the plant addresses it, because the contamination enters downstream.**

> **So converting an intermittent supply to a continuous one is a public health measure of the first order, and it is usually achieved not by finding more water but by reducing losses and managing pressure — which brings the argument back to leakage control.**

**THE CHLORINE DEMAND AND THE BREAK-POINT, FOR COMPLETENESS:**

| Stage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Chlorine added first reacts with reducing agents — iron, manganese, sulphide, organics** ← | **Producing NO disinfecting residual at all** ← |
| **Further chlorine reacts with AMMONIA to form CHLORAMINES** ← | **A COMBINED residual, which disinfects weakly and slowly** ← |
| **Beyond a point, further chlorine DESTROYS the chloramines** ← | **And the measured residual actually FALLS as more is added** ← |
| **The minimum of that curve is the BREAK-POINT** ← | ← |
| **Beyond the break-point, added chlorine appears as FREE residual** ← | **Hypochlorous acid, which is the strong, fast disinfectant** ← |
| **BREAK-POINT CHLORINATION means dosing past that point** ← | **Which is what a properly operated plant does** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE COUNTER-INTUITIVE FEATURE OF THE CURVE AND IT HAS A PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE WORTH KNOWING: over part of the range, adding more chlorine REDUCES the residual.**

> **An operator who measures a low residual, increases the dose, and finds the residual has fallen further may conclude the test is faulty — when in fact he is on the descending limb and must push through the break-point.**

> **A residual measured without knowing whether it is FREE or COMBINED is therefore of limited value: 0.5 mg/l of free chlorine is good disinfection and 0.5 mg/l of combined chlorine is not.**

> **This is why the standard specifies a FREE residual, and why the field test kit must distinguish the two rather than reporting a single total figure.**

examTip.trick: **Evidence that the demand was satisfied, plus a continuing barrier in the distribution system** — where the plant cannot reach.
examTip.trap: **An intermittent supply SUCKS IN contamination whenever the mains drain** — through the same defects that leak out under pressure. A quality objection, not a convenience one.
examTip.mnemonic: **Past the BREAK-POINT the residual is FREE chlorine; before it, adding more can REDUCE the reading.** And 0.5 mg/l free is good disinfection while 0.5 combined is not.

questions.stem: RAINWATER HARVESTING as a domestic water source is characterised by:
options: A yield independent of the roof area
Water requiring no treatment whatever
A constant supply throughout the year
A yield proportional to the roof area and the rainfall
questions.solution:
**A yield proportional to the ROOF AREA and the RAINFALL, requiring STORAGE to bridge the dry season** — with the FIRST FLUSH needing to be diverted and the stored water still requiring disinfection.

**The yield calculation:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **Yield = roof PLAN area × rainfall × RUNOFF coefficient** ← | ← |
| **The runoff coefficient is 0.8 to 0.9 for a metal or tiled roof** ← | **Lower for a thatched or porous roof, which absorbs and evaporates a substantial part** ← |
| **A 100 m² roof in a place receiving 1,500 mm of rain yields about 120 to 135 m³ a year** ← | **100 × 1.5 × 0.85 = 127 m³** ← |
| **Which at 20 lpcd would serve a family of five for about three and a half years' worth of that ration** ← | **So the annual volume is generally ample; the difficulty is entirely one of TIMING** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE POINT ON WHICH RAINWATER HARVESTING TURNS AND IT IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY: the annual quantity is usually more than sufficient and the seasonal distribution is the problem.**

> **In Nepal, some 80 per cent of the rain falls in four monsoon months, and the driest period may be five or six months long.**

> **So the yield arrives when it is least needed and is absent when it is most needed — and the STORAGE required to bridge that gap is the whole cost of the system.**

> **A tank to carry a family through a six-month dry season at 20 lpcd is about 18 m³, which is a substantial structure — and it is the tank, not the roof or the gutters, that determines whether the scheme is affordable.**
