> **This is why rainwater harvesting is often designed as a SUPPLEMENTARY source, reducing the demand on a stressed main supply during and after the monsoon, rather than as a sole source requiring full seasonal storage.**

**THE QUALITY CONSIDERATIONS, WHICH ARE WHY OPTION (b) IS WRONG:**

| Contaminant | Note |
|---|---|
| **BIRD and animal droppings on the roof** ← | **The principal bacteriological hazard, and it is a real one** ← |
| **DUST, leaves, insects and debris** ← | ← |
| **Roofing material itself** ← | **Asbestos, lead flashing, bitumen and some paints can contaminate; a metal or tile roof is preferred** ← |
| **Atmospheric deposition** ← | **Near an industrial area or a busy road** ← |
| **Growth within the TANK** ← | **Algae if light enters, and mosquito breeding if it is not sealed** ← |

> **THE FIRST FLUSH DIVERTER IS THE SINGLE MOST EFFECTIVE QUALITY MEASURE AND ITS PRINCIPLE IS SIMPLE: the first few millimetres of rain wash the accumulated droppings and dust off the roof, and that water is by far the dirtiest.**

> **Diverting the first one or two millimetres of each storm — a few tens of litres from a domestic roof — removes the great majority of the contamination for the loss of a very small part of the yield.**

> **The device can be as simple as a vertical standpipe that fills first and is emptied manually, or a tipping bucket, and it costs almost nothing.**

> **Its omission, or its failure to be emptied between storms, is the commonest reason a rainwater system delivers poor water — and since it requires a small routine action by the householder, it is a maintenance-dependent measure and must be explained rather than merely installed.**

**THE OTHER ESSENTIALS OF A SOUND SYSTEM, IN BRIEF:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **A leaf SCREEN on the gutter and the inlet** ← | ← |
| **A DARK, SEALED tank with a screened overflow and vent** ← | **Excluding light stops algae; sealing excludes mosquitoes, which is important in dengue and malaria areas** ← |
| **A DRAW-OFF above the tank floor, and a washout at the floor** ← | **So the settled sediment is not drawn into the supply** ← |
| **Household DISINFECTION before drinking — boiling, chlorination or SODIS** ← | **Rainwater is not sterile and the tank is not a treatment plant** ← |
| **A means of using the water within a reasonable time** ← | **Water stored for many months in a warm tank deteriorates** ← |

> **The sealed tank in the second row deserves emphasis in a Nepali and South Asian context because of a hazard unconnected with drinking water: an open water storage tank is an ideal breeding site for Aedes mosquitoes, and dengue has spread widely in Nepal in recent years.**

> **So a rainwater tank that is not properly screened can create a vector-borne disease risk while solving a water supply problem — an instance of the water-related insect vector category from the disease classification, arising directly from a public health intervention.**

verification.notes: 100 m2 roof x 1.5 m rain x 0.85 = 127 m3 per year.

examTip.trick: **Yield = roof area × rainfall × runoff coefficient (0.8-0.9).** The annual quantity is usually ample; the STORAGE to bridge the dry season is the real cost.
examTip.trap: **Rainwater is NOT clean** — bird droppings, dust and roofing materials contaminate it, and it still needs household disinfection. The tank is not a treatment plant.
examTip.mnemonic: **Divert the FIRST FLUSH (1-2 mm)** — it carries most of the contamination for a tiny loss of yield. And SEAL the tank: an open one breeds Aedes mosquitoes.

questions.stem: In siting the INTAKE for a river water supply, the intake is best located:
options: On the outer bank of a bend
On the inner bank of a bend, where deposition keeps the bed level
Immediately downstream of the town, where the flow is greatest
At the centre of a straight reach, on the bed
questions.solution:
**On the OUTER bank of a bend, where the channel is deep and scouring, and UPSTREAM of the town's sewage outfalls and other pollution sources.**

**The considerations in siting a river intake:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **On the OUTER (concave) bank of a bend** ← | **The flow attacks the outer bank, so the channel there is DEEP and SCOURING — the intake stays in water and does not silt up** ← |
| **NOT on the inner bank** ← | **The inner bank is where DEPOSITION occurs, so an intake there silts up and eventually stands in a sand bar** ← (option b is inverted) |
| **UPSTREAM of all sewage outfalls, drains and industrial discharges** ← | **And upstream of the town itself, since the town generates diffuse pollution as well as point discharges** ← |
| **Where the water is DEEPEST at low flow, and free of eddies** ← | ← |
| **Accessible by road for construction and maintenance** ← | ← |
| **Above the highest flood level for the structure and the approach** ← | ← |
| **Clear of navigation channels, and of any reach liable to CHANNEL MIGRATION** ← | **A braided Himalayan river may abandon the reach entirely** ← |

> **THE OUTER-BANK PRINCIPLE IN THE FIRST TWO ROWS IS THE MOST USEFUL PIECE OF KNOWLEDGE IN INTAKE SITING AND IT FOLLOWS FROM THE SECONDARY CIRCULATION IN A BEND:**

> **Water moving round a bend is thrown outward by centrifugal effect at the surface and returns inward along the bed, setting up a spiral flow.**

> **That spiral scours the outer bank and the bed beside it, and deposits the material it carries on the inner bank.**

> **Hence the universal pattern: outer bank deep and eroding, inner bank shallow and building — the mechanism that makes a river meander in the first place.**

> **An intake on the outer bank is therefore self-cleaning, while one on the inner bank fights a continuous losing battle against deposition.**

> **The corollary is that the outer bank must be PROTECTED, since the same scour that keeps the intake in water is attacking the bank the intake stands on — so an outer-bank intake needs revetment and a founding level below the anticipated scour.**

**THE TYPES OF INTAKE, FOR CONTEXT:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **RIVER intake — a submerged or a wet/dry well intake tower** ← | **With screens, and often multiple draw-off levels** ← |
| **RESERVOIR intake — a tower with several draw-off levels** ← | **The multiple levels being the point, as discussed for eutrophication** ← |
| **CANAL intake — a chamber in the canal bank** ← | **With a bell mouth and a screen** ← |
| **LAKE intake — a submerged crib or a pipe extending into deep water** ← | **Placed well away from the shore, where the water is cleanest** ← |
| **SPRING and INFILTRATION GALLERY intakes** ← | **The gallery being a perforated pipe or a porous drain laid in a permeable bed beside or beneath a river, so that the water is naturally filtered before collection** ← |

> **THE INFILTRATION GALLERY IN THE LAST ROW DESERVES PARTICULAR ATTENTION IN A NEPALI CONTEXT AND IS OFTEN THE BEST ANSWER TO A DIFFICULT PROBLEM: a Himalayan river in the monsoon carries turbidity of thousands of NTU, which no small treatment plant can handle.**

> **A gallery laid in the river's own gravel bed draws water that has passed through several metres of that gravel, and it emerges with a turbidity a small fraction of the river's — the bed acting as a natural slow sand filter.**

> **It also draws a steadier quality and temperature, and it is invisible and unaffected by floating debris, boulders and floods that would destroy a surface intake.**

> **The limitations are that it needs a permeable bed of adequate thickness, its yield is limited by the bed's permeability and can decline as the bed silts up, and it cannot be inspected or cleaned easily once buried.**

> **But where the geology suits it, an infiltration gallery can replace both a surface intake and much of a treatment plant — which on a small hill scheme with no operator and no chemical supply is an enormous practical advantage, and it is the reason such galleries are so widely used for the country's smaller river-fed supplies.**

examTip.trick: **Outer (concave) bank of a bend — deep and scouring — and UPSTREAM of all discharges.** The inner bank is where deposition occurs and an intake there silts up.
examTip.trap: **The scour that keeps the intake in water is also attacking its bank** — so an outer-bank intake needs revetment and a founding level below the anticipated scour.
examTip.mnemonic: **An INFILTRATION GALLERY in the river's gravel bed replaces both intake and much of the treatment** — the bed is a natural slow sand filter. Ideal for a small hill scheme with no operator.

questions.stem: HDPE (high density polyethylene) pipe is particularly favoured for water supply in Nepal's hill areas because it:
options: Withstands higher internal pressures than steel
Is light, flexible and available in long coils
Requires no bedding or cover
Is immune to damage by rodents and by ultraviolet light
questions.solution:
**It is LIGHT, FLEXIBLE and available in long coils** — so it can be carried to sites without road access, laid round obstacles with few joints, and can tolerate ground movement without fracturing.

**Why those properties matter so much in the hills:**

| Property | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **LIGHT — about an eighth the weight of cast iron for the same duty** ← | **It can be carried by porters or mules where no vehicle can go, which for much of Nepal is decisive** ← |
| **Supplied in long COILS rather than short lengths** ← | **Far FEWER joints, and a joint is the commonest point of leakage and failure** ← |
| **FLEXIBLE** ← | **It follows the ground's contour and bends round obstacles without fittings, and it accommodates settlement and minor landslip movement** ← |
| **CORROSION-proof** ← | **Immune to the acidic soils and aggressive waters common in hill areas** ← |
| **Joined by heat FUSION, giving a joint as strong as the pipe** ← | **With no gasket to perish and no mechanical joint to pull out** ← |
| **Smooth bore, so low friction, and it does not tuberculate with age** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE PROPERTY THAT MATTERS MOST IN GEOLOGICALLY ACTIVE TERRAIN AND IT IS WORTH DWELLING ON: a rigid pipe in ground that moves will break.**

> **Nepal's hillsides creep, slip and settle continuously, and a cast iron or asbestos cement main crossing such ground fractures at the joints or in the barrel.**

> **A polyethylene pipe deflects instead, and can accommodate a considerable displacement before it is in distress — so it survives the slow ground movement that would sever a rigid main, and it survives earthquake ground strain far better.**

> **This makes HDPE not merely a convenient material for the hills but the technically appropriate one, and the ease of transport is a bonus rather than the whole justification.**

**ITS LIMITATIONS, WHICH OPTION (d) TOUCHES ON AND WHICH MUST BE RESPECTED:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **ULTRAVIOLET degradation** ← | **Exposed HDPE becomes brittle over years unless it is carbon-black stabilised — and even then, exposed pipe should be covered or painted** ← |
| **RODENT and termite attack** ← | **Rats gnaw polyethylene, and buried pipe in some soils is attacked — a real cause of leakage** ← |
| **Low resistance to high TEMPERATURE** ← | **Its pressure rating falls sharply as the temperature rises, so it must be de-rated where the pipe is exposed to the sun** ← |
| **Permeation by hydrocarbons** ← | **Petrol and solvents in contaminated ground can diffuse through the wall and taint the water** ← |
| **A high coefficient of thermal EXPANSION** ← | **So exposed pipe must be laid with slack or with expansion provision** ← |
| **Lower stiffness, so it needs careful BEDDING** ← | **It deflects under load, and a sharp stone under an unbedded pipe is a point of failure** ← (option c is wrong) |

> **THE UV POINT IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE COMMONEST FIELD FAILURE OF HDPE IN NEPAL AND IT IS ENTIRELY AVOIDABLE: pipe is delivered in coils, laid partly exposed across a gully or along a rock face, and left uncovered because burying it there is difficult.**

> **The exposed reach then degrades over five or ten years while the buried reaches remain sound, and the pipeline fails at exactly the points hardest to reach for repair.**

> **Covering, casing or painting the exposed lengths at construction is cheap and it is regularly omitted — so a specification for a hill pipeline should address exposed reaches explicitly rather than assuming the pipe will be buried throughout.**

**THE OTHER MATERIALS, FOR COMPARISON:**

| Material | Suited to |
|---|---|
| **DUCTILE IRON** ← | **Large mains under roads; strong, tough, and its joints accommodate some movement — the standard for urban trunk mains** ← |
| **CAST IRON** ← | **Obsolete for new work — brittle, and it tuberculates internally, losing capacity over decades** ← |
| **STEEL** ← | **Large diameters, high pressures, long spans and bridge crossings; needs careful corrosion protection** ← |
| **uPVC** ← | **Cheap, light, corrosion-proof; but BRITTLE, UV-sensitive, and it fails suddenly rather than deforming** ← |
| **GI (galvanised iron)** ← | **Small-diameter service connections and exposed work; corrodes at the threads** ← |
| **PSC and RCC** | **Very large gravity mains and low-pressure work** ← |

> **The uPVC entry is worth comparing directly with HDPE, since the two are often treated as interchangeable and are not: uPVC is stiffer and cheaper but BRITTLE, so it shatters under impact or ground movement, while HDPE deforms.**

> **In stable ground under a road, uPVC serves well. In moving hillside ground it is a poor choice for exactly the reason HDPE is a good one.**

examTip.trick: **Light, coiled (few joints), flexible, corrosion-proof, fusion-jointed** — portable to roadless sites and tolerant of ground movement.
examTip.trap: **It is NOT immune to UV or rodents, and it DOES need bedding** — exposed reaches degrade in years while buried ones stay sound, failing where repair is hardest.
examTip.mnemonic: **In moving hillside ground, HDPE DEFORMS where uPVC SHATTERS** — the two are not interchangeable, though they are often treated as such.

questions.stem: A SLUICE (gate) valve differs in function from a REFLUX (check, non-return) valve in that the sluice valve:
options: Allows flow in one direction only
Automatically releases air from the pipeline
Is operated to open, close or throttle the line at will
Reduces the downstream pressure to a set value
questions.solution:
**It is operated to OPEN, CLOSE or THROTTLE the line at will** — whereas a reflux valve operates automatically and permits flow in one direction only.

**The valves of a water distribution system:**

| Valve | Function |
|---|---|
| **SLUICE (gate) valve** ← | **Isolation — opened or closed by hand or actuator; the workhorse of a network, at every junction and at intervals along mains** ← |
| **REFLUX (check, non-return) valve** ← | **Permits flow in ONE direction only, automatically — placed on a pump's delivery to prevent backflow when the pump stops** ← (option a) |
| **AIR valve** ← | **Releases accumulated air at high points, and admits air when the line is drained** ← (option b) |
| **SCOUR (washout, blow-off) valve** ← | **At low points, to drain and flush the main of sediment** ← |
| **PRESSURE REDUCING valve** ← | **Maintains a set DOWNSTREAM pressure regardless of the upstream pressure** ← (option d) |
| **PRESSURE RELIEF valve** ← | **Opens to discharge when the pressure exceeds a set value — surge protection** ← |
| **BUTTERFLY valve** ← | **A disc rotating in the pipe; compact and quick to operate, used on large diameters** ← |
| **ALTITUDE valve** | **Closes when a service reservoir is full, preventing overflow** ← |

> **THE AIR VALVE AND THE SCOUR VALVE IN THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS ARE THE TWO MOST OFTEN OMITTED, AND THEIR PLACEMENT FOLLOWS A SIMPLE AND MEMORABLE RULE:**

> **AIR rises, so AIR VALVES go at the HIGH points — the summits of the pipeline's profile.**

> **SEDIMENT sinks, so SCOUR VALVES go at the LOW points — the valleys.**

> **A pipeline profile should therefore be drawn and the two sets of valves placed by inspection of it, which is a five-minute exercise that is regularly skipped on small schemes.**

**WHY THE AIR VALVE MATTERS MORE THAN IT SEEMS, WHICH IS WORTH EXPLAINING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Air collects at every summit in a pipeline** ← | **Released from solution as the pressure falls, and entrained at the intake or reservoir** ← |
| **An air pocket REDUCES the effective cross-section, restricting the flow** ← | **Acting as a partial blockage** ← |
| **A large pocket can stop the flow entirely — an AIR LOCK** ← | **Which is a common and baffling fault on a gravity main, since nothing is visibly wrong** ← |
| **Air also causes the pipe to SURGE and hammer as pockets move** ← | ← |
| **And on DRAINING, a main without air valves COLLAPSES** ← | **Because atmospheric pressure crushes the evacuated pipe — a real failure with thin-walled and plastic pipes** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW DESCRIBES THE CLASSIC UNEXPLAINED FAILURE OF A HILL GRAVITY MAIN AND IT IS WORTH RECOGNISING BY ITS SYMPTOMS: the scheme was commissioned and worked, and now delivers a fraction of its design flow with no visible leak or blockage.**

> **The usual cause is air accumulated at a summit — often after a supply interruption that let the main partly drain — and the remedy is simply to release it.**

> **A main with automatic air valves at every summit releases it continuously and the problem never arises; a main without them requires someone to know that the summits are the places to look.**

> **The fifth row's collapse mechanism is the same phenomenon in reverse and it deserves respect: a large-diameter thin-walled pipe has almost no resistance to external pressure, and draining it without admitting air can crush it flat.**

> **This is why air valves are DOUBLE-ACTING — releasing air on filling and ADMITTING it on emptying — and why a washout valve should never be opened on a main whose air valves are not working.**

> **A final practical note on the sluice valve itself: it should be used FULLY OPEN or FULLY CLOSED, and not for permanent throttling.**

> **A partly open gate is subject to vibration and cavitation damage to its seat and body, and its throttled position is neither recorded nor repeatable — so where a permanent flow or pressure reduction is wanted, a pressure reducing valve or an orifice plate is the correct device rather than a half-shut sluice valve.**

examTip.trick: **A sluice valve is OPERATED at will; a reflux valve acts AUTOMATICALLY in one direction.** Option (b) is an air valve, (d) a pressure reducing valve.
examTip.trap: **AIR rises so air valves go at HIGH points; SEDIMENT sinks so scour valves go at LOW points.** Draw the profile and place them by inspection.
examTip.mnemonic: **An unexplained loss of flow in a gravity main is usually an AIR LOCK at a summit.** And air valves must be DOUBLE-ACTING, or draining the main can crush it flat.

questions.stem: A BREAK PRESSURE TANK is provided on a gravity water supply pipeline in order to:
options: Store water for the peak hourly demand
Allow sediment to settle out of the flow
Provide a point at which the pipeline can be disinfected
Limit the static head in the pipeline below it by exposing the water to atmosphere
questions.solution:
**To LIMIT the static head in the pipeline below it by exposing the water to ATMOSPHERE** — so that a pipe of lower pressure rating can be used and the fittings and taps downstream are not over-pressurised.

**The problem it solves:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **A gravity scheme in the hills may have a source several hundred metres above the village** ← | **Which is what makes the scheme possible** ← |
| **The STATIC head in a continuous pipeline equals that full elevation difference** ← | **300 m of elevation gives 30 bar of static pressure at the bottom when no water is flowing** ← |
| **No ordinary HDPE or GI pipe, and certainly no tap or fitting, will withstand that** ← | ← |
| **A BREAK PRESSURE TANK interrupts the hydraulic continuity** ← | **The water enters, its surface is at atmospheric pressure, and it leaves through a separate outlet** ← |
| **So the static head below the tank is only the drop from THAT tank, not from the source** ← | ← |
| **Tanks are placed at intervals to keep each reach's static head within the pipe's rating** ← | **Commonly every 60 to 100 m of fall** ← |

> **THE 'STATIC' QUALIFICATION IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE POINT MOST WORTH UNDERSTANDING AND IT IS WHERE THE DANGER LIES: the pressure in a pipeline is greatest when NOTHING IS FLOWING.**

> **When water is flowing, friction consumes much of the head, and the pressure at any point is the elevation difference MINUS the friction loss to that point — which may be modest.**

> **When every tap is closed, the friction loss is zero and the pressure everywhere is the full static head.**

> **So a pipeline can operate perfectly for months and burst at night when the last tap is closed — and a designer who checks the pressure under flowing conditions only has checked the wrong case.**

> **The static head is always the governing case for pipe pressure rating, and it must be computed from the hydraulic grade line with NO flow.**

**THE DESIGN OF THE TANK ITSELF:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **Small — its purpose is to break the pressure, not to store** ← | **A few hundred litres to a cubic metre is usual, giving a short detention** ← (which is why option a is wrong) |
| **The INLET discharges above the water surface, or is otherwise vented** ← | **So that the hydraulic continuity is genuinely broken; a submerged inlet with no vent does not break the pressure** ← |
| **The OUTLET is set above the floor, with a washout below it** ← | **So sediment can be removed without entering the supply** ← |
| **An OVERFLOW sized for the full inflow** ← | **Since the tank will overflow whenever the downstream demand is less than the inflow, which is most of the time** ← |
| **A watertight, lockable COVER and a screened vent** ← | **The tank is an opening into the supply and a point of contamination** ← |
| **A float valve is sometimes fitted to stop the inflow when full** ← | **Which avoids wasting the source's water, but introduces a mechanism that can fail** ← |

> **THE OVERFLOW IN THE FOURTH ROW IS AN ASPECT OF BREAK PRESSURE TANKS THAT IS OFTEN MISUNDERSTOOD AND HAS A REAL CONSEQUENCE: unless a float valve stops the inflow, the tank overflows continuously whenever demand is below the source's yield.**

> **That is not a fault — the water was flowing down the hill anyway — but it means the overflow must be piped away properly to a safe discharge point.**

> **An overflow allowed to discharge onto the ground beside the tank saturates the soil, and on a steep hillside a continuously saturated patch is precisely how a landslide begins.**

> **So the overflow's discharge arrangement is a slope stability matter as much as a hydraulic one, and a break pressure tank that has quietly been irrigating a hillside for ten years is a recognised cause of failure of both the slope and the pipeline crossing it.**

> **THE SECOND ROW'S WARNING IS WORTH REPEATING AS A CHECK: a tank whose inlet pipe is submerged and whose cover is sealed with no vent has NOT broken the pressure — the water column is continuous and the full static head is transmitted straight through it.**

> **The break depends on a free water surface open to the atmosphere, and that is a detail to verify rather than assume.**

examTip.trick: **It exposes the water to atmosphere, so the static head below it starts again from that tank** — letting a lower-rated pipe be used. Not for storage.
examTip.trap: **Pipeline pressure is GREATEST when nothing flows** — friction consumes head only while flowing. A main can serve for months and burst at night when the last tap closes.
examTip.mnemonic: **Pipe the overflow properly** — a continuously saturated patch on a steep hillside is how a landslide starts. And a submerged unvented inlet does NOT break the pressure.

questions.stem: The BALANCING (storage) capacity of a service reservoir is most rigorously determined by:
options: Taking it as one-third of the maximum daily demand, as a rule of thumb
Plotting the cumulative inflow and the cumulative demand against time over the design day (a mass diagram) and measuring the greatest vertical separation between them
Multiplying the peak hourly demand by four hours
Taking it as the volume required for fire fighting alone
questions.solution:
**By plotting the CUMULATIVE inflow and the CUMULATIVE demand against time over the design day (a MASS DIAGRAM) and measuring the greatest vertical separation between them.**

**The method:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Plot cumulative INFLOW against time** ← | **A straight line if pumping is continuous; a series of straight segments if pumping is intermittent** ← |
| **Plot cumulative DEMAND against time on the same axes** ← | **A curve, steep during the morning and evening peaks and flat overnight** ← |
| **Where DEMAND exceeds inflow, the reservoir DEPLETES** ← | **The demand curve rising above the inflow line** ← |
| **Where inflow exceeds demand, it FILLS** ← | ← |
| **The required capacity is the sum of the maximum DEFICIT and the maximum SURPLUS** ← | **That is, the greatest vertical distance ABOVE the inflow line plus the greatest distance BELOW it** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE STEP MOST OFTEN GOT WRONG AND IT IS WORTH BEING PRECISE: the capacity is not the maximum deficit alone.**

> **The reservoir must hold the surplus accumulated during the low-demand hours AND be able to supply the deficit during the peak hours.**

> **Those two occur at different times of the day, so the tank must accommodate the total swing from its fullest to its emptiest — which is the sum of the two maxima measured from the inflow line.**

> **Taking only the deficit gives a tank that empties before the peak has passed.**

**WHAT ELSE THE RESERVOIR MUST HOLD, WHICH IS ADDED TO THE BALANCING VOLUME:**

| Component | Note |
|---|---|
| **BALANCING storage** ← | **From the mass diagram, as above — typically a third to a half of the day's demand for intermittent pumping, much less for continuous** ← |
| **BREAKDOWN (emergency) reserve** ← | **To maintain supply while a pump, a main or the plant is out of service — commonly 4 to 8 hours of average demand** ← |
| **FIRE reserve** ← | **A volume sufficient for a fire of the design duration — significant in a small town, trivial in a large one** ← (option d is only this part) |
| **DEAD storage below the outlet** ← | **Which is not available and must be added to the total depth** ← |

> **THE TOTAL COMMONLY WORKS OUT AT A THIRD TO A HALF OF THE MAXIMUM DAILY DEMAND, WHICH IS WHERE OPTION (a)'S RULE OF THUMB COMES FROM — and the rule is a reasonable starting figure while being no substitute for the calculation.**

> **Its weakness is that the balancing volume depends entirely on the PUMPING PATTERN, which the rule of thumb takes no account of.**

| Pumping pattern | Balancing storage required |
|---|---|
| **CONTINUOUS pumping over 24 hours** ← | **SMALL — the inflow line is a single straight line closely following the average demand** ← |
| **Pumping for 8 hours a day** ← | **LARGE — the whole day's supply arrives in a third of the day and must be stored** ← |
| **Pumping timed to COINCIDE with the demand peaks** ← | **Smaller still than continuous, in principle — but it requires the pumps and mains to be sized for the peak, which costs more than the tank saved** ← |

> **THE COMPARISON BETWEEN THE FIRST TWO ROWS IS THE PRACTICAL DESIGN TRADE AND IT IS WORTH SEEING AS SUCH: a longer pumping day means a smaller reservoir, and a shorter pumping day means a bigger one.**

> **Continuous pumping minimises the tank but requires the pumps to run all day, which costs energy at whatever tariff applies around the clock and gives no window for maintenance without a standby.**

> **Pumping for a shorter period allows the use of OFF-PEAK electricity tariffs, which in many countries are substantially cheaper, and concentrates the operator's attention — at the cost of a larger tank and larger pumps.**

> **So the pumping hours and the reservoir capacity are decided together, on the balance between the energy tariff and the cost of storage, rather than either being fixed first.**

> **In a Nepali context with unreliable power, a further consideration usually dominates: the tank must be large enough to ride through a power outage of the length that actually occurs — which may set the capacity well above anything the mass diagram indicates.**

examTip.trick: **Mass diagram: cumulative inflow against cumulative demand.** The capacity is the maximum DEFICIT plus the maximum SURPLUS — the full swing, not the deficit alone.
examTip.trap: **Balancing storage depends entirely on the PUMPING PATTERN** — small for continuous pumping, large for an 8-hour day. The one-third rule of thumb ignores this.
examTip.mnemonic: **Add breakdown reserve (4-8 hours) and fire reserve to the balancing volume.** And in Nepal, the tank must ride through the power outages that actually occur.

questions.stem: Compared with a DEAD-END (tree) distribution layout, a GRID or RING layout has the advantage that:
options: It requires a shorter total length of pipe
It is simpler to design and to analyse
Water can reach any point by more than ONE route
It needs no valves
questions.solution:
**Water can reach any point by MORE THAN ONE ROUTE** — so a burst or a repair isolates a smaller area, the water does not stagnate at ends, and the pressures are more uniform.

**The layouts compared:**

| Layout | Description |
|---|---|
| **DEAD-END (tree, branching)** ← | **A main with branches and sub-branches, each terminating** ← |
| **GRIDIRON** ← | **A rectangular grid of interconnected mains — every junction fed from several directions** ← |
| **RING (circular)** ← | **A closed loop main around the area, with branches inward** ← |
| **RADIAL** ← | **The area divided into zones, each fed radially outward from its own central service reservoir** ← |

| Property | DEAD-END | GRID / RING |
|---|---|---|
| **Pipe length and cost** | **LESS — the cheapest layout** ← (so option a favours dead-end) | **More** ← |
| **Design and analysis** | **SIMPLE — the flow in every pipe is determined by the demand beyond it** ← (option b favours dead-end) | **INDETERMINATE — requires iterative network analysis** ← |
| **Effect of a burst or a repair** | **Everything BEYOND the break loses supply** ← | **Only the immediate area, the flow re-routing around the loop** ← |
| **STAGNATION** | **At every dead end, where water sits and the chlorine residual decays** ← | **Little — the water circulates** ← |
| **Pressure uniformity** | **Poor; the far ends are weak** ← | **Good** ← |
| **Fire fighting** | **A single main limits the flow available at any point** ← | **Several mains can feed a hydrant** ← |

> **THE STAGNATION ROW IS THE WATER QUALITY ARGUMENT AND IT IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN UNDERWEIGHTED IN A DESIGN THAT IS THINKING ABOUT HYDRAULICS: a dead end is where the water is OLDEST.**

> **Water reaching a dead end has travelled the whole length of the network and then stopped, and it moves only when a consumer at that end draws it.**

> **In that time the chlorine residual decays, sediment settles, biofilm develops on the pipe wall, and any taste or odour problem is at its worst.**

> **So consumer complaints about water quality cluster at the ends of a dead-end network, and the same locations are where a contamination event would go undetected longest.**

> **Which is why a dead-end network requires a programme of regular FLUSHING at its extremities — a real operating cost, and one that a looped network largely avoids.**

**THE PRACTICAL RESOLUTION, SINCE BOTH LAYOUTS HAVE MERIT:**

| Situation | Layout |
|---|---|
| **A town with a regular street pattern and adequate resources** ← | **GRID for the main streets, with short dead-end branches into lanes** ← |
| **A hill town with a single access road along a ridge** ← | **Necessarily dead-end — the topography permits nothing else** ← |
| **A rural scheme with scattered settlements** ← | **Dead-end, the cost of looping being prohibitive for the length involved** ← |
| **A dense city core** | **Grid, with looping and district metering** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE COMMON NEPALI CASE AND IT SHOULD BE ACKNOWLEDGED HONESTLY: a settlement strung along a ridge road has one route for its main and no possibility of a loop.**

> **The layout is dictated by the topography rather than chosen, and the design must then MANAGE the dead-end's disadvantages rather than avoid them — washouts at the ends for flushing, valves at intervals to limit the area isolated by a repair, and a residual chlorine monitoring point at the extremity where the problem will appear first.**

> **The general principle worth carrying is that where a layout's weaknesses cannot be designed out, they should be designed FOR: the operating provisions that mitigate them are cheap at construction and impossible to retrofit.**

> **THE ANALYSIS DIFFICULTY IN THE SECOND PROPERTY ROW IS WORTH A CLOSING NOTE, since it is the reason grids were historically avoided: the flow distribution in a looped network is statically indeterminate, and before computers it had to be solved by hand iteration — the HARDY CROSS method, which converges but is laborious.**

> **That obstacle has entirely disappeared, and a network of any size is now analysed in seconds by software.**

> **So one of the historical arguments for dead-end layouts no longer applies, and the choice today rests on pipe cost and topography alone.**

examTip.trick: **Multiple routes to every point** — smaller isolation on a repair, no stagnation, uniform pressures, better fire flows. Dead-end is cheaper and simpler.
examTip.trap: **A dead end is where the water is OLDEST** — decayed residual, settled sediment, biofilm. Consumer complaints cluster there, and it needs a flushing programme.
examTip.mnemonic: **Where a weakness cannot be designed out, design FOR it** — washouts, sectioning valves and a residual monitoring point at the extremity. Cheap now, impossible to retrofit.

questions.stem: In the HARDY CROSS method of analysing a looped water distribution network, the flows are adjusted iteratively until, in every loop:
options: The velocity is the same in every pipe
The algebraic sum of the head losses around the loop is zero
The diameter of every pipe is the same
The total length of pipe in each loop is equal
questions.solution:
**The algebraic sum of the HEAD LOSSES around the loop is ZERO, while continuity of flow is satisfied at every junction.**

**The two conditions the solution must satisfy:**

| Condition | Statement |
|---|---|
| **CONTINUITY at each junction** ← | **The flow in equals the flow out — a statement of mass conservation, analogous to Kirchhoff's current law** ← |
| **ENERGY around each loop** ← | **The algebraic sum of the head losses, taken consistently round the loop, is ZERO — because a point cannot have two different pressures, analogous to Kirchhoff's voltage law** ← |

> **THE ANALOGY WITH AN ELECTRICAL NETWORK IN BOTH ROWS IS EXACT AND WORTH HOLDING, because it makes the method's logic obvious: pipes are resistors, flows are currents, and heads are voltages.**

> **The only difference is that head loss varies with the SQUARE of the flow rather than linearly with it, which is what makes the problem non-linear and forces an iterative solution.**

> **A linear network can be solved directly; a water network cannot, and Hardy Cross is essentially a Newton-type iteration on the loop equations.**

**THE PROCEDURE:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. ASSUME a flow in every pipe, satisfying continuity at every junction** ← | **Any set that satisfies continuity will do; a sensible guess converges faster** ← |
| **2. Compute the head loss in each pipe, h_f = r Qⁿ** ← | **n = 2 for Darcy-Weisbach, 1.85 for Hazen-Williams** ← |
| **3. Sum the head losses round each loop, with SIGN** ← | **Clockwise flows positive, anticlockwise negative, consistently** ← |
| **4. If the sum is not zero, compute a CORRECTION for the loop** ← | **ΔQ = −Σh_f / (n Σ(h_f/Q))** ← |
| **5. Apply the correction to every pipe in the loop** ← | **Which preserves continuity automatically, since the same amount is added round a closed loop** ← |
| **6. For a pipe COMMON to two loops, apply BOTH corrections** ← | **With the appropriate signs — the step most often got wrong** ← |
| **7. Repeat until the corrections are negligible** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW CONTAINS THE ELEGANCE OF THE METHOD AND IT IS WORTH APPRECIATING: adding the same correction to every pipe round a closed loop cannot violate continuity at any junction, because whatever extra flow arrives at a junction from one side leaves it on the other.**

> **So the iteration can adjust the loop equations freely without ever disturbing the junction equations, which is precisely why the method converges reliably and why the initial guess need only satisfy continuity.**

> **That is a genuinely clever piece of construction, and it is what made hand analysis of looped networks practicable at all.**

> **THE SHARED-PIPE RULE IN THE SIXTH ROW IS THE COMMONEST ERROR IN EXAMINATION AND IN PRACTICE: a pipe belonging to two loops receives its own loop's correction AND, with reversed sign, the adjacent loop's.**

> **Omitting the second correction leaves the two loops inconsistent and the iteration converging slowly or not at all.**

> **The sign convention is where the mistake is made, and the reliable way to avoid it is to fix a positive direction for each loop at the outset, mark it on the sketch, and never depart from it.**

**AND A NOTE ON WHAT HAS SUPERSEDED IT, WHICH IS WORTH KNOWING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Hardy Cross is a LOOP-based method, solving for flow corrections** ← | ← |
| **The NODAL method solves instead for the HEADS at the junctions** ← | **Which is often more convenient, since heads are what the designer wants to know** ← |
| **Modern software (EPANET and its relatives) uses a GRADIENT or global method** ← | **Solving all the equations simultaneously by matrix methods, which converges far faster and handles pumps, valves and tanks** ← |
| **Hardy Cross remains the method taught, because it is doable by hand and it makes the two governing conditions explicit** ← | ← |

> **The last row is the honest justification for still learning it: nobody analyses a real network by hand any longer, but a designer who has done a Hardy Cross iteration understands what the software is solving and can recognise when its answer is implausible.**

> **That is a real benefit — the commonest failure in computer-aided design is accepting an output that violates something obvious — and it is worth the labour of one hand calculation to acquire.**

examTip.trick: **Σh_f = 0 round each loop, with continuity at every junction** — Kirchhoff's two laws, with head loss going as Q² instead of linearly.
examTip.trap: **A pipe shared by two loops takes BOTH corrections**, with the appropriate signs. Fix a positive direction for each loop on the sketch and never depart from it.
examTip.mnemonic: **ΔQ = −Σh_f/(n·Σ(h_f/Q))**, n = 2 for Darcy and 1.85 for Hazen-Williams. Adding the same ΔQ round a closed loop cannot break continuity — that is the method's trick.

questions.stem: A 200 mm diameter pipe 1,000 m long carries 40 litres per second. Taking the Darcy friction factor as 0.02, the head loss due to friction is about:
questions.solution:
**About 8.3 m.**

**The calculation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Cross-sectional area** | **A = πD²/4 = π × 0.2²/4 = 0.031416 m²** ← |
| **Velocity** | **V = Q/A = 0.040/0.031416 = 1.273 m/s** ← |
| **Darcy-Weisbach** | **h_f = f L V² / (2 g D)** ← |
| **Substituting** | **= 0.02 × 1,000 × 1.273² / (2 × 9.81 × 0.2)** ← |
| **Numerator** | **= 0.02 × 1,000 × 1.6205 = 32.41** ← |
| **Denominator** | **= 3.924** ← |
| **h_f** | **= 32.41 / 3.924 = 8.26 m, about 8.3 m** ← |

> **So the friction head loss is approximately 8.3 metres, that is 8.3 m per kilometre — a slope of about 1 in 120.**

**THE STRUCTURE OF THE FORMULA IS WORTH READING, BECAUSE ITS SENSITIVITIES DECIDE EVERY PIPE-SIZING DECISION:**

| Observation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **h_f varies with V²** ← | **DOUBLING the flow through a given pipe QUADRUPLES the head loss** ← |
| **And V = Q/A, with A proportional to D²** ← | **So for a given Q, h_f varies as 1/D⁴ from the velocity term** ← |
| **Combined with the D in the denominator, h_f varies as 1/D⁵** ← | **Which is an extraordinarily strong dependence** ← |
| **So increasing the diameter by 15 per cent HALVES the head loss** ← | **1.15⁵ = 2.0** ← |

> **THE FIFTH-POWER RELATIONSHIP IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE SINGLE MOST USEFUL FACT IN PIPELINE DESIGN AND IT IS WORTH COMMITTING TO MEMORY: head loss goes as the inverse FIFTH power of the diameter.**

> **This means a modest increase in pipe size produces a dramatic reduction in friction, which is why the ECONOMIC diameter calculation exists at all: the pipe cost rises roughly with D or D², while the pumping cost falls with D⁵.**

> **It also means that a small reduction in diameter — a pipe supplied one size smaller than specified, or a main narrowed by tuberculation — has a disproportionate effect on capacity.**

> **An old cast iron main whose bore has been reduced 10 per cent by tuberculation has lost about 40 per cent of its capacity at the same head loss, which is why old mains deliver so much less than their nominal size suggests and why cleaning and relining them is so worthwhile.**

**THE ALTERNATIVE FORMULAE, AND WHEN EACH IS USED:**

| Formula | Note |
|---|---|
| **DARCY-WEISBACH: h_f = fLV²/(2gD)** ← | **The fundamental and dimensionally correct one; f depends on the Reynolds number and the relative roughness, from the Moody diagram or the Colebrook-White equation** ← |
| **HAZEN-WILLIAMS: V = 0.849 C R^0.63 S^0.54** ← | **Empirical, for water at ordinary temperatures; C is the roughness coefficient (100 for old cast iron, 140 for new plastic)** ← |
| **MANNING: V = (1/n) R^(2/3) S^(1/2)** ← | **Chiefly for open channels and part-full sewers** ← |

> **THE PRACTICAL DISTINCTION IS THAT HAZEN-WILLIAMS IS FAR MORE CONVENIENT AND DARCY-WEISBACH IS MORE CORRECT, and the choice is worth making consciously.**

> **Hazen-Williams needs only a single coefficient C and requires no iteration, which is why it dominates water distribution practice and why network software offers it as a default.**

> **But it is calibrated for water at about 15 °C in the turbulent range, and it becomes inaccurate at very high or very low velocities, in small pipes, and for fluids other than water.**

> **Darcy-Weisbach applies to any fluid at any velocity, at the cost of needing f from the Moody diagram or an iterative solution of Colebrook-White — which a computer does instantly and a candidate in an examination does not.**

> **Hence the convention: Hazen-Williams for routine water distribution design, Darcy-Weisbach whenever the conditions are unusual or the accuracy matters.**

examTip.trap: **h_f varies as 1/D⁵** — so 15 % more diameter halves the loss, and a bore reduced 10 % by tuberculation loses 40 % of its capacity.
examTip.mnemonic: **Hazen-Williams is convenient (one coefficient C, no iteration); Darcy-Weisbach is correct (any fluid, any velocity).** Use the first for routine water work.

questions.stem: THRUST BLOCKS are provided at bends, tees and dead ends of a pressurised water main in order to:
options: Resist the unbalanced hydraulic thrust that arises wherever the flow changes direction or the pipe terminates
Support the weight of the pipe and its contents
Prevent the pipe from floating when the ground is waterlogged
Provide access for maintenance of the fitting
questions.solution:
**To RESIST the UNBALANCED HYDRAULIC THRUST that arises wherever the flow changes direction or the pipe terminates** — transferring it into the surrounding soil, so that the joints are not pulled apart.

**Where the thrust comes from:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **In a STRAIGHT pipe the pressure acts equally in opposite directions and CANCELS** ← | **So there is no net force along the pipe** ← |
| **At a BEND, the pressure forces on the two legs do NOT cancel** ← | **Their resultant acts outward along the bisector of the bend** ← |
| **At a TEE, a REDUCER, a VALVE or a DEAD END, the same imbalance arises** ← | ← |
| **The magnitude is large: T = 2 p A sin(θ/2) for a bend of angle θ** ← | ← |
| **A 300 mm main at 6 bar with a 90-degree bend gives a thrust of about 60 kN** ← | **Six tonnes, acting continuously** ← |
| **Nothing in a flexible (socket and spigot) joint resists it** ← | **The joint transmits pressure but not tension, so the pipe simply pulls out of the socket** ← |

> **THE SIXTH ROW IS THE POINT ON WHICH THE WHOLE MATTER TURNS AND IT DISTINGUISHES ONE KIND OF PIPELINE FROM ANOTHER: a flexible-jointed pipeline has no longitudinal strength across its joints.**

> **A welded steel or a fusion-welded HDPE pipeline is continuous, and it can carry the thrust as tension in the pipe wall along its own length — so it needs no thrust block, only anchorage where it changes direction abruptly.**

> **A ductile iron or uPVC main with push-fit joints cannot: each joint is a sliding fit sealed by a rubber ring, and any longitudinal pull separates it.**

> **So the presence or absence of thrust blocks depends on the JOINTING system, and this is one of the most consequential differences between pipe types.**

> **A designer who specifies push-fit pipe and omits thrust blocks has designed a pipeline that will disassemble itself at every bend the first time it is pressurised.**

**THE MAGNITUDE OF THE THRUST, BY FITTING:**

| Fitting | Thrust |
|---|---|
| **90-degree bend** ← | **T = 2 p A sin 45° = 1.414 p A** ← |
| **45-degree bend** ← | **0.765 p A — much less, which is why two 45s are preferable to one 90 where the space allows** ← |
| **DEAD END or a closed valve** ← | **T = p A — the FULL pressure on the full area, and the largest single case for a given pipe** ← |
| **TEE (on the branch)** ← | **p A of the branch** ← |
| **REDUCER** | **p times the difference in areas** ← |

> **THE DEAD END IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE CASE MOST OFTEN OVERLOOKED AND IT IS THE MOST SEVERE: a capped end or a closed valve takes the full static pressure on the full bore.**

> **And it arises in a situation where it is easily forgotten — during CONSTRUCTION, when a main is laid, capped and pressure-tested before its continuation is built.**

> **Pressure-testing a main against a temporary cap without an adequate temporary thrust block is a genuine hazard: a 300 mm cap at 10 bar carries about 7 tonnes, and when it lets go the cap becomes a projectile.**

> **Injuries and deaths have resulted, which is why the temporary end restraint for a pressure test is a specific safety item rather than a construction detail.**

**THE DESIGN OF THE BLOCK ITSELF, IN BRIEF:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Bearing area sized on the SOIL's safe bearing capacity in the HORIZONTAL direction** ← | **Which is much lower than its vertical capacity, and must be taken against UNDISTURBED ground** ← |
| **Cast against undisturbed soil, NOT against backfill** ← | **Backfill will yield, and the block moves with it** ← |
| **Positioned so the resultant passes through the bearing face** ← | **Or the block rotates** ← |
| **Where soil bearing is inadequate, use TIED joints or anchor blocks instead** ← | **Restraining the pipe longitudinally rather than bearing against the soil** ← |
| **Concrete must not encase the joint itself** ← | **The joint must remain accessible and free to flex, so the block bears on the fitting's body** ← |

> **The second row is the requirement most often violated on site and it defeats the block entirely: a block cast into loose backfill in an oversized trench has nothing to push against.**

> **The trench at a bend must therefore be cut to the block's exact profile in undisturbed ground, which takes care and is inconvenient — and a block cast into a convenient rectangular hole and backfilled around is a block that will migrate.**

examTip.trick: **Pressure forces cancel in a straight pipe and do not at a bend, tee or dead end** — and a push-fit joint carries no tension, so the pipe pulls out.
examTip.trap: **A DEAD END takes the full pA — the largest case** — and it arises during pressure TESTING against a temporary cap. A 300 mm cap at 10 bar is 7 tonnes and becomes a projectile.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cast against UNDISTURBED soil, never backfill**, and size the area on the soil's HORIZONTAL bearing capacity. Welded steel and fused HDPE need no blocks — they carry it as tension.

questions.stem: WATER HAMMER in a pumping main is most severe when:
options: A valve is closed rapidly, or a pump stops suddenly
The pump is started gradually
The pipeline is very short and the velocity low
An air valve is left open at a summit
questions.solution:
**When a valve is closed RAPIDLY, or a pump STOPS suddenly** — the moving column of water being decelerated abruptly, so its momentum is converted into a pressure wave that travels along the pipe at the speed of sound in water.

**The mechanism:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Water flowing in a pipe has MOMENTUM** ← | **ρ A L V for a column of length L** ← |
| **Stopping it requires a FORCE, and force × time = momentum change** ← | ← |
| **So the SHORTER the stopping time, the GREATER the force** ← | **And hence the greater the pressure rise** ← |
| **The pressure rise appears as a WAVE travelling back along the pipe** ← | **At the wave speed, typically 1,000 to 1,400 m/s in a rigid pipe and much less in a flexible one** ← |
| **It reflects at the reservoir and returns, oscillating and decaying** ← | ← |
| **For INSTANTANEOUS closure the rise is ΔH = aV/g (the Joukowsky value)** ← | **Independent of the pipe's length — a is the wave speed and V the initial velocity** ← |

> **THE JOUKOWSKY RESULT IN THE LAST ROW GIVES A STRIKING NUMBER THAT IS WORTH COMPUTING ONCE: with a wave speed of 1,200 m/s and a velocity of 1.5 m/s, ΔH = 1,200 × 1.5/9.81 = 183 metres.**

> **That is 18 bar of pressure rise from stopping a flow of a modest 1.5 m/s — added to whatever static pressure was already there.**

> **It is why water hammer bursts pipelines, and why the surge pressure rather than the working pressure frequently governs the pipe's pressure class.**

> **The velocity dependence also explains a design rule: keeping the velocity in a pumping main modest — 1 to 2 m/s — limits the surge as well as the friction, and a main sized for high velocity to save capital cost brings a surge problem with it.**

**WHAT DETERMINES WHETHER CLOSURE IS 'RAPID', WHICH IS THE KEY DISTINCTION:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The wave takes a time 2L/a to travel to the far end and back** ← | **The PIPE PERIOD** ← |
| **If the valve closes in LESS than 2L/a, the closure is RAPID** ← | **The reflected wave has not yet returned to relieve the pressure, so the full Joukowsky rise occurs** ← |
| **If it closes in MORE than 2L/a, the closure is SLOW** ← | **The returning wave relieves the pressure progressively and the rise is less** ← |
| **For a 2 km main at 1,200 m/s, 2L/a is 3.3 seconds** ← | **So any closure faster than about 3 seconds is 'rapid' — which includes almost any valve slammed by hand** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW GIVES THE PRACTICAL MEASURE OF THE PROBLEM AND IT IS SOBERING: on a main of ordinary length, 'rapid' means a few seconds.**

> **So a valve that an operator considers to have been closed carefully — over five or ten seconds — may still be a rapid closure on a long main, and certainly is on a short one.**

> **This is why valve closure times on large mains are specified and why powered valves are given a controlled closing rate rather than being allowed to slam.**

**THE PROTECTIVE MEASURES:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **SLOW-closing valves, and specified closure times** ← | **The cheapest measure where it suffices** ← |
| **A FLYWHEEL on the pump, increasing its inertia** ← | **So it runs down slowly rather than stopping abruptly** ← |
| **AIR VESSEL (surge vessel)** ← | **A pressure vessel with a cushion of compressed air, which supplies water into the main as the pressure falls and absorbs it as the pressure rises** ← |
| **SURGE TANK or a standpipe open to atmosphere** ← | **The same device as in a hydropower scheme** ← |
| **Pressure RELIEF valve** ← | **Discharging to waste when a set pressure is exceeded** ← |
| **A ONE-WAY surge tank, admitting water only** ← | **Preventing the negative pressure phase, which is often the more dangerous** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW POINTS AT THE PART OF THE PHENOMENON THAT IS MOST OFTEN OVERLOOKED AND FREQUENTLY DOES THE REAL DAMAGE: the NEGATIVE pressure phase.**

> **When a pump stops, the column downstream continues to move away and the pressure behind it FALLS — often to below atmospheric.**

> **If it falls to the vapour pressure, the water column SEPARATES and a vapour cavity forms.**

> **When the column returns and the cavity collapses, the two masses of water meet at speed and the resulting pressure spike can far exceed the original Joukowsky rise.**

> **Meanwhile the sub-atmospheric pressure can COLLAPSE a thin-walled pipe, and can suck contaminated groundwater in through any defect — a water quality hazard as well as a structural one.**

> **So surge analysis must examine the low-pressure envelope as carefully as the high, and protection against column separation is often the governing requirement on a pipeline with a high summit.**

verification.notes: Joukowsky: dH = aV/g = 1200 x 1.5/9.81 = 183 m. Pipe period 2L/a = 2 x 2000/1200 = 3.3 s.

examTip.trick: **Rapid valve closure or sudden pump stoppage** — momentum destroyed quickly means a large force. ΔH = aV/g, about 183 m for V = 1.5 m/s and a = 1,200 m/s.
examTip.trap: **'Rapid' means faster than the pipe period 2L/a — a few SECONDS on an ordinary main.** So a valve closed 'carefully' over five seconds is still a rapid closure.
examTip.mnemonic: **The NEGATIVE phase often does the damage** — column separation, cavity collapse with a spike above Joukowsky, pipe collapse, and contaminated groundwater sucked in through defects.

questions.stem: The OPERATING POINT of a centrifugal pump installed in a pipeline is found:
options: At the pump's maximum efficiency, whatever the pipeline
At the shut-off head of the pump
Where the pump's HEAD-DISCHARGE characteristic intersects the system (pipeline) characteristic
At the point of maximum discharge the pump can deliver
questions.solution:
**Where the pump's HEAD-DISCHARGE characteristic INTERSECTS the SYSTEM (pipeline) characteristic** — the system curve being the static lift plus the friction loss, which rises with the square of the discharge.

**The two curves:**

| Curve | Shape |
|---|---|
| **PUMP characteristic (H against Q)** ← | **FALLING — the head the pump can generate DECREASES as the discharge increases; highest at zero flow (the shut-off head)** ← |
| **SYSTEM characteristic** ← | **RISING — static lift (a constant) plus friction loss (proportional to Q²)** ← |
| **Their INTERSECTION is the operating point** ← | **The only condition at which the head the pump produces equals the head the system demands** ← |

> **THE OPERATING POINT IS DETERMINED BY THE SYSTEM AS MUCH AS BY THE PUMP, AND THAT IS THE POINT OF THE QUESTION: a pump does not have a discharge of its own.**

> **The same pump in a short pipeline delivers a large flow at a low head; in a long pipeline it delivers a small flow at a high head.**

> **So a pump cannot be selected from its own curve alone — the pipeline's curve must be drawn first, and the pump then chosen so that the intersection falls at or near the pump's BEST EFFICIENCY POINT.**

> **Which is why option (a) is wrong but points at the design objective: the pump does not automatically run at its best efficiency, and making it do so is the whole art of pump selection.**

**WHY RUNNING AWAY FROM THE BEST EFFICIENCY POINT MATTERS, WHICH IS MORE THAN A MATTER OF ENERGY COST:**
| Condition | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Running at the best efficiency point** ← | **Maximum efficiency, smooth flow through the impeller, minimum vibration** ← |
| **Running at much LOWER flow than BEP** ← | **RECIRCULATION within the impeller, radial thrust on the shaft, vibration, bearing and seal wear, and overheating — a pump throttled hard is being damaged** ← |
| **Running at much HIGHER flow than BEP** ← | **CAVITATION risk rises sharply, and the motor may be overloaded** ← |
| **Running at SHUT-OFF (against a closed valve)** ← | **All the input power becomes heat in the casing; the water boils within minutes and the pump is destroyed** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS A REAL OPERATIONAL HAZARD AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING: a centrifugal pump running against a fully closed delivery valve is not idling harmlessly.**

> **The motor continues to deliver its power, the water in the casing cannot escape, and there is nothing to carry the heat away — so the temperature rises rapidly, the water flashes to steam, and the pump seizes or the casing fails.**

> **A few minutes is enough on a large pump. This is why a minimum-flow bypass is fitted to pumps that might be run against a closed valve, and why 'no flow' protection is a standard interlock.**

**THE SHAPE OF THE SYSTEM CURVE HAS A USEFUL CONSEQUENCE WORTH KNOWING:**

| Case | Note |
|---|---|
| **A system dominated by STATIC lift (a deep well, a high reservoir)** ← | **The system curve is nearly FLAT, so the operating point is insensitive to friction and the flow is stable** ← |
| **A system dominated by FRICTION (a long main, little lift)** ← | **The curve is STEEP, so the flow is sensitive to any change in roughness or in the pump's condition** ← |
| **A steep system curve makes THROTTLING an inefficient way to control flow** ← | **Since the throttling loss is a large fraction of the head** ← |
| **On such a system, VARIABLE SPEED control saves much more energy** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS CONTAIN THE MODERN ENERGY-SAVING ARGUMENT AND IT IS A LARGE ONE: throttling a pump to reduce its flow wastes the throttled head as heat, and the pump still consumes nearly its full power.**

> **Reducing the SPEED instead reduces the flow proportionally, the head as the square of the speed, and the POWER as the CUBE of the speed — the affinity laws.**

> **So a 20 per cent reduction in speed gives about a 20 per cent reduction in flow and a 50 per cent reduction in power, whereas throttling to the same flow saves very little.**

> **That cubic relationship is why variable speed drives repay their cost quickly on any pump whose duty varies, and it is one of the few genuinely large and easily obtained energy savings available in a water utility.**

examTip.trick: **The intersection of the falling PUMP curve with the rising SYSTEM curve** (static lift plus friction ∝ Q²). A pump has no discharge of its own.
examTip.trap: **Running well off the best efficiency point damages the pump** — recirculation and radial thrust at low flow, cavitation at high flow. At shut-off the water boils in minutes.
examTip.mnemonic: **Affinity laws: flow ∝ N, head ∝ N², POWER ∝ N³.** So a 20 % speed cut halves the power, while throttling to the same flow saves almost nothing.

questions.stem: CAVITATION in a centrifugal pump occurs when:
options: The absolute pressure at the impeller inlet falls to the water's vapour pressure
The pump is run at too low a speed
Air is deliberately introduced to prime the pump
The delivery head is lower than the pump's rating
questions.solution:
**When the absolute pressure at the impeller INLET falls to the water's VAPOUR PRESSURE**, so vapour bubbles form and then COLLAPSE violently as they pass into the higher-pressure region — pitting the impeller and causing noise and vibration.

**The mechanism:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Water is accelerated into the impeller's eye, so its pressure FALLS** ← | **The lowest pressure in the whole pump is just at the impeller inlet** ← |
| **If that pressure reaches the VAPOUR pressure, the water BOILS — at ambient temperature** ← | **Boiling is a matter of pressure as much as of temperature** ← |
| **Vapour bubbles form and are carried into the impeller** ← | ← |
| **A few millimetres further on, the pressure has risen and the bubbles COLLAPSE** ← | **Implosively, in microseconds** ← |
| **Each collapse drives a microjet of water at the metal surface at enormous local pressure** ← | **Progressively removing material — the surface is PITTED, as though corroded** ← |
| **The symptoms are a loud crackling noise, vibration, falling head and discharge, and eventual impeller destruction** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW CONTAINS THE FACT THAT MAKES CAVITATION POSSIBLE AT ALL AND IT IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY: water at 20 °C boils at an absolute pressure of about 2.3 kPa, which is a vacuum of some 97 per cent.**

> **So cavitation requires the pressure at the impeller inlet to be very low indeed, and everything that lowers it contributes: a high suction LIFT, a long or narrow suction pipe, a partly closed suction valve, a clogged strainer, high ALTITUDE, and warm water.**

> **The remedy is therefore always to RAISE the pressure available at the pump's inlet, and the parameter that measures it is the NET POSITIVE SUCTION HEAD.**

**THE NPSH CONDITION, WHICH IS THE DESIGN CHECK:**

| Quantity | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **NPSH AVAILABLE (NPSHa)** ← | **What the INSTALLATION provides: atmospheric head, minus the static suction lift, minus the suction friction losses, minus the vapour pressure head** ← |
| **NPSH REQUIRED (NPSHr)** ← | **What the PUMP needs, from the manufacturer's curve — it INCREASES with discharge** ← |
| **The condition** ← | **NPSHa > NPSHr, with a margin of at least 0.5 to 1.0 m** ← |

> **THE PRACTICAL LIMIT ON SUCTION LIFT FOLLOWS DIRECTLY AND IS WORTH KNOWING AS A NUMBER: atmospheric pressure is 10.3 m of water at sea level, and after deducting the vapour pressure, the friction losses and the pump's NPSHr, the practical suction lift is about 6 to 7 metres — and less at altitude.**

| Altitude | Atmospheric head | Practical suction lift |
|---|---|---|
| **Sea level** | **10.3 m** | **6 to 7 m** ← |
| **1,400 m (Kathmandu)** ← | **About 8.7 m** ← | **About 5 m** ← |
| **3,000 m** ← | **About 7.2 m** ← | **3 to 4 m** ← |

> **THE ALTITUDE EFFECT IN THIS TABLE IS A GENUINELY IMPORTANT PRACTICAL POINT IN NEPAL AND IT IS REGULARLY MISSED: a pump installation that works perfectly in the Terai may cavitate at the same suction lift in Kathmandu, and will certainly do so at 3,000 m.**

> **The pump is identical and the pipework is identical; only the atmospheric pressure has changed, and it has taken away 1.6 m of the available suction head between the plain and the valley.**

> **So a standard design replicated up the hill without adjusting the suction arrangement will cavitate — and the symptom will be reported as a faulty pump rather than as a siting error.**

> **The remedies are all about geometry: lower the pump relative to the water level, shorten and enlarge the suction pipe, remove bends and fittings from it, or best of all use a SUBMERSIBLE or a vertical turbine pump so that the impeller is below the water and the suction lift is negative.**

> **That last option removes the problem entirely rather than managing it, which is why submersible pumps have become standard for deep wells and for any duty where suction lift would be marginal.**

verification.notes: Atmospheric head 10.3 m at sea level, about 8.7 m at 1400 m altitude; practical suction lift 6-7 m falling to about 5 m.

examTip.trick: **The pressure at the impeller inlet reaches VAPOUR pressure, bubbles form and implode** — pitting the metal, with a loud crackling and falling output.
examTip.trap: **NPSHa > NPSHr with a margin** — and NPSHr RISES with discharge, so a pump can cavitate when run at high flow even if it is fine at its duty point.
examTip.mnemonic: **Altitude steals suction head** — 10.3 m at sea level but 8.7 m in Kathmandu, so a Terai design cavitates in the valley. A SUBMERSIBLE removes the problem entirely.

questions.stem: Two identical centrifugal pumps connected in SERIES, as compared with the same two in PARALLEL, will:
options: Deliver twice the discharge at the same head
Deliver the same head and the same discharge as one pump alone
Deliver half the head and half the discharge
Deliver approximately twice the head at a given discharge
questions.solution:
**Deliver approximately TWICE the HEAD at a given discharge** — whereas in parallel they deliver approximately twice the DISCHARGE at a given head.

**The two arrangements:**

| Arrangement | Effect | Used when |
|---|---|---|
| **SERIES — the delivery of one feeds the suction of the next** ← | **HEADS ADD at the same discharge** ← | **The HEAD required exceeds what one pump can generate — a high lift** ← |
| **PARALLEL — both draw from the same suction and deliver into the same main** ← | **DISCHARGES ADD at the same head** ← | **The FLOW required exceeds what one pump can deliver, or standby and part-load flexibility is wanted** ← |

> **THE WORD 'APPROXIMATELY' IN BOTH CASES IS IMPORTANT AND IT IS THE PART MOST OFTEN MISSED, so it is worth explaining why the doubling is never exact:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The combined curve is drawn by adding heads (series) or flows (parallel) at each point** ← | ← |
| **But the OPERATING POINT is still the intersection with the SYSTEM curve** ← | **And the system curve has not changed** ← |
| **In PARALLEL, the higher flow means MORE FRICTION in the common main** ← | **So the system curve rises, and the combined operating point is at a HIGHER head and LESS than twice the flow** ← |
| **The steeper the system curve, the LESS parallel pumping gains** ← | **On a friction-dominated system, adding a second pump in parallel may increase the flow by only 30 or 40 per cent** ← |
| **In SERIES, the higher head means more flow, hence more friction, so again less than the arithmetic sum** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE PRACTICAL WARNING AND IT IS A COMMON DISAPPOINTMENT IN OPERATION: a utility installs a second identical pump in parallel expecting to double its output, and obtains a third more.**

> **The reason is entirely in the pipeline: doubling the flow quadruples the friction loss, which consumes most of the second pump's contribution.**

> **So a parallel pump is effective on a system dominated by STATIC lift, where the system curve is flat, and disappointing on one dominated by friction.**

> **A utility wanting to double its delivery through an existing main must usually enlarge the main as well as adding a pump — and the main is the greater part of the cost, which is why 'just add another pump' rarely works as hoped.**

**THE PRACTICAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR EACH ARRANGEMENT:**

| Arrangement | Considerations |
|---|---|
| **SERIES** | **The second pump's casing must withstand the FULL combined pressure — its suction is already at the first pump's delivery pressure** ← |
| ← | **A MULTISTAGE pump is series operation within one casing, and is the normal solution for a high head** ← |
| ← | **If one pump fails, the other cannot deliver against the full head, so there is no partial redundancy** ← |
| **PARALLEL** | **Each pump needs its own NON-RETURN valve, or the running pump will drive water backwards through the idle one** ← |
| ← | **Pumps of DISSIMILAR characteristics in parallel can conflict — the weaker one may deliver nothing, or be driven backwards** ← |
| ← | **Gives genuine STANDBY and allows the number running to be matched to the demand** ← |

> **THE NON-RETURN VALVE IN THE FOURTH ROW IS AN ABSOLUTE REQUIREMENT AND ITS OMISSION HAS AN IMMEDIATE CONSEQUENCE: with two pumps on a common delivery and one running, the delivery pressure acts on the idle pump's outlet.**

> **Water then flows backwards through the idle pump, spinning its impeller in reverse — so the running pump is pumping in a circle and delivering far less than it should, while the idle pump is being driven as a turbine.**

> **The utility sees a pump running and an inexplicably low delivery, and the cause is not visible from outside.**

> **THE DISSIMILAR-PUMP WARNING IN THE FIFTH ROW IS THE OTHER COMMON ERROR AND IT ARISES NATURALLY OVER TIME: pumps are replaced one at a time as they fail, and a station that began with three identical sets ends with three different ones.**

> **If their shut-off heads differ substantially, the pump with the lower shut-off head cannot deliver at all when the stronger one is running — its non-return valve simply stays shut.**

> **So it consumes power, gets hot, and delivers nothing, while the operator believes two pumps are working.**

> **Matching pump characteristics when replacing one of a parallel set is therefore not a preference but a requirement, and it is worth recording the original curves in the station so the requirement can be met years later.**

examTip.trick: **Series adds HEADS; parallel adds DISCHARGES.** Series for a high lift, parallel for more flow and for standby.
examTip.trap: **Never exactly double** — in parallel, twice the flow means four times the friction, so the gain may be only 30-40 % on a friction-dominated system. Enlarging the main is usually needed too.
examTip.mnemonic: **Each parallel pump needs its own NON-RETURN valve**, or the running one drives water backwards through the idle one. And match characteristics when replacing one of a set.

questions.stem: A DISTRICT METERED AREA (DMA) is established in a water distribution network in order to:
options: Increase the pressure available to consumers in that area
Isolate a discrete zone hydraulically and meter all flow into and out of it
Allow the area to be supplied from a different source
Provide a point at which the water can be re-chlorinated
questions.solution:
**To ISOLATE a discrete zone hydraulically and METER all flow into and out of it** — so that the zone's night-time minimum flow can be measured and compared with its legitimate use, revealing the volume of LEAKAGE.

**How the method works:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The network is divided into zones of typically 500 to 3,000 connections** ← | **By closing boundary valves, so each zone has only one or two metered inlets** ← |
| **The inflow is metered CONTINUOUSLY** ← | ← |
| **The MINIMUM NIGHT FLOW — usually between 2 and 4 a.m. — is identified** ← | **When legitimate consumption is at its lowest** ← |
| **Legitimate night use is estimated and deducted** ← | **A small allowance per property, plus any known industrial night use** ← |
| **What remains is LEAKAGE** ← | **And it is measured rather than guessed** ← |
| **A rise in the minimum night flow over time indicates a NEW leak** ← | **Which can then be located within that zone rather than across the whole town** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW CONTAINS THE INSIGHT ON WHICH THE WHOLE TECHNIQUE RESTS AND IT IS AN ELEGANT ONE: at three in the morning, almost nobody is using water, so almost everything flowing into the zone is leaking out of it.**

> **During the day, consumption and leakage are mixed and cannot be separated by any measurement at the inlet.**

> **At night, consumption nearly vanishes and leakage does not — leaks run at a constant rate around the clock — so the two are separated automatically by the passage of time.**

> **That is why the minimum night flow is such a powerful indicator, and why it requires no assumptions about consumer behaviour beyond the fact that people sleep.**

**WHY THE ZONING MATTERS AS MUCH AS THE METERING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A single meter on a whole town's supply tells you the total loss and nothing about WHERE it is** ← | **Which is of little operational use** ← |
| **A DMA localises the loss to a few kilometres of main and a few hundred properties** ← | **Which a leak detection crew can survey in a day or two** ← |
| **It also allows zones to be RANKED, so effort goes where the loss is greatest** ← | ← |
| **And it allows the effect of a repair to be VERIFIED** ← | **The night flow drops by the amount of the leak found, which confirms the leak was the one being sought** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS AN UNDERAPPRECIATED BENEFIT AND IT MAKES THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A PROGRAMME AND AN ACTIVITY: without a DMA, a utility repairs leaks and never knows whether its losses have fallen.**

> **With one, every repair produces a measurable step change in the night flow, so the programme's effectiveness is demonstrable and the crews' work is verifiable.**

> **That measurability is what allows a leakage programme to be funded and sustained, since it can be shown to be returning water rather than merely consuming budget.**

**THE COMPLEMENTARY MEASURE, WHICH IS WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE IT IS OFTEN THE CHEAPEST:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **PRESSURE MANAGEMENT — reducing the pressure to the minimum adequate** ← | **Leakage from a given hole varies with roughly the SQUARE ROOT of the pressure, or more for a split in a plastic pipe** ← |
| **So reducing the pressure by 30 per cent can cut leakage by 20 to 40 per cent** ← | **Without finding or repairing a single leak** ← |
| **It also reduces the rate at which NEW leaks and bursts occur** ← | **High pressure is what causes most bursts** ← |
| **Achieved with pressure reducing valves at the DMA inlets** ← | **Often modulated to allow higher pressure at the demand peak and lower at night** ← |

> **THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS TOGETHER MAKE PRESSURE MANAGEMENT THE MOST COST-EFFECTIVE LEAKAGE MEASURE AVAILABLE AND IT IS WORTH PUTTING FIRST: it reduces the existing leakage immediately and reduces the creation of new leakage indefinitely.**

> **No excavation is needed, no leak need be found, and the saving begins the day the valve is set.**

> **The limit is that consumers must still receive an adequate pressure — typically a minimum of 7 to 10 m at the highest fitting served — so the scope depends on how much surplus pressure the zone had.**

> **In a network with a wide range of ground levels, the low-lying zones often have far more pressure than they need, and those are precisely the zones where pressure management yields most.**

examTip.trick: **Meter a small isolated zone and read its MINIMUM NIGHT FLOW** — at 3 a.m. consumption nearly vanishes but leakage does not, so the two separate themselves.
examTip.trap: **A single town meter gives the total loss and no idea where it is** — the value is in LOCALISING it to a few hundred properties a crew can survey.
examTip.mnemonic: **Pressure management is the cheapest measure** — leakage goes as roughly √pressure, so a 30 % cut saves 20-40 % with no excavation, and it prevents new bursts too.

questions.stem: A CROSS-CONNECTION in a water supply system is dangerous because it can permit:
options: An excessive pressure to develop in the mains
Air to be drawn into the pipeline at high points
Backflow of contaminated water into the potable supply
Loss of the chlorine residual by chemical reaction
questions.solution:
**BACKFLOW of contaminated water into the potable supply, when the supply pressure falls below that of the contaminated source** — a risk realised by BACK-SIPHONAGE or by BACK-PRESSURE.

**The two mechanisms of backflow:**

| Mechanism | Cause |
|---|---|
| **BACK-SIPHONAGE** ← | **The supply pressure falls BELOW atmospheric — from a main burst, a fire draw-off, a pump starting, or a supply interruption — and the sub-atmospheric main SUCKS water back through any submerged outlet** ← |
| **BACK-PRESSURE** ← | **The contaminated system is at a HIGHER pressure than the supply — a boosted circuit, a boiler, a pressurised process vessel, or simply a tank at a greater height — and it pushes its contents into the main** ← |

> **THE FIRST MECHANISM IS THE MORE COMMON AND THE SITUATIONS THAT CREATE IT ARE ENTIRELY ORDINARY, which is what makes it dangerous:**

| Example | Note |
|---|---|
| **A hose left submerged in a bucket, a tank, a drain or a swimming pool** ← | **The classic case, and it needs no defective plumbing at all** ← |
| **A tap below the rim of a basin or a cistern** ← | **Where the outlet can become submerged if the fitting overflows** ← |
| **A hose connected to a chemical sprayer or a fertiliser applicator** ← | **A recognised cause of serious poisoning incidents** ← |
| **A submerged inlet to a livestock trough** ← | ← |
| **A pipe connected to both the mains and a private well or tanker supply** ← | **The most serious form, since it connects an entire unverified source to the network** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW EXPLAINS WHY THE PRIMARY DEFENCE IS SO SIMPLE AND SO EFFECTIVE: an AIR GAP.**

> **If the outlet is above the flood level of the receiving vessel by at least twice the pipe's diameter, no siphon can form and no backflow is physically possible whatever the pressures.**

> **This is why every properly designed tap discharges ABOVE the rim of its basin, why a cistern's inlet is above its overflow level, and why a hose should never be left with its end submerged.**

> **It is a purely geometric protection requiring no device, no maintenance and no testing — which makes it the most reliable safeguard available, and the one to prefer wherever the layout permits.**

**THE HIERARCHY OF BACKFLOW PREVENTION, IN DESCENDING ORDER OF RELIABILITY:**

| Device | Note |
|---|---|
| **AIR GAP (physical separation)** ← | **Absolute, and cannot fail — the preferred solution** ← |
| **Reduced pressure zone (RPZ) assembly** ← | **Two check valves with a relief valve between them, which dumps to atmosphere if either fails — for high hazard connections** ← |
| **Double check valve assembly** ← | **Two independent check valves in series — for moderate hazard** ← |
| **Single check valve** ← | **Minimal protection; a single mechanical device that can be held open by grit** ← |
| **Vacuum breaker** ← | **Admits air to break a siphon; protects against back-siphonage only, NOT against back-pressure** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS A DISTINCTION THAT MATTERS IN SELECTION AND IS OFTEN MUDDLED: a vacuum breaker admits air when the pressure falls, which defeats back-siphonage.**

> **It does nothing whatever against BACK-PRESSURE, because in that case the supply pressure has not fallen — the contaminated side has simply risen above it, and the vacuum breaker has no reason to open.**

> **So a vacuum breaker on a connection to a pressurised process or a boosted circuit is no protection at all, and the device must be chosen for the mechanism that actually threatens.**

> **THE UNDERLYING PRINCIPLE IS WORTH STATING AS A CLOSING POINT, BECAUSE IT REVERSES A NATURAL ASSUMPTION: a water main is not a one-way street.**

> **A network is a pressurised system whose pressure varies constantly and can locally reverse, and every connection to it is a potential inlet as well as an outlet.**

> **In an INTERMITTENT supply, where the mains empty daily, that reversal is not an occasional event but a routine one — so cross-connection control is far more important in such a system than in a continuously pressurised one, and it is precisely where it receives least attention.**

examTip.trick: **Backflow — by back-SIPHONAGE (supply pressure falls) or back-PRESSURE (the contaminated side is higher).** Two distinct mechanisms.
