examTip.trap: **A VACUUM BREAKER protects only against back-siphonage** — under back-pressure the supply has not fallen, so it never opens. Choose the device for the mechanism.
examTip.mnemonic: **An AIR GAP cannot fail** — an outlet above the flood level by twice its diameter makes backflow physically impossible. Prefer geometry to devices.

questions.stem: In a town water distribution network, both a MINIMUM and a MAXIMUM pressure are specified. The MAXIMUM is limited because excessive pressure:
options: Increases leakage and the frequency of bursts, wastes water at every tap
Reduces the water's chlorine residual
Causes the water to become turbid
Prevents the water reaching upper floors
questions.solution:
**Because excessive pressure INCREASES LEAKAGE and the frequency of BURSTS, wastes water at every tap, and can damage domestic fittings and appliances.**

**The pressure requirements:**

| Requirement | Typical value |
|---|---|
| **MINIMUM residual pressure at the consumer's connection** ← | **7 m for a single storey, 12 m for two storeys, 17 m for three — about 5 m per additional floor plus a working residual** ← |
| **Minimum for FIRE fighting at a hydrant** ← | **Higher, and often the governing minimum in a commercial area** ← |
| **MAXIMUM pressure** ← | **Commonly limited to about 55 to 70 m (5.5 to 7 bar)** ← |
| **Where the topography would give more** ← | **The network is ZONED by elevation, with pressure reducing valves or separate service reservoirs for each zone** ← |

> **THE FOUR CONSEQUENCES OF EXCESSIVE PRESSURE ARE WORTH SEPARATING, BECAUSE THEY ARE OF QUITE DIFFERENT KINDS:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **LEAKAGE increases** ← | **Flow through an existing hole rises with roughly the square root of the pressure, and through a split in a plastic pipe considerably faster** ← |
| **BURSTS become more frequent** ← | **High pressure both stresses the pipe continuously and amplifies every surge — and burst frequency rises steeply with pressure** ← |
| **CONSUMER WASTAGE increases** ← | **A tap at 60 m delivers far more than the user wants or notices; the excess simply runs down the drain** ← |
| **DAMAGE to fittings and appliances** ← | **Taps, cisterns, water heaters and washing machines are rated for a modest pressure, and their washers and seals fail early above it** ← |
| **And NOISE and water hammer in the plumbing** | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN OVERLOOKED AND IT IS A SURPRISINGLY LARGE EFFECT: consumption itself rises with pressure.**

> **A person washing their hands opens the tap and closes it when finished; the volume delivered in that time is proportional to the flow, and the flow depends on the pressure.**

> **So a network at high pressure delivers more water for the same activity, and the excess is genuine waste that no leak detection will find because it passes through the meter as legitimate consumption.**

> **This is part of the reason pressure management reduces total demand and not merely leakage, and it means the water saved is greater than a leakage calculation alone would suggest.**

**THE ZONING SOLUTION IN THE FOURTH ROW OF THE FIRST TABLE IS THE STANDARD ANSWER IN HILLY TOWNS AND IT IS WORTH SETTING OUT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A town with 200 m of relief cannot be served from one reservoir** ← | **The high ground would have no pressure and the low ground far too much** ← |
| **So it is divided into PRESSURE ZONES of perhaps 40 to 60 m of elevation each** ← | ← |
| **Each zone has its own service reservoir, or is fed through a pressure reducing valve** ← | ← |
| **The zones are kept hydraulically SEPARATE, with closed boundary valves** ← | **And those valves must stay closed — a boundary valve opened during a repair and left open destroys the zoning** ← |
| **Each zone can then be metered as a DMA as well** ← | **The two purposes coinciding conveniently** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE OPERATIONAL FAILURE THAT UNDOES PRESSURE ZONING AND IT HAPPENS CONSTANTLY: a valve is opened to maintain supply during a repair, the repair is completed, and nobody closes it again.**

> **The two zones are then connected, the higher-pressure zone feeds the lower one, and consumers in the low zone receive the full head from the upper reservoir.**

> **Their fittings begin to fail and their leakage rises, and the cause is a valve position that no record shows.**

> **This is why a network's valve positions must be recorded and audited, and why a zoned network needs a valve register as much as it needs a pipe drawing — an unglamorous administrative measure without which the hydraulic design does not survive contact with operation.**

> **The minimum in the first table deserves a closing word too: the 7 m figure is at the CONNECTION, not at the tap, and it must be measured at the point and the time of least favourable conditions — the highest property, at the peak hour, with the reservoir at its lowest.**

> **A network that meets 7 m on average and 2 m at the worst point and hour has not met the requirement, and the consumers at that point are the ones who will complain.**

examTip.trick: **More leakage, more bursts, more consumer wastage, damaged fittings.** Minimum about 7 m for one storey rising 5 m per floor; maximum about 55-70 m.
examTip.trap: **Consumption itself rises with pressure** — a tap open for the same time delivers more. So pressure management cuts demand as well as leakage.
examTip.mnemonic: **A boundary valve opened for a repair and left open destroys the zoning** — the low zone then gets the upper reservoir's full head. Hence a valve REGISTER, audited.

questions.stem: A FERRULE, as used in a domestic water service connection, is:
options: The meter that records the consumer's consumption
The valve on the consumer's side of the boundary
The pipe connecting the meter to the house
The small valve or fitting tapped directly into the distribution main
questions.solution:
**The SMALL VALVE or fitting tapped directly into the distribution main**, forming the start of the service connection and allowing it to be shut off at the main.

**The parts of a house service connection, in order from the main:**

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **FERRULE** ← | **Tapped into the main; the connection's origin, and it can be closed to isolate the service without shutting the main** ← |
| **GOOSE NECK (a short flexible or curved length)** ← | **An S-shaped bend immediately after the ferrule, which absorbs relative movement between the main and the service pipe** ← |
| **SERVICE (communication) PIPE** ← | **Running from the main to the property boundary** ← |
| **STOP COCK at the boundary, in a surface box** ← | **The utility's isolating valve, and the usual limit of its responsibility** ← |
| **WATER METER** ← | **Recording the consumption** ← (option a) |
| **Consumer's STOP VALVE** ← | **Under the consumer's control** ← (option b) |
| **SUPPLY PIPE within the property** ← | ← (option c) |

> **THE GOOSE NECK IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE COMPONENT WHOSE PURPOSE IS LEAST OBVIOUS AND MOST WORTH KNOWING: it is a deliberate loop of slack in the pipe.**

> **A main and a service pipe move independently — the main is large and rigid and settles with the road, while the service pipe is small and is disturbed by the footway, by the property's own settlement and by traffic vibration.**

> **A rigid connection between them concentrates that relative movement at the tapping, which is a small threaded hole in the main's wall and the weakest point in the arrangement.**

> **The goose neck absorbs the movement in bending instead, so the tapping is not stressed.**

> **Service connection leaks at the ferrule are among the commonest leaks in any network, and a missing or straightened goose neck is a frequent reason.**

**WHY SERVICE CONNECTIONS MATTER MORE THAN THEIR SIZE SUGGESTS, WHICH IS THE PRACTICAL POINT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A network has ONE service connection per property — thousands of them** ← | **Each with a tapping, a ferrule, joints, a stopcock and a meter** ← |
| **So the great majority of the network's JOINTS and fittings are in its service connections** ← | ← |
| **And a large share of total LEAKAGE is there rather than in the mains** ← | **Commonly half or more in an older network** ← |
| **Yet they are small, shallow, numerous and individually trivial** ← | **So they receive far less attention than a trunk main** ← |
| **Their leaks are also the hardest to find** ← | **Small flows, often running into a drain or a soakaway without surfacing** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE CONCLUSION THAT SHOULD DIRECT A LEAKAGE PROGRAMME AND IT IS ROUTINELY MISSED: most of the water lost is lost from the smallest pipes.**

> **A programme concentrating on the mains, which are visible, mapped and substantial, may address the minority of the loss.**

> **The service connections, which are unmapped, undocumented and often installed informally over decades, hold the majority — and the only economic way to deal with them in a badly deteriorated network is often wholesale REPLACEMENT of the service pipes rather than repair.**

> **That is expensive and unglamorous and it is frequently what the technical evidence points to.**

**A CLOSING NOTE ON METERING, SINCE IT SITS IN THIS LIST:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A meter records CONSUMPTION and thereby permits volumetric charging** ← | ← |
| **Metered consumers use substantially LESS water than unmetered ones** ← | **Typically 15 to 30 per cent less, and the reduction persists** ← |
| **Meters also localise loss** ← | **The difference between the zone's inflow and the sum of its meters is the loss** ← |
| **But a meter UNDER-registers at very low flows** ← | **So a slow leak inside the property may pass unrecorded, and a network's apparent loss includes meter error** ← |
| **And a meter is a maintenance liability** ← | **It must be read, tested, and replaced periodically** ← |

> **The second row is the strongest argument for metering and it is a behavioural rather than a technical one: a consumer who pays by volume uses less, and continues to use less.**

> **That reduction is obtained without any works, and it is the largest single demand-side saving available to a utility — which is why metering is treated as a supply augmentation measure as much as a revenue measure.**

examTip.trick: **The ferrule is the fitting tapped into the MAIN** — the origin of the service connection. Then goose neck, service pipe, boundary stopcock, meter.
examTip.trap: **The GOOSE NECK is deliberate slack** absorbing relative movement between main and service pipe. Straightened or omitted, the tapping is stressed and leaks.
examTip.mnemonic: **Most of a network's JOINTS — and often most of its LEAKAGE — are in the service connections**, not the mains. And metering cuts consumption 15-30 % with no works at all.

questions.stem: The conventional treatment train for a turbid surface water is, in the correct order:
options: Filtration, coagulation, sedimentation, disinfection
Screening, then aeration where required, then coagulation and flocculation, then sedimentation, then filtration, then disinfection
Disinfection, screening, sedimentation, filtration
Coagulation, filtration, sedimentation, screening, disinfection
questions.solution:
**SCREENING, then AERATION where required, then COAGULATION and FLOCCULATION, then SEDIMENTATION, then FILTRATION, then DISINFECTION.**

**The train, with each unit's purpose:**

| Unit | Removes or achieves |
|---|---|
| **SCREENING** ← | **Floating debris, leaves, fish, rags — protecting the plant's mechanical equipment** ← |
| **AERATION (where needed)** ← | **Iron, manganese, CO₂, H₂S, taste and odour** ← |
| **Plain SEDIMENTATION or a grit chamber (where the turbidity is very high)** ← | **Coarse silt and sand, before chemicals are spent on it** ← |
| **COAGULATION (rapid mix)** ← | **Destabilises colloids chemically** ← |
| **FLOCCULATION (slow mix)** ← | **Grows the destabilised particles into settleable flocs** ← |
| **SEDIMENTATION (clarification)** ← | **Removes the bulk of the floc — typically 90 per cent of the solids** ← |
| **FILTRATION** ← | **Removes the residual floc and the protozoan cysts, polishing to below 1 NTU** ← |
| **DISINFECTION** ← | **Kills the remaining pathogens and leaves a residual** ← |
| **Any further steps — softening, fluoridation, pH correction** | **As required** ← |

> **THE ORDER IS NOT ARBITRARY AND EACH POSITION CAN BE JUSTIFIED, WHICH IS THE POINT OF THE QUESTION:**

| Why this order | Note |
|---|---|
| **SCREENING comes FIRST because debris would damage or block everything downstream** ← | **A rag in a chemical dosing pump or a log against a flocculator paddle** ← |
| **Coarse SEDIMENTATION before coagulation, where turbidity is extreme** ← | **Because coagulant spent on sand that would settle anyway is wasted, and the chemical cost of a 2,000 NTU monsoon flow is otherwise prohibitive** ← |
| **COAGULATION before FLOCCULATION, and both before SEDIMENTATION** ← | **The floc must exist before it can settle** ← |
| **SEDIMENTATION before FILTRATION** ← | **The filter would block within minutes if it received the full floc load; the clarifier removes 90 per cent and the filter polishes the rest** ← |
| **DISINFECTION LAST** ← | **So the disinfectant is not consumed by the organic matter and turbidity that the earlier stages remove — and so no unit downstream can recontaminate** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW EXPRESSES THE ESSENTIAL RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN THE CLARIFIER AND THE FILTER AND IT IS WORTH FIXING FIRMLY: they are not alternatives but a sequence with a strict division of labour.**

> **The clarifier does the BULK removal cheaply, using nothing but gravity and time.**

> **The filter does the FINAL polishing, and it can only do so if the load reaching it is already small.**

> **A filter asked to do the clarifier's work blocks in minutes and spends most of its time backwashing, consuming its own output.**

> **This is why direct filtration — omitting the clarifier — is possible only on a water of consistently low turbidity, and why it is unsuitable for a Himalayan river whose monsoon turbidity is measured in thousands of NTU.**

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT ORDERING PRINCIPLE OF ALL AND IT DESERVES ITS PLACE: disinfection is the LAST barrier, and nothing may come after it that could reintroduce contamination.**

> **This is why the clear water reservoir after chlorination must be covered and sealed, why filter backwash water is never returned downstream of the chlorination point, and why any repair to a unit downstream of chlorination requires the unit to be disinfected before it is returned to service.**

> **The train is arranged as a series of BARRIERS, each catching what the previous one missed — the MULTIPLE BARRIER principle — and the barriers must be in the right order, with the most reliable last.**

> **A plant whose sequence is disturbed, or in which one barrier is bypassed 'temporarily', has lost more protection than the arithmetic suggests, because the barriers are complementary: the filter removes what chlorine cannot kill, and the chlorine kills what the filter cannot remove.**
tags: clarifier and filter division of labour

examTip.trick: **Screen, aerate, coagulate, flocculate, settle, filter, disinfect.** Each unit prepares the water for the next.
examTip.trap: **The clarifier does BULK removal and the filter POLISHES** — they are a sequence, not alternatives. A filter given the full floc load blocks in minutes.
examTip.mnemonic: **Disinfection is LAST and nothing may follow it that could recontaminate** — hence sealed clear water tanks, and backwash never returned downstream of chlorination.

questions.stem: In a water treatment plant, a COARSE SCREEN (bar rack) differs from a FINE SCREEN in that the coarse screen:
options: Is placed after the sedimentation tank
Is made of woven wire mesh
Removes dissolved impurities
Has openings of the order of 50 to 100 mm and stops large floating objects
questions.solution:
**It has openings of the order of 50 to 100 mm and stops LARGE floating objects — logs, branches and animals** — while a fine screen with openings of 5 to 20 mm removes smaller debris, leaves and fish.

**The screens, in the order water meets them:**

| Screen | Opening | Removes |
|---|---|---|
| **TRASH RACK / COARSE screen (bar rack)** ← | **50 to 100 mm** ← | **Logs, branches, drifting timber, dead animals, large rubbish** ← |
| **MEDIUM screen** | **20 to 50 mm** | **Smaller branches, plastic, rags** ← |
| **FINE screen** ← | **5 to 20 mm** ← | **Leaves, twigs, fish, weed** ← |
| **MICROSTRAINER (rotating drum, 20 to 60 micron fabric)** ← | **Microns** ← | **ALGAE and fine suspended matter, in place of or ahead of coagulation on a low-turbidity water** ← |

> **THE PROGRESSION FROM COARSE TO FINE IS ESSENTIAL AND ITS LOGIC IS THE SAME AS FOR THE TREATMENT TRAIN AS A WHOLE: each screen protects the next.**

> **A fine screen presented with a log would be destroyed by it; a coarse screen alone would pass everything a pump could choke on.**

> **So the screens are graded, and the coarse one takes the mechanical punishment while the fine one does the detailed work.**

**THE DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS FOR A SCREEN, WHICH ARE MORE INTERESTING THAN THE OPENING SIZES:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **The approach VELOCITY must be low — about 0.6 to 1.0 m/s** ← | **Too high and the debris is pressed against the bars and cannot be raked off; too low and silt deposits in the approach channel** ← |
| **The screen is INCLINED at 45 to 60 degrees to the horizontal** ← | **So that the rake can drag the debris up and out, and so the effective opening area is greater than the channel's section** ← |
| **A HEAD LOSS develops across the screen and INCREASES as it blocks** ← | **Which is why the differential head is monitored — it is the indicator that cleaning is due** ← |
| **The screen must be CLEANABLE, by hand rake or mechanically** ← | ← |
| **The debris must go SOMEWHERE** ← | **A screening handling and disposal arrangement is part of the design, not an afterthought** ← |
| **A blocked screen can cause the upstream level to rise and OVERTOP the channel** ← | **Or, on an intake, starve the plant entirely** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST USEFUL OPERATIONAL POINT AND IT IS THE BASIS OF SCREEN CONTROL: the head loss across a screen is a direct measure of how blocked it is.**

> **A clean screen loses a few centimetres; a blocked one can lose a metre or more.**

> **So a simple pair of level gauges either side of the screen tells the operator when to clean it, and on a mechanically raked screen that differential is what triggers the rake automatically.**

> **It is a good example of a measurement that requires no instrument beyond a scale on a wall and yet controls the process reliably.**

> **THE SIXTH ROW DESCRIBES THE FAILURE THAT MAKES SCREENS IMPORTANT OUT OF PROPORTION TO THEIR SIMPLICITY, and it is a monsoon problem: a river in flood carries an extraordinary quantity of floating debris.**

> **A screen that copes all year can be blanketed within minutes by a raft of vegetation, and the plant's inflow stops at exactly the moment the river is at its most abundant.**

> **So screen capacity and cleaning arrangements must be sized for the flood condition and not for the average, and a manually raked screen on a Himalayan river in the monsoon needs staff present rather than a periodic visit.**

> **The corollary is that a plant should have some means of continuing briefly when the screens block — a bypass with a coarser screen, or storage ahead of the plant — because the alternative is an interruption to the town's supply caused by an excess rather than a shortage of water, which is both avoidable and hard to explain.**

Logs, branches and animals — while a fine screen with openings of 5 to 20 mm removes smaller debris, leaves and fish.

examTip.trick: **Coarse 50-100 mm for logs and animals; fine 5-20 mm for leaves and fish.** Microstrainers work in microns and remove algae.
examTip.trap: **Approach velocity 0.6-1.0 m/s** — too fast presses debris onto the bars so it cannot be raked; too slow silts the channel.
examTip.mnemonic: **The HEAD LOSS across a screen measures how blocked it is** — two level gauges control the cleaning. And size the screens for the MONSOON debris raft, not the average.

questions.stem: A rectangular sedimentation tank 30 m long and 8 m wide treats 4.0 million litres per day. Its SURFACE LOADING (overflow) RATE is:
options: 16.7 m³ per m² per day
4.2 m³ per m² per day
33.3 m³ per m² per day
8.3 m³ per m² per day
questions.solution:
**16.7 m³ per m² per day.**

**The calculation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Plan area** | **30 × 8 = 240 m²** ← |
| **Flow** | **4.0 MLD = 4,000 m³/day** ← |
| **Surface loading rate = flow ÷ PLAN AREA** ← | **= 4,000 / 240** ← |
| **Evaluating** | **= 16.67, about 16.7 m³/m²/day** ← |

> **So the overflow rate is 16.7 m³/m²/day, which is within the usual range of 15 to 30 for a plain sedimentation tank and 20 to 40 for a coagulated one.**

**WHY THE SURFACE LOADING RATE IS THE GOVERNING PARAMETER, AND NOT THE DETENTION TIME, IS THE POINT WORTH UNDERSTANDING:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The surface loading rate has the units of a VELOCITY** ← | **m³/m²/day is metres per day — 16.7 m/day, that is 0.19 mm/s** ← |
| **It is the CRITICAL SETTLING VELOCITY of the tank** ← | **Any particle whose fall velocity EXCEEDS it will be removed; any slower particle will be carried out** ← |
| **So the tank's performance depends only on its PLAN AREA and the flow** ← | **And NOT on its depth** ← |
| **Which is the same result derived for the hydropower settling basin** ← | **The identical relation, reached in a different subject** ← |

> **THE DEPTH-INDEPENDENCE IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE CLASSIC AND SURPRISING RESULT OF IDEAL SETTLING THEORY, AND IT IS WORTH SEEING WHY: a particle in a deeper tank has further to fall, but it also has proportionately longer to fall, because the tank holds more water at the same flow.**

> **The two effects cancel exactly, so a shallow tank of a given plan area removes the same particles as a deep one.**

> **This is the basis of the SHALLOW DEPTH settling devices — tube settlers and plate settlers — which insert inclined plates or tubes into a tank to multiply its effective plan area many times over within the same footprint.**

> **A tank fitted with tube settlers can handle several times the flow of the same tank without them, which makes them the standard way of upgrading an overloaded clarifier without building a new one.**

> **Depth is nevertheless chosen deliberately, for reasons the ideal theory does not capture: sludge storage, keeping the flow tranquil, and avoiding scour of settled sludge from the floor.**

**THE DETENTION TIME, FOR COMPLETENESS AND BECAUSE IT IS OFTEN ASKED TOGETHER:**

| Quantity | Working |
|---|---|
| **Assuming a depth of 3 m, the volume** | **240 × 3 = 720 m³** ← |
| **Flow per hour** | **4,000/24 = 166.7 m³/h** ← |
| **Detention time** | **720/166.7 = 4.3 hours** ← |
| **Which is within the usual 2 to 6 hours** ← | ← |

> **THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN THE TWO IS WORTH NOTING: the detention time equals the depth divided by the surface loading rate, so specifying any two of depth, detention time and overflow rate fixes the third.**

> **Here 3 m ÷ 16.7 m/day = 0.18 day = 4.3 hours, which confirms the arithmetic and is a useful check.**

> **A further practical parameter is the WEIR LOADING at the outlet — the flow per metre of weir length, usually kept below about 250 m³/m/day — because an overloaded weir draws the flow upward too strongly near the outlet and lifts settled floc back into it.**

> **A clarifier with a correct surface loading rate and an overloaded outlet weir will carry floc over, and the cause is often looked for in the coagulation when it lies in the outlet geometry — which is why the weir length is designed rather than left to whatever the tank's width happens to provide.**

verification.notes: 4000 m3/day / 240 m2 = 16.67 m3/m2/day; detention at 3 m depth = 720/166.7 = 4.3 h.

examTip.trick: **Flow ÷ PLAN AREA = 4,000/240 = 16.7 m³/m²/day.** Note the units are a velocity: the tank's critical settling velocity.
examTip.trap: **Performance depends on plan area, NOT depth** — deeper means further to fall but proportionately longer to do it. Hence tube settlers, which multiply the effective area.
examTip.mnemonic: **Detention time = depth ÷ overflow rate** — a useful cross-check. And watch the WEIR LOADING: an overloaded outlet weir lifts settled floc back into the flow.

questions.stem: A COAGULANT AID such as polyelectrolyte or activated silica is added in water treatment in order to:
options: Replace the primary coagulant entirely
Raise the pH into the optimum range for coagulation
Strengthen and enlarge the floc so that it settles faster and resists breaking up
Disinfect the water before filtration
questions.solution:
**To STRENGTHEN and enlarge the floc so that it settles faster and resists breaking up** — allowing a lower dose of the primary coagulant and a higher throughput.

**The coagulants and the aids:**

| Chemical | Role |
|---|---|
| **ALUM — aluminium sulphate** ← | **The standard PRIMARY coagulant; cheap, effective, and consumes alkalinity; optimum pH 6.5 to 7.5** ← |
| **FERRIC chloride and ferric sulphate** ← | **Primary coagulants; effective over a WIDER pH range (about 5 to 9) than alum, and better for colour removal — but they stain and are more corrosive** ← |
| **PAC — poly-aluminium chloride** ← | **A pre-hydrolysed aluminium coagulant; effective at lower doses, consumes less alkalinity, works better in cold water, and produces less sludge — dearer per kilogram and often cheaper in use** ← |
| **POLYELECTROLYTES (polymers)** ← | **Coagulant AIDS, and sometimes primary coagulants; long-chain molecules that BRIDGE between particles** ← |
| **ACTIVATED SILICA** ← | **A coagulant aid, forming a tough floc** ← |
| **LIME, soda ash, sodium bicarbonate** ← | **pH and ALKALINITY correction, not coagulation** ← (which is option b) |
| **Bentonite CLAY** ← | **A WEIGHTING agent, added to a very low-turbidity water to give the floc something to form around** ← |

> **THE POLYMER'S MECHANISM IN THE FOURTH ROW IS DIFFERENT IN KIND FROM ALUM'S, AND THE DISTINCTION IS THE HEART OF THE QUESTION:**

| Coagulant | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **ALUM and ferric salts** ← | **CHARGE NEUTRALISATION — a highly charged metal ion compresses the repulsive layer so particles can approach** ← |
| **POLYELECTROLYTES** ← | **BRIDGING — a long molecule adsorbs onto several particles at once and physically ties them together** ← |

> **Because the polymer works by physically linking particles rather than by altering their charge, it produces a floc that is LARGER and much TOUGHER — it holds together under the shear of the flocculator, the launders and the filter.**

> **That toughness is the practical benefit: a fragile alum floc can be broken by a pump, a sharp bend or an over-vigorous flocculator, and once broken it does not re-form.**

> **A polymer-strengthened floc survives the journey to the clarifier and the filter, so more of it is actually removed.**

**THE PRACTICAL BENEFITS AND THE CAUTIONS:**

| Benefit | Caution |
|---|---|
| **A faster-settling floc, so a higher plant throughput** ← | **The DOSE is critical and small — typically 0.1 to 1.0 mg/l** ← |
| **A lower primary coagulant dose, so less sludge** ← | **OVERDOSING is worse than underdosing: excess polymer RE-STABILISES the particles by coating them, and the floc disperses** ← |
| **Better performance in cold water and at low turbidity** ← | **Polymers must be made up carefully — a dry polymer added to water clumps into an unusable gel unless wetted correctly** ← |
| **Longer filter runs, since the floc does not break through** ← | **Only APPROVED polymers may be used for potable water, and to the approved maximum dose** ← |

> **THE OVERDOSING WARNING IN THE SECOND ROW IS A GENUINELY COUNTER-INTUITIVE AND EXPENSIVE TRAP AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING: with alum, a somewhat excessive dose is merely wasteful.**

> **With a polymer it is actively harmful. Beyond the optimum, the polymer coats each particle completely instead of bridging between particles — and a fully coated particle has no free surface for another polymer chain to attach to.**

> **The particles are then STERICALLY stabilised, repelling one another by the physical bulk of their coatings, and the suspension becomes more stable than it was before any polymer was added.**

> **So the operator who sees a poor floc, doubles the polymer dose and finds the water worse has met exactly this effect — and the remedy is to REDUCE the dose, which requires knowing that the curve has a maximum.**

> **This is precisely why the JAR TEST is indispensable for polymer dosing: the optimum is a narrow window and it cannot be found by extrapolation from either side.**

examTip.trick: **A stronger, larger floc that settles faster and resists shear** — allowing less primary coagulant and more throughput. Option (b) is lime, not a coagulant aid.
examTip.trap: **Alum works by CHARGE NEUTRALISATION; polymers by BRIDGING** — long molecules physically tying particles together, which is why the floc is so much tougher.
examTip.mnemonic: **Polymer OVERDOSE re-stabilises the suspension** — a fully coated particle has no free surface to bridge to. The curve has a maximum, so the jar test is essential.

questions.stem: The JAR TEST is carried out in a water treatment plant in order to:
options: Measure the turbidity of the raw water
Determine the optimum coagulant dose and pH for the water being treated on that day
Test the strength of the concrete in the treatment tanks
Measure the residual chlorine in the treated water
questions.solution:
**To determine the OPTIMUM COAGULANT DOSE and pH for the water being treated on that day**, by dosing several samples differently and comparing the floc formed and the settled turbidity.

**The procedure:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Fill 4 to 6 jars with the RAW water** ← | **The same water the plant is treating at that moment** ← |
| **Dose each with a DIFFERENT coagulant dose** ← | **Spanning the expected optimum — say 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 mg/l of alum** ← |
| **Stir RAPIDLY for a minute** ← | **Simulating the flash mixer** ← |
| **Then stir SLOWLY for 15 to 30 minutes** ← | **Simulating the flocculator** ← |
| **Stop and allow to SETTLE for 30 minutes** ← | **Simulating the clarifier** ← |
| **Observe the FLOC — its size, its speed of settling, its clarity — and measure the SETTLED TURBIDITY** ← | ← |
| **The optimum is the LOWEST dose giving satisfactory settled turbidity** ← | **Not the dose giving the very best result regardless of quantity** ← |

> **THE PROCEDURE'S DESIGN IS ITS WHOLE VALUE AND IT IS WORTH NOTICING WHAT IT IS DOING: the jar test is a SCALE MODEL of the plant.**

> **The rapid stir represents the flash mixer, the slow stir the flocculator, and the quiescent settling the clarifier — in the same sequence and in comparable proportions of time.**

> **So its result is directly transferable to the plant, which is why a simple set of beakers and a paddle stirrer can determine the operation of a multi-million-rupee works.**

> **It is one of the most cost-effective pieces of apparatus in engineering, and its absence or disuse is one of the commonest causes of a plant running badly.**

**WHY THE TEST MUST BE REPEATED RATHER THAN DONE ONCE, WHICH IS THE OPERATIONAL POINT:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **The optimum dose depends on the raw water's TURBIDITY, which varies daily and hourly in the monsoon** ← | ← |
| **It depends on the ALKALINITY and pH, which also vary** ← | ← |
| **It depends on the TEMPERATURE — coagulation is slower and needs more coagulant in cold water** ← | **Which matters in a Nepali winter** ← |
| **And on the nature of the turbidity — fine clay, algae or colour each behave differently** ← | ← |
| **So a dose set once and left is right only by coincidence** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW DESCRIBES THE UNIVERSAL FAILING OF POORLY RUN PLANTS AND IT IS WORTH STATING BLUNTLY: a fixed coagulant dose is wrong most of the time.**

> **Set too high, it wastes chemical, produces excess sludge, and may depress the pH out of the optimum range — making the treatment worse as well as dearer.**

> **Set too low, the floc does not form, the clarifier passes solids, the filters block quickly, and the filtered turbidity rises — so the plant's protection against cysts is lost.**

> **Since the raw water turbidity in a Himalayan river can change by two orders of magnitude within a day, the correct dose can change by a factor of five within the same day — which no fixed setting can accommodate.**

> **So a jar test at the start of each shift, and more often when the river is rising, is not a laboratory nicety but the principal means by which the plant is actually controlled.**

> **A useful refinement worth knowing: the test should also VARY THE pH at the best dose found, by adding lime or acid to different jars, because the optimum dose and the optimum pH interact.**

> **A dose that performs poorly at the raw water's own pH may perform excellently a half-unit higher, so testing dose alone can lead to a large and unnecessary chemical bill — and on a soft, low-alkalinity water it is the pH rather than the dose that usually needs attention.**

examTip.trick: **Several jars, different doses: rapid stir, slow stir, settle, then compare floc and settled turbidity.** The optimum is the LOWEST adequate dose.
examTip.trap: **The jar test is a SCALE MODEL of the plant** — rapid mix, flocculation and clarification in sequence. That is why its result transfers directly.
examTip.mnemonic: **A fixed dose is wrong most of the time** — the optimum changes with turbidity, alkalinity and temperature. In a Himalayan monsoon it can change fivefold in a day.

questions.stem: In the design of a FLOCCULATOR, the product of the VELOCITY GRADIENT G and the detention time t (the dimensionless value Gt) is specified because:
options: It determines the tank's structural thickness
It fixes the coagulant dose required
It measures the chlorine demand of the water
It measures the total number of particle collisions the water experiences
questions.solution:
**It measures the total number of PARTICLE COLLISIONS the water experiences** — enough collisions being needed to grow the floc, while too high a G tears the floc apart.

**The two quantities and their roles:**

| Quantity | Meaning | Typical value |
|---|---|---|
| **G — the VELOCITY GRADIENT, in s⁻¹** ← | **The rate of shear in the water; it measures how vigorously adjacent parcels of water move past one another, and hence the RATE of particle collisions** ← | **20 to 75 s⁻¹ for flocculation** ← |
| **t — the DETENTION time** ← | **How long the water is subjected to that shear** ← | **20 to 40 minutes** ← |
| **Gt — their product, dimensionless** ← | **The TOTAL number of collisions — the cumulative opportunity for floc growth** ← | **30,000 to 150,000** ← |
| **G for RAPID mixing (coagulation), by contrast** ← | **Very much higher** ← | **500 to 1,000 s⁻¹ for 30 to 60 seconds** ← |

> **THE CONTRAST BETWEEN THE FIRST AND FOURTH ROWS QUANTIFIES THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN COAGULATION AND FLOCCULATION AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL THING IN THIS ANSWER: rapid mixing uses a G an order of magnitude higher for a time two orders of magnitude shorter.**

> **High G disperses the coagulant instantly, which is what coagulation needs.**

> **Low G for a long period grows the floc gently, which is what flocculation needs.**

> **And the reason flocculation cannot simply use a high G to save time is the second half of the answer: shear both BUILDS and BREAKS floc.**

**THE COMPETING EFFECTS, WHICH ARE THE WHOLE OF FLOCCULATOR DESIGN:**

| Effect of increasing G | Note |
|---|---|
| **MORE collisions per second, so faster floc growth** ← | **The beneficial effect** ← |
| **But greater SHEAR STRESS on the flocs already formed** ← | **The harmful effect** ← |
| **Below about 20 s⁻¹, collisions are too few and flocculation is impracticably slow** ← | ← |
| **Above about 75 s⁻¹, the flocs are torn apart as fast as they grow** ← | **And beyond that the floc size actually DECREASES with more energy** ← |
| **So there is an OPTIMUM G, and it is a maximum rather than a direction** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE STRUCTURAL FEATURE OF THE PROBLEM AND IT RECURS THROUGHOUT THIS SUBJECT: more energy is not better beyond a point.**

> **This is why a flocculator's paddles turn slowly — a tip speed of only 0.2 to 0.7 m/s — and why a flocculator that is stirred too vigorously produces a fine, slow-settling floc that looks like a coagulation failure.**

> **An operator diagnosing poor floc should therefore check the flocculator SPEED as well as the chemical dose, and reducing the speed is as likely to help as increasing the dose.**

**TAPERED FLOCCULATION IS THE REFINEMENT THAT FOLLOWS FROM ALL THIS, AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Early in the flocculator, the particles are SMALL and numerous** ← | **They are not fragile, and they need many collisions — so a HIGH G is appropriate** ← |
| **Later, the flocs are LARGE and delicate** ← | **They break easily, and need only gentle contact — so a LOW G is appropriate** ← |
| **So the flocculator is divided into compartments with DECREASING paddle speeds** ← | **Perhaps 50, 35 and 20 s⁻¹ in three stages** ← |
| **This grows the floc faster AND delivers it intact** ← | **Better than any single uniform G could achieve** ← |

> **Tapered flocculation is a genuinely elegant piece of process design: it recognises that the optimum condition CHANGES as the process proceeds, and it varies the condition to match rather than compromising on a single average.**

> **The same idea appears in the flow from the flocculator to the clarifier, which must be as gentle as the last flocculation stage — so the connecting channel is sized for a low velocity and the inlet to the clarifier is baffled rather than being a jet.**

> **A plant with beautifully tapered flocculation and a sharp bend or a pump between the flocculator and the clarifier has destroyed its floc on the way, and the clarifier will underperform for a reason that no examination of either unit would reveal.**

examTip.trick: **G is the collision RATE, t the time, so Gt is the total number of collisions.** Flocculation: G 20-75 s⁻¹ for 20-40 min, Gt 30,000-150,000.
examTip.trap: **Rapid mix uses G of 500-1,000 for 30-60 SECONDS** — an order of magnitude more shear for two orders less time. Opposite requirements, adjacent units.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shear both builds and BREAKS floc, so G has an optimum.** Hence TAPERED flocculation — high G early for small tough particles, low G later for large delicate ones.

questions.stem: A CLARIFLOCCULATOR is a treatment unit in which:
options: Flocculation and filtration are carried out in one structure
Coagulation and disinfection occur simultaneously
Flocculation takes place in a central compartment and sedimentation in a surrounding annular zone of the same circular tank
Sludge is thickened before disposal
questions.solution:
**FLOCCULATION takes place in a central compartment and SEDIMENTATION in a surrounding annular zone of the same circular tank** — saving land and the connecting channel between the two processes.

**Its arrangement:**

| Zone | Function |
|---|---|
| **The central CIRCULAR compartment, with a slow stirrer** ← | **FLOCCULATION — the water enters here and the floc is grown** ← |
| **The flow passes outward under a skirt into the ANNULUS** ← | **A gentle transfer with no channel, pump or bend** ← |
| **The surrounding annular zone** ← | **SEDIMENTATION — the flow moves slowly outward and upward while the floc settles** ← |
| **A peripheral launder collects the clarified water** ← | **Giving a very long weir length, which keeps the weir loading low** ← |
| **A rotating scraper on the floor** ← | **Moving the sludge to a central hopper for withdrawal** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW CONTAINS THE UNIT'S REAL ADVANTAGE AND IT IS NOT THE ONE USUALLY QUOTED: the transfer from flocculation to sedimentation is as gentle as it can possibly be.**

> **The land saving is real but modest; the process benefit is that the floc, having been grown carefully, is not then pumped, bent round a corner or dropped over a weir before it reaches the settling zone.**

> **It simply drifts outward under a skirt at a very low velocity, arriving intact.**

> **Given how easily floc is broken — the point that closes the flocculation question — that is a substantial advantage, and it is why a clariflocculator often outperforms separate units of the same nominal capacity.**

**THE CLARIFIER TYPES, FOR COMPARISON:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **HORIZONTAL FLOW rectangular tank** ← | **The simplest; long and narrow, with the flow from end to end and a scraper travelling along it** ← |
| **RADIAL FLOW circular tank** ← | **Inlet at the centre, flow outward and upward, collection at the periphery** ← |
| **CLARIFLOCCULATOR** ← | **Flocculation and clarification combined — this question** ← |
| **TUBE or PLATE settler** ← | **Inclined tubes or plates inserted into a tank, multiplying the effective settling area within the same footprint** ← |
| **SOLIDS CONTACT (upflow) clarifier** ← | **The incoming water is mixed with previously formed sludge, so the new floc has abundant nuclei to build on — a much faster and more robust process** ← |
| **DISSOLVED AIR FLOTATION (DAF)** ← | **The opposite approach: fine air bubbles attach to the floc and FLOAT it to the surface, where it is skimmed off — used where the floc is light, as with algae or coloured water** ← |

> **THE SOLIDS CONTACT PRINCIPLE IN THE FIFTH ROW IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING BECAUSE IT ADDRESSES A REAL WEAKNESS OF CONVENTIONAL TREATMENT: floc formation requires particles to find one another, and in a low-turbidity water there are few particles to find.**

> **A solids contact clarifier recirculates settled sludge back into the incoming water, so every incoming particle immediately meets an existing floc to attach to.**

> **This makes the process far less sensitive to raw water turbidity, and it means the unit performs well on a clear water where a conventional plant would struggle to form any floc at all.**

> **It is the same reasoning that leads to adding bentonite clay to a very clear water — supply the nuclei that the water lacks — achieved by recycling rather than by purchase.**

> **THE DAF OPTION IN THE LAST ROW DESERVES A NOTE BECAUSE IT INVERTS THE WHOLE PROBLEM: where the floc is nearly neutrally buoyant, settling it is slow and difficult, and floating it is easy.**

> **Algal floc and the floc from a highly coloured upland water are both of this kind, so DAF is the process of choice for them and can be several times faster than sedimentation.**

> **Its cost is the energy needed to saturate the recycle stream with air under pressure, which is significant — so it is used where sedimentation performs badly rather than as a general alternative.**

> **The general lesson worth carrying is that the choice of clarifier follows from the FLOC's character, which follows from the raw water's character: heavy silt-based floc settles readily, light algal or colour-based floc does not, and a unit chosen without regard to which is present may be the wrong machine entirely.**

examTip.trick: **Flocculation in a central compartment, sedimentation in the surrounding annulus** of one circular tank.
examTip.trap: **The real benefit is the GENTLE transfer** — no channel, pump or weir between the two, so the floc arrives intact. The land saving is secondary.
examTip.mnemonic: **Solids contact clarifiers recycle sludge to supply the NUCLEI a clear water lacks; DAF FLOATS a light floc instead of settling it.** Choose by the floc's character.

questions.stem: A RAPID GRAVITY SAND FILTER is operated at a filtration rate of the order of:
options: 2 to 5 m³ per m² per day
20 to 30 m³ per m² per day
1,000 m³ per m² per day
100 to 150 m³ per m² per day
questions.solution:
**100 to 150 m³ per m² per day** — that is, about 4 to 6 metres per hour.

**The two filter types compared:**

| Property | SLOW sand filter | RAPID sand filter |
|---|---|---|
| **Filtration rate** | **2 to 5 m³/m²/day** ← (option a) | **100 to 150 m³/m²/day — some 30 times faster** ← |
| **Effective sand size** | **0.2 to 0.3 mm — FINE** ← | **0.45 to 0.7 mm — COARSER** ← |
| **Bed depth** | **0.9 to 1.1 m** | **0.6 to 0.75 m** ← |
| **Pre-treatment needed** | **NONE, or plain sedimentation only** ← | **Coagulation, flocculation and clarification are ESSENTIAL** ← |
| **How it works** | **Biologically, through the SCHMUTZDECKE** ← | **Physically and by adsorption within the bed depth** ← |
| **Cleaning** | **SCRAPING the top 20 to 25 mm off, every few weeks to months** ← | **BACKWASHING with reversed flow, every 24 to 48 hours** ← |
| **Land required** | **Very LARGE** ← | **Small** ← |
| **Operating skill and chemicals** | **Little of either** ← | **Continuous chemical dosing and skilled operation** ← |
| **Bacterial removal** | **Excellent, 99 to 99.9 per cent** ← | **Good but less complete, so disinfection is essential** ← |

> **THE THIRTY-FOLD DIFFERENCE IN RATE IS THE HEADLINE, BUT THE FOURTH AND EIGHTH ROWS ARE WHAT ACTUALLY DECIDE WHICH TO BUILD, and the choice is a genuine one rather than a matter of modernity:**

| Situation | Choice |
|---|---|
| **A large town, expensive land, a reliable chemical supply, trained staff** ← | **RAPID sand filter** ← |
| **A small town or a rural scheme, land available, no chemical supply chain, minimal operator training** ← | **SLOW sand filter** ← |
| **A raw water of consistently LOW turbidity** ← | **Slow sand filter serves excellently** ← |
| **A raw water of high and variable turbidity** ← | **Slow sand filter CLOGS rapidly and becomes unmanageable; a rapid filter with proper pre-treatment is needed** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE LIMITATION THAT RULES OUT SLOW SAND FILTERS ON MOST HIMALAYAN RIVERS AND IT SHOULD BE ACKNOWLEDGED: a slow sand filter receiving 500 NTU water blinds within hours.**

> **It is a superb process for a clear or moderately turbid water and an unusable one for a monsoon-turbid river, because its cleaning cycle is measured in weeks and its clogging would be measured in hours.**

> **So the attraction of a chemical-free, low-skill process runs directly into the reality of the raw water, and the usual resolution is to precede it with a roughing filter or to draw from an infiltration gallery instead — which returns to the point made earlier about galleries doing much of a plant's work.**

**THE SCHMUTZDECKE IN THE FIFTH ROW IS THE SLOW SAND FILTER'S DISTINCTIVE FEATURE AND IT IS WORTH EXPLAINING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A biological MAT develops on the sand's surface over a week or two** ← | **Algae, bacteria, protozoa and their secretions** ← |
| **It removes organisms by PREDATION and by biological action, not merely by straining** ← | **Which is why its removal of bacteria is so much better than a rapid filter's** ← |
| **It takes time to RIPEN, so a newly cleaned filter must be run to waste for a day or two** ← | **The ripening period, during which its output is not yet fit** ← |
| **So the filter must never be allowed to dry out or be disinfected** ← | **Killing the schmutzdecke destroys the process** ← |
| **And its cleaning is by SCRAPING, not backwashing** ← | **Backwashing would destroy the mat that does the work** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE OPERATIONAL INSTRUCTION THAT MOST OFTEN GOES WRONG AND IT IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE TO ANYONE TRAINED ON RAPID FILTERS: a slow sand filter must NOT be chlorinated or allowed to dry.**

> **An operator who cleans and disinfects it as good hygiene would suggest has killed the biological population that provides most of its treatment, and the filter will then perform poorly for weeks until the mat re-establishes.**

> **This is a striking instance of a process whose active agent is alive, so that the maintenance regime appropriate to a physical filter is actively destructive — and it is why slow sand filtration needs its own operating instructions rather than an adaptation of conventional practice.**
tags: choice by raw water and resources

examTip.trick: **Rapid: 100-150 m³/m²/day (4-6 m/h). Slow: 2-5 m³/m²/day** — some 30 times slower, with finer sand and a deeper bed.
examTip.trap: **A slow sand filter needs NO chemicals but blinds on turbid water** — hours instead of weeks. So it suits a clear source and a low-skill setting, not a monsoon river.
examTip.mnemonic: **The SCHMUTZDECKE is alive** — never chlorinate or dry a slow sand filter, clean it by SCRAPING not backwashing, and run to waste while it ripens.

questions.stem: In a rapid gravity sand filter, BACKWASHING is carried out by:
options: Draining the filter and scraping the top layer of sand away
Reversing the flow upward through the bed at a rate high enough to expand (fluidise) it
Adding a chemical to dissolve the accumulated solids
Increasing the downward flow rate to flush the solids through the underdrain
questions.solution:
**By reversing the flow UPWARD through the bed at a rate high enough to EXPAND (fluidise) it**, so the accumulated solids are released and carried away to waste.

**The process:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The filter is taken off line and drained to just above the sand** ← | ← |
| **Clean water is admitted UPWARD through the underdrains** ← | **At 5 to 10 times the filtration rate — 0.3 to 0.9 m³/m²/min** ← |
| **The bed EXPANDS by 20 to 50 per cent and becomes FLUIDISED** ← | **The grains separate and move, rubbing against one another** ← |
| **The accumulated floc is dislodged and carried up with the wash water** ← | ← |
| **The dirty wash water overflows into wash water troughs and goes to waste** ← | ← |
| **Backwashing lasts 5 to 15 minutes and uses 2 to 5 per cent of the filter's output** ← | ← |
| **AIR SCOUR or surface wash is often used first, to break up the surface crust** ← | **Air agitation being much more effective than water alone at scrubbing the grains** ← |

> **THE FLUIDISATION IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE ESSENTIAL MECHANISM AND IT IS WORTH BEING PRECISE ABOUT: the bed must EXPAND, not merely have water passed up through it.**

> **Below the fluidisation velocity, the water flows up through a stationary bed and dislodges very little.**

> **At and above it, the drag on each grain exceeds its submerged weight, the grains lift and separate, and the bed behaves as a dense fluid in which the grains circulate and abrade one another.**

> **That abrasion is what actually cleans the sand, so a backwash rate below the fluidisation velocity fails almost entirely — and a filter backwashed at too low a rate progressively accumulates dirt however often it is washed.**

> **The required rate depends on the sand's size and the water's TEMPERATURE, since cold water is more viscous and fluidises the bed at a lower velocity — so a rate set in summer may over-expand the bed in winter and wash sand away.**

**THE AIR SCOUR IN THE LAST ROW IS THE MOST VALUABLE REFINEMENT AND ITS REASON IS MECHANICAL:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Water backwash alone lifts and separates the grains but does not scrub them hard** ← | **In a fluidised bed the grains move with the water, so their relative motion is modest** ← |
| **AIR bubbles rising through the bed create violent local agitation** ← | **Grains are thrown against one another, and the attached floc is scoured off** ← |
| **So air-plus-water backwash cleans far more thoroughly than water alone** ← | **And uses less water doing it** ← |
| **The sequence is usually air alone, then air and water, then water alone to carry the dirt away** ← | ← |

> **WHAT HAPPENS WHEN BACKWASHING IS INADEQUATE IS THE PRACTICAL SUBJECT WORTH KNOWING, AND IT PRODUCES A RECOGNISABLE SET OF FAULTS:**

| Fault | Cause and appearance |
|---|---|
| **MUD BALLS** ← | **Floc and sand agglomerating into lumps that sink into the bed; they grow, occupy the bed's volume and destroy its uniformity** ← |
| **Bed CRACKING and shrinkage** ← | **The dirty bed contracts and cracks, and the water then SHORT-CIRCUITS down the cracks with no filtration at all** ← |
| **AIR BINDING** ← | **Air released from solution accumulates in the bed, blocking part of it and increasing the head loss; it also blows the bed apart when backwashing starts** ← |
| **NEGATIVE HEAD** ← | **Where the head loss through the upper bed exceeds the water depth above it, the pressure in the bed falls below atmospheric — which releases dissolved air and causes air binding** ← |
| **Loss of MEDIA** ← | **From backwashing too vigorously, or from a damaged underdrain** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE MOST DANGEROUS FAULT BECAUSE IT IS INVISIBLE AND ITS EFFECT IS TOTAL: a cracked bed passes water through the cracks without filtering it at all.**

> **The filter's flow is unchanged and its head loss may even fall, so the instruments give no warning — while the filtrate turbidity rises and the cyst barrier is gone.**

> **THE FOURTH ROW EXPLAINS HOW TO PREVENT MUCH OF THIS BY DESIGN RATHER THAN OPERATION: keeping an adequate DEPTH OF WATER above the bed ensures the pressure within it stays above atmospheric even when the head loss is high, which prevents negative head and therefore prevents air binding.**

> **A filter box designed with a shallow water depth to save on wall height will develop negative head at quite modest head losses, and will then suffer air binding for the rest of its life — a permanent operating problem created by a small saving in construction.**

examTip.trick: **Reverse the flow upward fast enough to FLUIDISE the bed** — 5-10 times the filtration rate, expanding it 20-50 %, using 2-5 % of the output.
examTip.trap: **Below the fluidisation velocity the wash achieves almost nothing** — and the velocity depends on temperature, since cold water is more viscous.
examTip.mnemonic: **A CRACKED bed short-circuits with no filtration and no instrument warning.** And adequate water DEPTH above the bed prevents negative head, hence air binding.

questions.stem: When chlorine is added to water, the disinfecting species formed are HYPOCHLOROUS ACID (HOCl) and the HYPOCHLORITE ion (OCl⁻). Their relative proportions and effectiveness are such that:
options: HOCl is some 80 to 100 times more effective as a disinfectant than OCl⁻, and it predominates at low pH
OCl⁻ is the more effective, and it predominates below pH 7
Both are equally effective, so pH does not matter
Neither disinfects; the disinfection is done by the chloride ion
questions.solution:
**HOCl is some 80 to 100 times more effective as a disinfectant than OCl⁻, and it PREDOMINATES at LOW pH** — so disinfection is much more effective in slightly acidic water than in alkaline water.

**The equilibrium:**

| Reaction | Note |
|---|---|
| **Cl₂ + H₂O → HOCl + H⁺ + Cl⁻** ← | **Chlorine hydrolyses in water** ← |
| **HOCl ⇌ H⁺ + OCl⁻** ← | **And the hypochlorous acid then dissociates, reversibly** ← |
| **The equilibrium depends on pH, with a pK of about 7.5** ← | ← |

| pH | HOCl | OCl⁻ |
|---|---|---|
| **6.0** ← | **About 97 %** ← | **3 %** |
| **7.0** ← | **About 78 %** ← | **22 %** |
| **7.5** ← | **About 50 %** ← | **50 % — the crossover** ← |
| **8.0** ← | **About 22 %** ← | **78 %** |
| **9.0** ← | **About 3 %** ← | **97 %** ← |

> **THE PRACTICAL SIGNIFICANCE OF THIS TABLE IS LARGE AND IT IS OFTEN UNDERAPPRECIATED: raising the pH from 7 to 8 reduces the proportion of the effective species from 78 per cent to 22 per cent — a fall of more than three times in disinfecting power for the same measured chlorine residual.**

> **So a residual of 0.5 mg/l at pH 7 and a residual of 0.5 mg/l at pH 8.5 are not equivalent, and the second may be quite inadequate.**

> **The reason is that HOCl is a NEUTRAL molecule and OCl⁻ is negatively charged — and a bacterial cell wall is also negatively charged, so it repels the ion while the neutral molecule passes through it freely.**

> **That electrostatic explanation is worth knowing because it makes the eighty-fold difference intelligible rather than arbitrary: one species can get inside the cell and the other largely cannot.**

**THE CONSEQUENCES FOR PRACTICE:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Disinfection should be carried out at the LOWEST practicable pH** ← | **Below 7.5 if possible** ← |
| **A plant that softens with lime, raising the pH to 9 or more, must RECARBONATE before chlorinating** ← | **Or the disinfection will be ineffective at any reasonable dose** ← |
| **The chlorine RESIDUAL required rises with pH** ← | **Which is why standards sometimes specify a higher residual for higher-pH water** ← |
| **But pH cannot be lowered indefinitely** ← | **Corrosive water attacks the pipes and dissolves metals, so a pH of 6.5 to 8.5 is the practical range** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW STATES THE COMPETING CONSTRAINT AND IT IS A REAL ONE: low pH favours disinfection and promotes CORROSION.**

> **A water at pH 6.5 disinfects well and dissolves iron from the mains, copper from the plumbing and lead from any lead solder or service pipe present — which is a health hazard of its own.**

> **So the pH is a compromise between disinfection efficiency, corrosion control and the coagulation optimum, none of which coincide exactly — and a plant's pH regime is settled by weighing all three rather than optimising any one.**

**AND THE CT CONCEPT, WHICH IS HOW DISINFECTION IS ACTUALLY SPECIFIED:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Disinfection depends on the CONCENTRATION of disinfectant AND the CONTACT TIME** ← | **Their product, CT, in mg-min/l** ← |
| **A given organism requires a given CT for a given degree of inactivation** ← | **So a high concentration for a short time and a low concentration for a long time can be equivalent** ← |
| **The CT required depends on the ORGANISM, the pH and the TEMPERATURE** ← | **Rising steeply as the temperature falls** ← |
| **Bacteria need a very small CT; VIRUSES more; GIARDIA much more; CRYPTOSPORIDIUM more than chlorine can practically deliver** ← | ← |
| **So the CONTACT TANK's volume and its hydraulic efficiency are as important as the dose** ← | **A tank that short-circuits gives some of the water far less contact time than its nominal detention suggests** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE DESIGN POINT THAT FOLLOWS AND IT IS FREQUENTLY NEGLECTED: a chlorine contact tank must be designed for PLUG FLOW, with baffles, so that no parcel of water passes through faster than the design contact time.**

> **A simple rectangular tank without baffles can pass a substantial fraction of its flow through in a quarter of the nominal detention time, and that fraction receives a quarter of the intended CT.**

> **Since the whole point of disinfection is that ALL the water is treated, the worst-served fraction governs — and a nominal 30-minute contact tank delivering 8 minutes to a tenth of the flow has not disinfected that tenth.**

> **This is measured by a TRACER test and expressed as t₁₀ — the time by which the first 10 per cent of a tracer has emerged — and it is t₁₀ rather than the nominal detention that belongs in the CT calculation.**

examTip.trick: **HOCl is 80-100 times better and dominates at LOW pH** — 78 % at pH 7 but only 22 % at pH 8. The crossover is pH 7.5.
examTip.trap: **HOCl is neutral and OCl⁻ is negatively charged, like the cell wall** — so one enters the cell and the other is repelled. That is why the difference is so large.
examTip.mnemonic: **CT = concentration × contact TIME, and use t₁₀ not the nominal detention** — an unbaffled tank passes some water through in a quarter of the time, and that fraction governs.

questions.stem: SUPER-CHLORINATION followed by DE-CHLORINATION is practised when:
options: The water is very soft and low in alkalinity
The water contains excessive fluoride
A large chlorine dose is needed to overcome a heavy chlorine demand or to deal with a badly contaminated water
The water must be softened before distribution
questions.solution:
**When a LARGE chlorine dose is needed to overcome a heavy chlorine demand or to deal with a badly contaminated water** — the excess then being removed with sulphur dioxide or activated carbon so that the water is palatable.

**The forms of chlorination practice:**

| Practice | Meaning and purpose |
|---|---|
| **PLAIN chlorination** ← | **Chlorine as the ONLY treatment — used for a clear, uncontaminated groundwater or spring** ← |
| **PRE-chlorination** ← | **Applied BEFORE the other treatment units — controls algae in the clarifier, aids iron and manganese oxidation, and reduces the load on later disinfection** ← |
| **POST-chlorination** ← | **After filtration — the normal disinfection step, and the last barrier** ← |
| **DOUBLE chlorination** ← | **Both pre and post** ← |
| **BREAK-POINT chlorination** ← | **Dosing past the break-point so that a FREE residual is obtained** ← |
| **SUPER-chlorination** ← | **A dose far above the demand — 5 to 15 mg/l or more — for a heavily contaminated water, an epidemic, or a new or repaired main** ← |
| **DE-chlorination** ← | **Removing the excess afterwards, with sulphur dioxide, sodium bisulphite, sodium thiosulphate or activated carbon** ← |

> **THE PAIRING OF THE LAST TWO IS THE POINT OF THE QUESTION AND ITS LOGIC IS STRAIGHTFORWARD: the large dose is needed for the disinfection and is intolerable for the consumer.**

> **Chlorine is detectable by taste and smell at well below 1 mg/l, and at 5 mg/l the water is thoroughly unpalatable.**

> **An unpalatable supply is not merely a nuisance — consumers reject it and revert to a source they prefer, which may be a contaminated well or river.**

> **So a supply that is safe and undrinkable can be worse for public health than one that is slightly less safe and accepted, and the de-chlorination step exists to avoid that outcome.**

> **That is a genuine public health argument rather than a matter of customer service, and it is worth being able to state.**

**WHERE SUPER-CHLORINATION IS ACTUALLY USED:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **DISINFECTION of a new or repaired main before commissioning** ← | **Typically 20 to 50 mg/l held for 24 hours, then flushed to waste — the commonest use** ← |
| **During or after an epidemic, or after a flood** ← | **Where the contamination is known to be heavy** ← |
| **A source of high and variable chlorine demand** ← | **Where a normal dose would be entirely consumed** ← |
| **Shock dosing to control biofilm or nuisance organisms in a network** ← | ← |
| **Emergency treatment of a suspect source** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE ROUTINE APPLICATION AND IT IS AN IMPORTANT PROCEDURE THAT IS OFTEN SKIPPED: a newly laid main has been handled by workers, has had soil and water in it, and may contain rodents, debris and mud.**

> **Commissioning it without disinfection introduces all of that into the supply, and the consequences have included documented outbreaks.**

> **The procedure is to flush, then fill with a strong chlorine solution, hold it for 24 hours, test that a substantial residual remains — which proves the demand was satisfied — then flush thoroughly to waste and confirm by bacteriological sampling before connecting.**

> **The flushing to waste in the last step matters environmentally too: 50 mg/l of chlorine is toxic to fish and aquatic life, so a large volume of super-chlorinated water must be de-chlorinated or discharged where it can do no harm — a point regularly overlooked when a main is flushed into the nearest drain or stream.**

> **THE PRE-CHLORINATION IN THE SECOND ROW OF THE FIRST TABLE HAS BECOME LESS FAVOURED AND THE REASON IS WORTH KNOWING: applying chlorine to the RAW water, which is rich in natural organic matter, is exactly the condition that forms the most trihalomethanes and other disinfection by-products.**

> **Post-chlorination applies it to water from which most of the organic matter has already been removed, so far fewer by-products form.**

> **So the modern preference is to avoid pre-chlorination where possible, and to use potassium permanganate or a different oxidant where an early oxidation step is genuinely needed for algae or manganese — an example of a practice that was standard for decades being reconsidered as a new consequence came to light.**

examTip.trick: **A heavy dose for a heavy demand, then remove the excess** with sulphur dioxide, bisulphite or activated carbon so the water is drinkable.
examTip.trap: **A safe but unpalatable supply is rejected**, and consumers revert to a contaminated source they prefer — which can be worse for health. Hence de-chlorination.
examTip.mnemonic: **New and repaired mains need 20-50 mg/l for 24 hours before commissioning** — and the flush water is toxic to fish, so it cannot simply go into the nearest stream.

questions.stem: Compared with chlorination, disinfection by ULTRAVIOLET (UV) irradiation has the fundamental limitation that it:
options: Leaves no residual disinfectant
Is ineffective against bacteria
Produces large quantities of disinfection by-products
Raises the water's temperature substantially
questions.solution:
**It leaves NO RESIDUAL disinfectant**, so it gives no protection against contamination entering the distribution system downstream — and it is ineffective if the water is turbid or coloured, since the radiation cannot penetrate.

**The disinfectants compared:**

| Disinfectant | Residual? | Effective against Crypto? | By-products | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **CHLORINE (gas or hypochlorite)** ← | **YES — its great advantage** ← | **NO** ← | **THMs and HAAs** ← | **Cheap, simple, universally available** ← |
| **CHLORAMINE** ← | **Yes, and it is very PERSISTENT** ← | **No** | **Fewer THMs** | **Weak and slow, so it is used for the residual rather than for primary disinfection** ← |
| **CHLORINE DIOXIDE** ← | **Yes, briefly** | **Partly** | **Chlorite and chlorate** | **Effective over a wide pH range; must be generated on site** ← |
| **OZONE** ← | **NO — it decomposes in minutes** ← | **YES, effectively** ← | **BROMATE, where bromide is present** ← | **A very powerful oxidant, excellent for taste, odour and colour; expensive, generated on site** ← |
| **UV irradiation** ← | **NO** ← | **YES, very effectively and at low dose** ← | **NONE** ← | **Simple, no chemical, no by-products — this question** ← |

> **THE RESIDUAL COLUMN IS THE DECISIVE PRACTICAL DISTINCTION AND IT EXPLAINS WHY CHLORINE HAS NOT BEEN DISPLACED DESPITE ITS DRAWBACKS:**

> **A disinfectant that leaves no residual protects the water only at the point of treatment.**

> **From there onward the water travels through kilometres of pipe with thousands of joints, and any ingress is unopposed.**

> **So ozone and UV must be followed by a small chlorine or chloramine dose purely to establish a residual — which means they SUPPLEMENT chlorination rather than replacing it.**

> **Their value is in doing the primary disinfection better, particularly against chlorine-resistant organisms, while chlorine retains the distribution-system role for which nothing else serves.**

**UV's PARTICULAR STRENGTHS AND WEAKNESSES ARE WORTH SETTING OUT, SINCE IT IS INCREASINGLY USED:**

| Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|
| **Highly effective against CRYPTOSPORIDIUM and GIARDIA, which chlorine cannot touch** ← | **No residual whatever** ← |
| **NO chemicals to buy, store, handle or dose** ← | **Requires a RELIABLE electricity supply — it stops instantly in a power cut** ← |
| **NO by-products, no taste, no odour** ← | **Needs LOW turbidity: suspended particles shield organisms from the light** ← |
| **Very short contact time — seconds** ← | **The lamps FOUL and must be cleaned, and they lose output with age** ← |
| **Compact, and simple to operate** ← | **No easy way to verify performance in real time — the dose is inferred from lamp output and flow, not measured on the water** ← |
| **Does not alter the water's chemistry at all** ← | **Organisms can in principle REPAIR UV damage (photoreactivation), though this is not significant at proper doses** ← |

> **THE THIRD WEAKNESS IS THE ONE THAT LINKS BACK TO FILTRATION AND IT IS WORTH EMPHASISING: UV requires CLEAR water, because a shielded organism is an untreated organism.**

> **A particle a few tens of microns across can harbour bacteria in its interior where the radiation does not reach, and it passes through the reactor unharmed.**

> **So UV is a POLISHING disinfectant applied to filtered water, and it is quite unsuitable for a turbid source — which is the same requirement, for a different physical reason, that makes low filtered turbidity so important for chlorination.**

> **THE SECOND WEAKNESS IS THE DECISIVE ONE IN A NEPALI CONTEXT AND IT SHOULD BE STATED PLAINLY: UV stops the instant the power fails.**

> **There is no residual protection, no reservoir of disinfectant and no grace period — untreated water passes straight through a dark reactor, and unless an interlock closes a valve, it enters the supply.**

> **Chlorination, by contrast, continues to protect for hours through the residual already in the network even if the dosing stops.**

> **So in a system with unreliable power, UV requires a genuinely reliable standby supply and a fail-safe valve interlock, and without both it is less safe than the chlorination it might replace — which is a good illustration of why a technically superior process can be the wrong choice in a particular setting.**

examTip.trick: **No residual, and it needs CLEAR water** — a particle shields the organisms inside it. Excellent against cryptosporidium, which chlorine cannot touch.
examTip.trap: **Ozone and UV SUPPLEMENT chlorination rather than replacing it** — both need a small chlorine or chloramine dose afterwards purely for the distribution residual.
examTip.mnemonic: **UV stops the instant the power fails, with no grace period** — untreated water passes through a dark reactor. Chlorine's residual keeps protecting for hours.

questions.stem: In the LIME-SODA process of water softening, the SODA ASH (sodium carbonate) is required in addition to lime because:
options: It raises the pH further than lime can
It acts as a coagulant for the precipitated sludge
It removes the carbonate hardness that lime cannot
Lime alone removes only carbonate (temporary) hardness
questions.solution:
**LIME alone removes only CARBONATE (temporary) hardness** — the soda ash is needed to convert the NON-CARBONATE (permanent) hardness into a removable carbonate form.

**What each chemical does:**

| Chemical | Removes |
|---|---|
| **LIME, Ca(OH)₂** ← | **CARBONATE hardness — the bicarbonates of calcium and magnesium — by converting them to insoluble CaCO₃ and Mg(OH)₂, which precipitate** ← |
| **SODA ASH, Na₂CO₃** ← | **NON-CARBONATE hardness — the sulphates and chlorides — by supplying the CARBONATE ion that precipitates the calcium as CaCO₃, leaving sodium sulphate or chloride in solution** ← |

> **THE ESSENTIAL DIFFERENCE IS WHAT EACH CHEMICAL SUPPLIES AND IT IS WORTH SEEING CLEARLY:**

> **Bicarbonate hardness already CONTAINS the carbonate needed to precipitate it — it need only be converted from bicarbonate to carbonate, and adding lime (a base) does exactly that.**

> **Sulphate and chloride hardness contains NO carbonate at all, so no amount of lime will precipitate it — the carbonate ion must be brought in from outside, and soda ash brings it.**

> **Hence the division of labour: lime for what is already half-way there, soda ash for what is not.**

> **A useful check on any softening calculation is that the soda ash requirement should be proportional to the NON-carbonate hardness alone — if a calculation shows soda ash needed for a water with no permanent hardness, something has gone wrong.**

**THE PRACTICAL FEATURES OF THE PROCESS:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **The process is carried out at a HIGH pH — 9.5 to 10.5, or above 11 for magnesium removal** ← | **Magnesium hydroxide needs a higher pH than calcium carbonate to precipitate** ← |
| **EXCESS LIME is added where magnesium must be removed** ← | **The 'excess lime' process** ← |
| **The water leaves at a high pH and must be RECARBONATED** ← | **By bubbling CO₂ through it, to bring the pH down and to stabilise the remaining carbonate — otherwise scale deposits in the mains** ← |
| **A LARGE volume of sludge is produced** ← | **Calcium carbonate and magnesium hydroxide — its disposal is a substantial part of the process's cost** ← |
| **It cannot achieve zero hardness** ← | **A residual of 30 to 50 mg/l remains, limited by the solubility of the precipitates themselves** ← |
| **It also removes iron, manganese, some heavy metals and many bacteria** ← | **Incidental benefits of a high-pH precipitation process** ← |

> **THE RECARBONATION IN THE THIRD ROW IS NOT OPTIONAL AND ITS OMISSION HAS TWO CONSEQUENCES, both of which matter:**

> **First, water leaving at pH 10.5 will DEPOSIT the calcium carbonate that is still on the point of precipitating, and it does so in the distribution mains — scaling and eventually blocking them.**

> **Second, as the pH question established, chlorine at pH 10.5 is almost entirely present as the ineffective hypochlorite ion, so disinfection would fail.**

> **So recarbonation is required for the mains' sake and for the disinfection's, and a softening plant without it produces water that is neither stable nor safely disinfectable.**

**THE ALTERNATIVE PROCESS, FOR COMPARISON:**

| Process | Note |
|---|---|
| **LIME-SODA** ← | **Chemical precipitation; suited to LARGE plants and HIGH hardness; produces sludge; leaves 30-50 mg/l residual hardness** ← |
| **ION EXCHANGE (zeolite / resin)** ← | **Calcium and magnesium are exchanged for SODIUM on a resin bed; achieves essentially ZERO hardness; no sludge** ← |
| **Ion exchange's regeneration** ← | **The resin is regenerated with brine (common salt), producing a concentrated BRINE waste that must be disposed of** ← |
| **And it adds SODIUM to the water** ← | **Which matters for anyone on a low-sodium diet, and it makes the water unsuitable for irrigation** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS ARE THE PRICE OF ION EXCHANGE'S NEATNESS AND THEY DECIDE WHERE IT IS APPROPRIATE: it produces no sludge but does produce a brine, and a brine is harder to dispose of than a sludge.**

> **A calcium carbonate sludge is inert and can be landfilled or even used; a concentrated sodium chloride brine cannot be put anywhere without harming soil, groundwater or a watercourse — the same disposal difficulty met with reverse osmosis reject.**

> **And the sodium it adds is a genuine consideration: softening a hard water by ion exchange can raise its sodium substantially, which is why whole-house softening is often applied only to the hot water supply and the drinking tap left hard.**

> **So the two processes are not simply large-scale and small-scale versions of the same thing: they leave different residues, produce different treated waters, and suit different circumstances.**

examTip.trick: **Lime handles CARBONATE hardness, which already contains its own carbonate; soda ash SUPPLIES carbonate for the sulphates and chlorides.**
examTip.trap: **Recarbonation is essential** — otherwise the water scales the mains, and at pH 10.5 chlorine is nearly all the ineffective hypochlorite ion.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lime-soda leaves a SLUDGE; ion exchange leaves a BRINE and adds SODIUM.** A brine is harder to dispose of than a sludge, which is why the choice is not just about scale.

questions.stem: POWDERED or GRANULAR ACTIVATED CARBON is used in water treatment principally to remove:
options: Suspended solids and turbidity
Taste, odour, colour
Dissolved calcium and magnesium hardness
Bacteria and viruses
questions.solution:
**TASTE, ODOUR, COLOUR, and dissolved ORGANIC compounds including pesticides and algal toxins** — by ADSORPTION onto its very large internal surface area.

**How it works:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Activated carbon is made by charring and then activating a carbonaceous material** ← | **Coconut shell, coal, wood or lignite** ← |
| **The activation creates an enormous internal PORE structure** ← | **A surface area of 500 to 1,500 m² per GRAM — a handful has the area of a football pitch** ← |
| **Dissolved organic molecules ADSORB onto that surface** ← | **Held by van der Waals forces — a physical process, not a chemical reaction** ← |
| **It is therefore effective against DISSOLVED organics, which no filter can remove** ← | **And ineffective against dissolved inorganic salts, which do not adsorb** ← |
| **The carbon eventually SATURATES and must be replaced or reactivated** ← | **Its capacity is finite, and once exhausted it does nothing** ← |

> **THE SURFACE AREA FIGURE IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE WHOLE BASIS OF THE MATERIAL AND IT IS WORTH APPRECIATING: adsorption is a surface phenomenon, so capacity is proportional to area.**

> **An ordinary solid's external surface is negligible for this purpose; activated carbon's internal surface is thousands of times greater than its external one, which is what makes the process practicable at all.**

> **The pores must also be of the right SIZE — large enough for the target molecule to enter and small enough to hold it strongly — which is why carbons are made from different feedstocks for different duties, and why a carbon that performs well on one contaminant may perform poorly on another.**

**THE TWO FORMS AND WHEN EACH IS USED:**

| Form | Application |
|---|---|
| **PAC — POWDERED activated carbon** ← | **Dosed into the water as a slurry and removed with the floc in the clarifier; used INTERMITTENTLY, for a seasonal taste and odour episode or an accidental spill** ← |
| **GAC — GRANULAR activated carbon** ← | **A fixed bed through which the water passes, often replacing the sand in a filter or as a separate contactor; used CONTINUOUSLY where the problem is permanent** ← |

> **THE CHOICE BETWEEN THEM TURNS ON WHETHER THE PROBLEM IS OCCASIONAL OR CONSTANT, AND THAT IS A USEFUL WAY TO SEE IT:**

> **PAC requires no capital works — it can be dosed into an existing plant with a slurry feeder — but its carbon is used once and discarded with the sludge, so it is expensive per kilogram of contaminant removed.**

> **GAC requires a bed, vessels and a regeneration or replacement arrangement, but its carbon can be REACTIVATED thermally and reused many times, so it is much cheaper in continuous service.**

> **A plant facing algal taste and odour for six weeks a year will use PAC; one treating a permanently contaminated source will install GAC.**

> **This is a good illustration of the general principle that a treatment's cost structure — capital against consumable — should be matched to the duration of the problem, and that the cheaper process in continuous use may be the dearer one for an occasional need.**

**A FEATURE OF GAC BEDS WORTH KNOWING, BECAUSE IT IS BOTH A BENEFIT AND A HAZARD:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A GAC bed in continuous service develops a BIOLOGICAL population** ← | **Bacteria colonise the carbon, feeding on the adsorbed organics** ← |
| **This BIOLOGICALLY ACTIVE CARBON extends the bed's life considerably** ← | **The bacteria consume the organics, continuously regenerating the adsorption sites — so the bed lasts far longer than its adsorptive capacity alone would allow** ← |
