| **Which is a genuine and valuable effect, and it is exploited deliberately** ← | **Particularly when preceded by ozone, which breaks organics into more biodegradable fragments** ← |
| **But the bed is then a bacterial REACTOR sitting in the treatment train** ← | **And it sheds bacteria into the water leaving it** ← |
| **So a GAC bed must be followed by DISINFECTION, and must never be the last unit** ← | ← |

> **The last row is the practical rule that follows and it is an important one: activated carbon is a poor place for the treatment train to end.**

> **It removes what chlorine cannot deal with and it introduces bacteria that chlorine must then deal with — so the two are complementary in a specific order, carbon before chlorine.**

> **Reversing them wastes the chlorine on the carbon, which adsorbs and destroys it, and leaves the bacteria from the bed untreated: a sequence error that defeats both units at once.**

examTip.trick: **Adsorption of DISSOLVED organics — taste, odour, colour, pesticides, algal toxins** — on 500-1,500 m² per gram of internal surface.
examTip.trap: **PAC for occasional problems (dosed and discarded), GAC for continuous ones (fixed bed, reactivated and reused).** Match the cost structure to the duration.
examTip.mnemonic: **A GAC bed becomes a bacterial reactor and sheds organisms** — so carbon BEFORE chlorine, never after. Reversed, the carbon destroys the chlorine and the bacteria pass.

questions.stem: Among the pressure-driven membrane processes, the one capable of removing DISSOLVED SALTS and therefore of desalinating water is:
options: Microfiltration (MF)
Ultrafiltration (UF)
Reverse osmosis (RO)
Nanofiltration (NF), which removes salts completely
questions.solution:
**REVERSE OSMOSIS (RO).**

**The membrane processes, in order of decreasing pore size:**

| Process | Removes | Typical pressure |
|---|---|---|
| **MICROFILTRATION (MF)** ← | **Suspended solids, BACTERIA, protozoan CYSTS — about 0.1 micron** ← | **0.5 to 2 bar** ← |
| **ULTRAFILTRATION (UF)** ← | **All the above plus VIRUSES and large organic molecules — about 0.01 micron** ← | **1 to 5 bar** ← |
| **NANOFILTRATION (NF)** ← | **All the above plus HARDNESS and larger dissolved organics — but it passes monovalent salts substantially, so it is a 'softening membrane' rather than a desalinating one** ← (which is why option d overstates it) | **5 to 15 bar** ← |
| **REVERSE OSMOSIS (RO)** ← | **Essentially EVERYTHING, including monovalent dissolved salts — the only one that desalinates** ← | **15 to 80 bar** ← |

> **THE PRESSURE COLUMN TELLS THE ECONOMIC STORY OF THIS TABLE AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL THING IN IT: the finer the separation, the higher the pressure and the greater the energy cost.**

> **MF and UF are essentially very fine filters, operating at pressures comparable with a domestic supply.**

> **RO must overcome the water's OSMOTIC pressure as well as the flow resistance, and osmotic pressure rises with salinity — so desalinating seawater requires 55 to 80 bar while brackish water needs 15 to 25.**

> **That is why RO's energy cost is an order of magnitude above UF's, and why RO is used only where dissolved salts genuinely must be removed rather than as a general-purpose treatment.**

**WHY 'REVERSE' OSMOSIS IS SO CALLED, WHICH MAKES THE PROCESS INTELLIGIBLE:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **In natural OSMOSIS, water moves through a semi-permeable membrane from the DILUTE side to the CONCENTRATED side** ← | **Driven by the difference in chemical potential — the osmotic pressure** ← |
| **It continues until the pressure difference balances the osmotic pressure** ← | ← |
| **REVERSE osmosis applies a pressure GREATER than the osmotic pressure to the concentrated side** ← | **Forcing water the other way — from concentrated to dilute** ← |
| **So pure water is pushed OUT of the salty water, leaving the salt behind** ← | **Which is the reverse of the natural direction, hence the name** ← |

> **THAT FRAMING ALSO EXPLAINS RO's TWO INHERENT LIMITATIONS, both of which are important:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **A concentrated REJECT (brine) stream is produced** ← | **Typically 15 to 50 per cent of the feed, containing all the removed salt in a smaller volume** ← |
| **Its disposal is genuinely difficult** ← | **It cannot go into a watercourse, onto land or into a sewer without consequence — the same problem as ion exchange brine and reservoir flushing effluent** ← |
| **The membrane FOULS and SCALES** ← | **Requiring careful pre-treatment, antiscalant dosing and periodic chemical cleaning** ← |
| **Recovery cannot approach 100 per cent** ← | **As water is removed, the remaining brine becomes more concentrated and its osmotic pressure rises, so the last of the water is the hardest to extract** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE FUNDAMENTAL LIMIT AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING RATHER THAN TREATING AS A PRACTICAL SHORTCOMING: the process gets harder as it proceeds.**

> **Recovering 50 per cent of the feed doubles the concentration of what remains and therefore roughly doubles its osmotic pressure; recovering 90 per cent multiplies it tenfold.**

> **So there is always a point beyond which the energy required exceeds what any plant would spend, and a reject stream is unavoidable.**

> **THE PRACTICAL CONCLUSION FOR WATER SUPPLY IS WORTH STATING, BECAUSE RO IS OFTEN PROPOSED WHERE IT IS NOT APPROPRIATE: RO removes everything, including the calcium and magnesium that are beneficial, and produces a water so pure that it is CORROSIVE and flat-tasting.**

> **RO permeate must therefore be remineralised or blended with a proportion of the feed before distribution, or it will attack the pipes and the consumers will dislike it.**

> **And it is a wholly disproportionate response to a problem that a simpler process would solve — the point made about iron removal — so the question to ask of any RO proposal is which specific dissolved constituent requires it, and whether that constituent could be dealt with another way or the source changed instead.**

examTip.trick: **MF: bacteria and cysts. UF: plus viruses. NF: plus hardness. RO: plus dissolved SALTS** — the only desalinating process.
examTip.trap: **NF passes monovalent salts substantially** — it is a softening membrane, not a desalinating one. And the pressure rises from 1 bar to 80 across the range.
examTip.mnemonic: **Recovery gets harder as it proceeds** — removing half the water doubles the brine's osmotic pressure. And RO permeate is CORROSIVE, so it must be remineralised or blended.

questions.stem: The SLUDGE produced by a conventional water treatment plant consists principally of:
options: The metal hydroxide floc from the coagulant together with the silt and organic matter removed from the raw water
Sewage solids
Pure calcium carbonate
Spent activated carbon only
questions.solution:
**The METAL HYDROXIDE floc from the coagulant together with the silt and organic matter removed from the raw water** — a bulky, gelatinous, difficult-to-dewater material whose disposal is a substantial and often neglected part of the plant's design.

**Where the sludge comes from and what it contains:**

| Source | Contribution |
|---|---|
| **CLARIFIER sludge** ← | **The great majority — aluminium or ferric hydroxide floc plus the raw water's silt, clay and organic matter** ← |
| **FILTER BACKWASH water** ← | **A large VOLUME of very dilute solids — 2 to 5 per cent of the plant's throughput** ← |
| **Softening sludge, where lime softening is practised** ← | **Calcium carbonate and magnesium hydroxide — much easier to handle, being crystalline** ← |
| **Spent activated carbon, where PAC is used** ← | **Mixed in with the clarifier sludge** ← |

> **THE ALUM SLUDGE IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE PROBLEMATIC MATERIAL AND ITS DIFFICULTY IS WORTH EXPLAINING, since it is not obvious:**

| Property | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **It is GELATINOUS — an amorphous hydroxide gel** ← | **It holds water within its structure rather than merely between its particles** ← |
| **So it dewaters very POORLY** ← | **A clarifier sludge at 1 per cent solids may reach only 15 to 25 per cent after mechanical dewatering** ← |
| **It is THIXOTROPIC** ← | **Apparently solid at rest and liquefying when disturbed, which makes it awkward to handle and to place** ← |
| **Its volume is LARGE relative to the water treated** ← | **Perhaps 0.5 to 2 per cent of the plant's throughput by volume** ← |
| **And the coagulant dose adds to it** ← | **Every kilogram of alum produces roughly half a kilogram of dry solids, on top of the raw water's own solids** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE CENTRAL DIFFICULTY AND IT DISTINGUISHES ALUM SLUDGE FROM ALMOST EVERYTHING ELSE: the water is bound within the gel and cannot be squeezed out.**

> **A crystalline sludge such as lime softening residue dewaters readily to 50 or 60 per cent solids, because its water sits between discrete particles and drains away.**

> **An alum floc's water is inside the floc's structure, and pressing it merely deforms the gel.**

> **So mechanical dewatering of alum sludge requires either a conditioning polymer, or freezing and thawing (which ruptures the gel structure), or simply a great deal of time in a drying bed — and the result is still a wet cake rather than a dry solid.**

**THE DISPOSAL OPTIONS, IN ROUGH ORDER OF FREQUENCY IN PRACTICE:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Discharge to a WATERCOURSE** ← | **Common, cheap, and increasingly unacceptable — it returns the removed solids to the river, smothers the bed and raises the turbidity downstream** ← |
| **SLUDGE LAGOONS or DRYING BEDS** ← | **The usual practical answer for a small or medium plant; large land requirement, and periodic desludging** ← |
| **Mechanical dewatering — centrifuge, filter press, belt press** ← | **For large plants where land is unavailable; needs polymer conditioning** ← |
| **Discharge to a SEWER, for treatment at the wastewater works** ← | **Convenient where a sewer exists with capacity, though the inert solids pass straight through and burden that plant's own sludge handling** ← |
| **LANDFILL or land application of the dewatered cake** ← | ← |
| **Beneficial reuse — brick making, cement manufacture, soil conditioner** ← | **Attractive in principle and limited in practice by the material's variability** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS WHAT MOST PLANTS ACTUALLY DO AND IT DESERVES A CLEAR STATEMENT OF THE OBJECTION: discharging clarifier sludge and backwash water to the river returns to it, in a concentrated slug, the material the plant was built to remove.**

> **The effect is worst in the dry season, when the river's flow is least and the discharge's proportion greatest — and it is precisely then that downstream users are most dependent on the river.**

> **It also returns the coagulant's aluminium, which is not naturally present in that form and is toxic to fish at quite low concentrations.**

> **THE PRACTICAL POINT FOR A DESIGNER IS THE ONE IN THE ANSWER ITSELF AND IT IS WORTH TAKING SERIOUSLY: sludge handling is a substantial part of a treatment plant and is regularly omitted from the design.**

> **A plant built without sludge facilities will discharge to the nearest watercourse because there is nowhere else for the material to go, and retrofitting lagoons requires land that was not acquired.**

> **So the land for sludge handling must be identified and acquired with the plant's own site, at the outset — and a feasibility study that costs the treatment units and omits the sludge works has understated both the cost and the land requirement of the scheme.**

examTip.trick: **Metal hydroxide floc plus the raw water's silt and organics** — bulky, gelatinous and very hard to dewater.
examTip.trap: **The water is bound INSIDE the gel, not between particles** — so pressing deforms it rather than draining it. 1 % solids reaches only 15-25 % after dewatering.
examTip.mnemonic: **Acquire the land for sludge handling with the plant's own site** — omitted, the plant discharges to the river, worst in the dry season when the river can least take it.

questions.stem: SODIS (solar water disinfection), as promoted for household use in Nepal and elsewhere, works by:
options: Boiling the water using a solar concentrator
Filtering the water through a solar-powered membrane
Exposing clear water in transparent PET bottles to full sunlight for about 6 hours
Adding a solar-activated chemical disinfectant
questions.solution:
**Exposing clear water in transparent PET bottles to full sunlight for about 6 hours**, the combined UV-A radiation and heat inactivating the pathogens.

**The method:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Fill clear PET plastic bottles, of 2 litres or less, with the water** ← | **Small bottles, so the light penetrates throughout** ← |
| **The water must be reasonably CLEAR — below about 30 NTU** ← | **Turbid water must be filtered or allowed to settle first, since particles shield the organisms** ← |
| **Shake the bottle three-quarters full to AERATE it, then fill completely** ← | **Oxygen assists the photochemical inactivation** ← |
| **Lay the bottles on a reflective or dark surface in FULL sunlight for 6 hours** ← | **Or for 2 consecutive days if the sky is more than half clouded** ← |
| **The combined UV-A and the temperature rise inactivate bacteria, viruses and protozoa** ← | ← |
| **Drink from the bottle, and do not store the water long** ← | **There is NO residual, so recontamination is possible** ← |

> **THE COMBINATION OF TWO MECHANISMS IN THE FIFTH ROW IS WHY THE METHOD WORKS AT ALL WITH SO LITTLE ENERGY, AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING: neither the UV-A nor the heat alone would be sufficient at these levels, and together they are.**

> **UV-A is a much weaker germicidal radiation than the UV-C used in a lamp, and sunlight delivers it at a modest intensity.**

> **The water in a bottle in the sun reaches perhaps 40 to 50 °C, which is well below pasteurisation temperature.**

> **But the two act SYNERGISTICALLY: the radiation damages the organisms and the elevated temperature both accelerates that damage and impairs the cells' ability to repair it.**

> **So the combined effect is far greater than the sum, and six hours suffices where either alone would take far longer.**

**ITS PLACE AMONG HOUSEHOLD WATER TREATMENT OPTIONS:**

| Method | Advantages | Limitations |
|---|---|---|
| **BOILING** ← | **Completely reliable, familiar, needs no equipment** ← | **Consumes a great deal of FUEL — which is expensive, causes indoor air pollution, and drives deforestation** ← |
| **SODIS** ← | **Free, needs only bottles and sunlight, no chemicals, no skill** ← | **Needs clear water and sunshine; small batches; no residual; bottles degrade and must be replaced** ← |
| **CHLORINE tablets or solution** ← | **Reliable, leaves a RESIDUAL, small and portable** ← | **Requires a supply chain and correct dosing; taste objections; ineffective against cryptosporidium** ← |
| **Ceramic or membrane FILTER (candle filters)** ← | **Removes turbidity and protozoa; no consumables beyond cleaning** ← | **Does not reliably remove viruses; the filter can crack undetected; needs cleaning discipline** ← |
| **BIOSAND filter** ← | **Effective and locally makeable; also removes turbidity** ← | **Heavy, needs a ripening period, and requires consistent use** ← |

> **THE BOILING ROW'S LIMITATION IS THE ONE THAT MAKES ALL THE ALTERNATIVES WORTH PURSUING AND IT IS OFTEN UNDERSTATED: boiling a family's drinking water requires roughly a kilogram of firewood per day.**

> **In a hill household that is a real burden of collection, a real cost if the fuel is bought, and a real health hazard from the smoke — indoor air pollution from cooking fires being itself a major cause of respiratory illness.**

> **So the advice to 'just boil it' carries costs that fall on the household and are easily overlooked by whoever gives the advice, and a method that avoids the fuel is genuinely valuable rather than merely cheaper.**

> **THE LAST LIMITATION OF SODIS DESERVES ITS OWN EMPHASIS BECAUSE IT APPLIES TO EVERY HOUSEHOLD METHOD: treated water with no residual is easily recontaminated by the container, the ladle and the hands that reach into it.**

> **Studies of household treatment repeatedly find that water safe at the point of treatment is contaminated at the point of USE — so a narrow-necked, covered storage vessel with a tap is as important as the treatment itself.**

> **This is the household-scale version of the distribution-system argument for a chlorine residual, and it reaches the same conclusion: treating the water is only half the problem, and protecting it afterwards is the other half.**

examTip.trick: **Clear water in PET bottles, full sun for 6 hours** — UV-A and heat acting together. Below about 30 NTU, and aerate by shaking first.
examTip.trap: **Neither UV-A nor 45 °C alone would suffice — they act SYNERGISTICALLY**, the heat accelerating the radiation damage and blocking the cells' repair.
examTip.mnemonic: **Boiling costs about a kilogram of firewood a day**, plus smoke and collection — a real burden that 'just boil it' overlooks. And protect the water AFTER treatment: no residual.

questions.stem: In estimating the quantity of SANITARY SEWAGE for the design of a sewer, the flow is normally taken as:
options: The full water supply rate, since all the water supplied returns as sewage
About 70 to 80 per cent of the water supplied, plus an allowance for groundwater infiltration
Twice the water supply rate
The rainfall on the catchment area alone
questions.solution:
**About 70 to 80 PER CENT of the water supplied, plus an allowance for GROUNDWATER INFILTRATION** — the balance of the supply being lost to consumptive uses that never reach the sewer.

**Where the missing 20 to 30 per cent goes:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **Garden and lawn WATERING** ← | **Evaporates or infiltrates; never reaches a drain** ← |
| **Water incorporated in PRODUCTS, in industry** ← | ← |
| **Evaporation from cooling and from washing** ← | ← |
| **Street washing and public standposts** ← | **Much of which runs to a storm drain rather than a sewer** ← |
| **Distribution LOSSES, which leak into the ground before reaching a consumer at all** ← | **A large item, as the demand question established** ← |
| **Water consumed in cooking and drinking** ← | **A small quantity** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE LARGEST OF THESE IN A LEAKY SYSTEM AND IT PRODUCES AN AWKWARD ASYMMETRY WORTH NOTING: water lost from the distribution system never reaches a house and therefore never reaches a sewer.**

> **So a town with 40 per cent distribution losses generates far less sewage relative to its water production than the 80 per cent rule suggests.**

> **The correct basis is therefore 70 to 80 per cent of the water actually CONSUMED — that is, delivered to premises — rather than of the water produced at the works, and confusing the two overestimates the sewage flow substantially.**

**THE INFILTRATION ALLOWANCE, WHICH IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE ANSWER:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Sewers are laid BELOW the water table in many places** ← | **And a sewer, unlike a water main, is not under internal pressure** ← |
| **So groundwater ENTERS through joints, cracks, defective manholes and unsealed connections** ← | **The pressure gradient is inward** ← |
| **Infiltration allowances of 5,000 to 50,000 litres per hectare per day are used, or per km of sewer per day** ← | **The range is wide because it depends entirely on the workmanship and the water table** ← |
| **INFLOW is a related but distinct problem** ← | **Storm water entering DIRECTLY through illegal roof and yard connections, or through manhole covers in a flooded street** ← |
| **Inflow is far more damaging than infiltration** ← | **Because it arrives suddenly and in enormous quantity, overwhelming the sewer and the treatment plant together** ← |

> **THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN INFILTRATION AND INFLOW IN THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS IS WORTH KEEPING CLEAR BECAUSE THE TWO CALL FOR DIFFERENT REMEDIES:**

> **INFILTRATION is groundwater seeping in continuously; it dilutes the sewage, wastes treatment capacity all year, and is remedied by repairing or relining the sewers.**

> **INFLOW is rainwater entering directly; it is intermittent, torrential, and remedied by disconnecting the illegal connections and sealing the covers.**

> **A separate sewerage system suffering heavy inflow behaves like a combined system during a storm — surcharging, overflowing and flooding basements — which defeats the whole purpose of having separated the two.**

> **And it is the commonest reason a nominally separate system fails to work as designed: the pipes were laid separately and the householders connected their roofs to whichever pipe was nearer.**

**THE PEAK FACTORS, WHICH COMPLETE THE ESTIMATE:**

| Flow | Note |
|---|---|
| **AVERAGE dry weather flow (DWF)** ← | **The basis of the calculation** ← |
| **PEAK flow, for sizing the sewer** ← | **2 to 3 times the average for a lateral, falling to about 1.5 times for a large trunk sewer** ← |
| **MINIMUM flow, for checking the self-cleansing velocity** ← | **About one-third to one-half of the average — and this is the case that must NOT be forgotten** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE CHECK THAT DISTINGUISHES SEWER DESIGN FROM WATER MAIN DESIGN AND IT IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN OMITTED: a sewer must work at its MINIMUM flow as well as its maximum.**

> **A water main sized for the peak simply runs slower at other times, which does no harm.**

> **A sewer running too slowly DEPOSITS its solids, and the deposit accumulates until the sewer blocks.**

> **So the sewer must be large enough to pass the peak AND steep enough to be self-cleansing at the minimum — two requirements that pull in opposite directions, since a larger pipe runs shallower and therefore slower at low flow.**

> **That tension is the central difficulty of sewer design, and it is why an over-sized sewer is a defective sewer rather than a conservative one.**

> **The peak factor falling with size in the second row is worth noting too: a lateral serves few properties whose peaks coincide, while a trunk sewer serves a whole town whose peaks are spread out in time by the travel time through the network — the same simultaneity reasoning met in water demand.**

examTip.trick: **70-80 % of the water CONSUMED, plus infiltration.** The rest goes to gardens, evaporation, products and distribution losses that never reach a house.
examTip.trap: **INFILTRATION is continuous groundwater seepage; INFLOW is storm water entering directly** through illegal roof connections. Inflow is far more damaging and defeats a separate system.
examTip.mnemonic: **A sewer must be checked at MINIMUM flow too** — too slow and it silts up. Peak sizing and minimum-flow velocity pull opposite ways, so an oversized sewer is a defective one.

questions.stem: A SEPARATE sewerage system is generally preferred to a COMBINED system principally because:
options: The treatment plant need be sized only for the sanitary flow
It requires a shorter total length of pipe
Storm water requires treatment as thorough as sewage does
Combined sewers cannot be laid in urban streets
questions.solution:
**Because the treatment plant need be sized only for the SANITARY flow, which is far smaller and far steadier than the combined storm flow** — so both the sewers and the works are smaller and there is no need for storm overflows discharging untreated sewage.

**The systems compared:**

| Aspect | SEPARATE | COMBINED |
|---|---|---|
| **Pipes** | **TWO — one for sewage, one for storm water** ← | **ONE, carrying both** ← |
| **Total pipe length and cost** | **GREATER — two systems to lay** ← (so option b favours combined) | **Less** ← |
| **Size of the sewage sewers** | **SMALL** ← | **LARGE — sized for the storm flow, which may be 50 to 100 times the sanitary flow** ← |
| **Treatment plant size** | **Sized for the sanitary flow only** ← | **Cannot be sized for the full storm flow — so overflows are essential** ← |
| **Storm OVERFLOWS discharging untreated sewage** | **NONE required** ← | **UNAVOIDABLE, and they discharge diluted raw sewage to a watercourse during every substantial storm** ← |
| **Self-cleansing in DRY weather** | **Achievable, the pipe being sized for the flow it carries** ← | **DIFFICULT — a large sewer carrying only the sanitary flow runs very shallow and silts up** ← |
| **Risk of misconnection** | **REAL — and it undermines the whole arrangement** ← | **Not applicable** ← |
| **Flooding of basements when surcharged** | **Storm water only** | **SEWAGE backs up into properties — far worse** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE DECISIVE ENVIRONMENTAL OBJECTION TO COMBINED SEWERS AND IT IS WORTH STATING CLEARLY: a combined system MUST overflow, by design.**

> **Its storm flow can be a hundred times its dry weather flow, and no treatment works could be built for that.**

> **So combined sewer overflows are provided, and every time it rains appreciably they discharge a mixture of storm water and raw sewage into the nearest watercourse.**

> **The sewage is diluted, which is the usual defence, but the discharge occurs precisely when the receiving water is turbid and its recreational and abstraction uses are already stressed — and the first flush of a storm carries the accumulated sewer deposits, so the early discharge is far stronger than the dilution suggests.**

> **A separate system has no such mechanism and needs none, which is why new systems are almost universally separate.**

**THE SIXTH ROW IS THE OPERATIONAL OBJECTION AND IT IS EQUALLY REAL:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A combined sewer is sized for the storm flow** ← | **So it may be 900 mm or 1,200 mm in diameter** ← |
| **In dry weather it carries only the sanitary flow** ← | **Perhaps a tenth of its capacity, so the depth of flow is a small fraction of the diameter** ← |
| **The velocity is then far below self-cleansing** ← | **And solids deposit along the invert** ← |
| **Those deposits are scoured out by the next storm** ← | **Producing the FIRST FLUSH phenomenon: the initial storm discharge is far more polluted than the sewage itself** ← |
| **So the deposition and the overflow problems compound one another** ← | ← |

> **THE SEVENTH ROW OF THE FIRST TABLE IS THE SEPARATE SYSTEM'S OWN WEAKNESS AND IT SHOULD NOT BE UNDERSTATED: two pipes in the street invite misconnection.**

> **A householder or a small builder connecting a new roof downpipe or a bathroom will connect to whichever pipe is convenient, and there is usually nothing to indicate which is which.**

> **A roof connected to the foul sewer imports storm water into a system with no capacity for it; a toilet connected to the storm drain discharges raw sewage into a watercourse continuously.**

> **The second is the more serious and it is entirely invisible until someone samples the storm outfall — which is why misconnection surveys, using dye or simply CCTV and observation, are a standard part of managing a separate system, and why the two pipes should be laid at clearly different levels and marked.**

> **THE PRACTICAL POSITION IN NEPAL IS WORTH NOTING AS A CLOSING POINT: most existing urban drainage is effectively combined, often consisting of open or covered street drains receiving both sewage and storm water.**

> **Converting to a separate system requires laying a new foul sewer throughout, which is expensive and disruptive — so the usual practical approach is an INTERCEPTOR: a foul sewer laid along the watercourse to intercept the dry weather flow from the existing drains and carry it to treatment, while allowing storm flows to overflow to the river as before.**

> **That is a compromise rather than a solution, and it accepts overflows in wet weather in exchange for treating the dry weather flow — but it treats the great majority of the annual pollution load for a fraction of the cost of full separation, which is a defensible allocation of limited resources.**

examTip.trick: **The works is sized for the sanitary flow alone, and no storm overflows are needed.** A combined system's storm flow can be 50-100 times its dry weather flow.
examTip.trap: **A combined system MUST overflow raw diluted sewage by design** — and the FIRST FLUSH scours the sewer's dry-weather deposits, so the early discharge is worse than the dilution implies.
examTip.mnemonic: **A separate system's weakness is MISCONNECTION** — a toilet on the storm drain discharges continuously and invisibly. And an INTERCEPTOR is the usual practical retrofit.

questions.stem: The SELF-CLEANSING VELOCITY in a sanitary sewer is normally specified as a minimum of about:
options: 0.6 to 0.8 m/s at the minimum flow
questions.solution:
**0.6 to 0.8 m/s at the minimum flow, with an upper limit of about 3 m/s** to avoid abrasion of the sewer's invert.

**The two limits and why each exists:**

| Limit | Value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **MINIMUM — self-cleansing velocity** ← | **0.6 m/s for a sanitary sewer, 0.8 m/s where grit is expected, and 0.9 to 1.0 m/s for a storm or combined sewer** ← | **Below it, the SOLIDS SETTLE and accumulate until the sewer blocks** ← |
| **MAXIMUM — non-scouring velocity** ← | **About 3 m/s, and up to 4 m/s for a well-made concrete or stoneware sewer** ← | **Above it, the GRIT in the flow ABRADES the invert, wearing a channel in it and eventually destroying the pipe** ← |

> **THE ABRASION MECHANISM IN THE SECOND ROW IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING BECAUSE IT IS OFTEN DISMISSED AS A THEORETICAL CONCERN AND IS NOT: sewage carries sand and grit, which is quartz and harder than concrete.**

> **At high velocity that grit acts as an abrasive slurry, and it acts continuously and always along the INVERT, where the flow is deepest and the grit travels.**

> **So a steep sewer wears a groove in its own bottom over years — the same phenomenon as turbine abrasion in a high-head hydropower plant, and for the same reason: wear rises steeply with velocity.**

> **A worn invert then leaks, admits roots, and eventually collapses, and it cannot be repaired without excavation or relining.**

> **This is why steep sewers in hilly towns need particular attention, and why drop manholes are used to take up level rather than allowing a sewer to run at an excessive gradient.**

**THE SIGNIFICANCE OF 'AT THE MINIMUM FLOW' IN THE ANSWER IS THE POINT THAT DISTINGUISHES A CORRECT DESIGN FROM AN INCORRECT ONE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A sewer's velocity depends on its GRADIENT and on the DEPTH of flow in it** ← | ← |
| **At low flow the depth is small, the hydraulic radius is small, and the velocity is LOW** ← | ← |
| **So a sewer that achieves 0.9 m/s when running half full may achieve only 0.4 m/s at its minimum night flow** ← | **And it will silt up every night** ← |
| **The self-cleansing check must therefore be made at the MINIMUM anticipated flow** ← | **Which for a new sewer serving a partly developed area may be a very small fraction of its design flow** ← |
| **This is why a sewer laid ahead of development silts up before the development arrives** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW DESCRIBES A COMMON AND FRUSTRATING SITUATION AND IT HAS NO WHOLLY SATISFACTORY ANSWER: a sewer sized for the ultimate development receives a small fraction of that flow for its first several years.**

> **It silts, it smells, it blocks, and it requires flushing repeatedly during the very period when nobody is yet paying for the service.**

> **The available responses are to lay the sewer STEEPER than the minimum gradient so that it is self-cleansing even at the early flow, to lay a smaller sewer initially and duplicate it later, or to accept a programme of flushing until the flow builds up.**

> **The first is usually the best where the topography allows, and it is one of the few cases where making a pipe steeper than necessary is positively desirable.**

**THE MINIMUM GRADIENTS THAT RESULT, WHICH ARE WORTH KNOWING AS FIGURES:**

| Sewer diameter | Approximate minimum gradient for self-cleansing |
|---|---|
| **150 mm** ← | **1 in 100 to 1 in 150** ← |
| **200 mm** | **1 in 150 to 1 in 200** ← |
| **250 mm** | **1 in 200** ← |
| **300 mm** | **1 in 250 to 1 in 300** ← |
| **600 mm** | **1 in 600 or flatter** ← |

> **The pattern is that LARGER sewers need FLATTER gradients, which is worth understanding rather than tabulating: a larger pipe has a larger hydraulic radius at the same proportional depth, so it achieves the same velocity on a gentler slope.**

> **A rough guide sometimes used is that the gradient in 1-in-N form can have N roughly equal to the diameter in millimetres — 1 in 150 for a 150 mm sewer, 1 in 300 for a 300 mm one — which is close enough for a preliminary layout and is easy to recall on site.**

An upper limit of about 3 m/s to avoid abrasion of the sewer's invert.

examTip.trick: **0.6-0.8 m/s minimum at MINIMUM flow; about 3 m/s maximum.** Below, solids deposit; above, grit abrades the invert.
examTip.trap: **The check is at MINIMUM flow, not design flow** — a sewer achieving 0.9 m/s half full may manage 0.4 m/s at night, and will silt every night.
examTip.mnemonic: **Larger sewers need flatter gradients** — roughly 1 in N where N is the diameter in mm. And lay a sewer steeper than necessary where development will be slow to arrive.

questions.stem: A 300 mm diameter sewer is laid at a gradient of 1 in 200. Taking Manning's n as 0.013, the velocity when the sewer is running FULL is about:
questions.solution:
**About 0.97 m/s.**

**The calculation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Hydraulic radius for a full circular pipe** ← | **R = A/P = (πD²/4)/(πD) = D/4 = 0.300/4 = 0.075 m** ← |
| **R^(2/3)** | **0.075^(2/3) = 0.1779** ← |
| **S^(1/2)** | **(1/200)^(1/2) = 0.0707** ← |
| **Manning: V = (1/n) R^(2/3) S^(1/2)** | **= (1/0.013) × 0.1779 × 0.0707** ← |
| **Evaluating** | **= 76.92 × 0.01258 = 0.968 m/s** ← |

> **So the full-bore velocity is about 0.97 m/s, which comfortably exceeds the self-cleansing minimum of 0.6 m/s.**

**The corresponding discharge, which usually follows:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Area** | **A = πD²/4 = π × 0.3²/4 = 0.0707 m²** ← |
| **Q = A V** | **= 0.0707 × 0.968 = 0.0684 m³/s** ← |
| **In litres per second** | **= 68.4 l/s** ← |

> **THE R = D/4 RESULT IN THE FIRST STEP IS WORTH COMMITTING TO MEMORY BECAUSE IT SAVES TIME AND IS EASY TO DERIVE: for a pipe running exactly full, the area is πD²/4 and the wetted perimeter is πD, so their ratio is D/4.**

> **The same result holds for a pipe running exactly HALF full — the area and the perimeter both halve, so the ratio is unchanged — which is a useful and slightly surprising fact.**

> **It means the velocity at half depth equals the velocity at full depth, since Manning's velocity depends only on R, n and S.**

> **And that leads directly to the most useful piece of knowledge about part-full sewers.**

**THE HYDRAULIC ELEMENTS OF A PART-FULL CIRCULAR SEWER, WHICH ARE GENUINELY COUNTER-INTUITIVE:**

| Depth ratio d/D | Velocity ratio v/V | Discharge ratio q/Q |
|---|---|---|
| **0.2** | **0.62** | **0.09** |
| **0.5 (half full)** ← | **1.00 — the SAME as full** ← | **0.50** |
| **0.8** ← | **1.14 — GREATER than full** ← | **0.98** |
| **0.94** ← | **1.14 — the MAXIMUM velocity** ← | **1.075 — the MAXIMUM discharge, GREATER than when full** ← |
| **1.0 (full)** | **1.00** | **1.00** |

> **THE FOURTH ROW CONTAINS THE RESULT THAT SURPRISES EVERYONE AND IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING: a circular sewer carries MORE than its full-bore discharge when running at about 94 per cent depth.**

> **The reason is that as the water rises through the last few per cent of the diameter, the added AREA is very small (the pipe is closing in at the top) while the added WETTED PERIMETER is relatively large.**

> **So the hydraulic radius DECREASES over that range, and with it the velocity — enough to more than offset the small gain in area.**

> **Hence both velocity and discharge peak just below full bore and then fall back.**

> **The practical consequence is that a sewer running just below full is at its most efficient, and that a sewer designed to run full at peak flow will in fact pass its peak at about 94 per cent depth with a small margin in hand — which is convenient, and is why sewers are conventionally designed to run about three-quarters to nine-tenths full at the peak rather than exactly full.**

> **Designing for exactly full is also avoided because a full pipe has no free surface, so it becomes a pressure conduit at the least excess flow, loses its ventilation, and can surcharge back into properties.**

examTip.trap: **R = D/4 for HALF full too** — area and perimeter both halve. So the velocity at half depth equals the velocity at full depth.
examTip.mnemonic: **Maximum discharge is at 0.94D, and it EXCEEDS the full-bore value** — the pipe closing in at the top adds perimeter faster than area, so R falls. Design for 0.75-0.9 full.

questions.stem: An EGG-SHAPED (ovoid) sewer section, narrow at the bottom and wider above, was traditionally used for COMBINED sewers because:
options: It is easier and cheaper to manufacture than a circular pipe
It resists external earth pressure better than any other shape
It provides a larger cross-sectional area for the same amount of material
The narrow invert keeps the depth of flow
questions.solution:
**The NARROW INVERT keeps the DEPTH of flow — and hence the velocity — higher at the small DRY WEATHER flow**, so the sewer remains self-cleansing despite being sized for a much larger storm flow.

**The problem it solves:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **A combined sewer must carry a storm flow perhaps 50 times its dry weather flow** ← | **So it is large** ← |
| **In a large CIRCULAR sewer, a small flow spreads across a wide invert** ← | **Giving a very shallow depth, a small hydraulic radius, and a low velocity** ← |
| **So it deposits its solids in dry weather — the difficulty identified earlier** ← | ← |
| **An EGG-SHAPED section has a narrow, deep invert** ← | **So the same small flow occupies a narrow channel and is DEEPER** ← |
| **A greater depth means a greater hydraulic radius and a higher velocity** ← | **So self-cleansing is maintained at low flow** ← |
| **While the wide upper portion provides the capacity for the storm flow** ← | ← |

> **THE SHAPE IS THEREFORE A DIRECT RESPONSE TO THE COMBINED SEWER'S CENTRAL DIFFICULTY, AND IT IS AN ELEGANT ONE: it varies its own hydraulic character with the depth of flow.**

> **At low flow it behaves like a small sewer, and at high flow like a large one — which is precisely what a combined sewer needs and what no single circular diameter can provide.**

> **This is the same design idea as tapered flocculation and multi-level intakes: where the required condition changes, vary the geometry to match rather than compromising on an average.**

**WHY EGG-SHAPED SEWERS ARE NO LONGER BUILT, WHICH IS WORTH KNOWING:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **They must be built IN SITU in brickwork or concrete, or specially moulded** ← | **A circular pipe is mass-produced and cheap** ← (which is why option a is inverted) |
| **They are structurally WEAKER than a circle under external pressure** ← | **A circle is the ideal shape for resisting uniform external load** ← (option b is inverted) |
| **They need careful construction and skilled bricklaying** ← | ← |
| **And SEPARATE systems have largely replaced combined ones** ← | **Removing the problem the shape existed to solve** ← |
| **Where a large combined sewer is still needed, a circular pipe with a CUNETTE is used instead** ← | **A small narrow channel formed in the invert, which achieves the same effect within a circular section** ← |

> **THE CUNETTE IN THE LAST ROW IS THE MODERN EQUIVALENT AND IT IS A NEAT SOLUTION: a small semicircular or V-shaped channel is formed in benching along the bottom of a large circular sewer.**

> **The dry weather flow runs in that channel, concentrated and therefore fast; the storm flow overtops it and uses the full section.**

> **So a mass-produced circular pipe is given the hydraulic behaviour of an egg-shaped one by a modest addition of concrete after laying, and the structural and manufacturing advantages of the circle are retained.**

**THE OTHER SEWER SECTIONS AND THEIR USES, FOR COMPLETENESS:**

| Section | Used for |
|---|---|
| **CIRCULAR** ← | **The great majority — mass produced, structurally efficient, hydraulically efficient when reasonably full** ← |
| **EGG-SHAPED (ovoid)** ← | **Old combined sewers — this question** ← |
| **HORSESHOE** ← | **Large sewers and tunnels, where headroom for access matters and the flat invert suits construction** ← |
| **RECTANGULAR (box)** ← | **Large storm drains, often cast in situ; simple to build and easy to inspect** ← |
| **U-shaped, and open channels** ← | **Storm drains in streets, where an open section can be cleaned by hand — the common arrangement in Nepali towns** ← |
| **SEMI-ELLIPTICAL** | **Very large sewers on good ground** ← |

> **The fifth row deserves a note in a Nepali context because it is what actually exists in most towns: an open or slab-covered rectangular street drain, carrying both storm water and sewage.**

> **Its hydraulic performance at low flow is poor for exactly the reason discussed — a wide flat invert — and it is cleaned by manual labour rather than by velocity.**

> **Providing even a rudimentary cunette in such drains, or simply giving them a proper longitudinal gradient and a defined invert, would greatly reduce the standing sewage and the associated nuisance — which is a modest and unglamorous intervention with a large effect on the immediate urban environment.**

examTip.trick: **A narrow invert keeps the small dry-weather flow DEEP and therefore fast** — self-cleansing in a sewer sized for a storm flow 50 times greater.
examTip.trap: **A circle is stronger and cheaper, not weaker and dearer** — options (a) and (b) are both inverted. The egg shape's only advantage is hydraulic.
examTip.mnemonic: **A CUNETTE gives a circular pipe the same behaviour** — a small channel formed in the invert, keeping the mass-produced pipe's structural advantages.

questions.stem: STONEWARE (salt-glazed vitrified clay) pipes have long been used for small sewers because they are:
options: Highly resistant to the acids and the sulphide attack found in sewage, and smooth-bored
Light, flexible and available in long coils
Immune to breakage under any handling
Suitable for large diameters and high external loads
questions.solution:
**Highly resistant to the ACIDS and the sulphide attack found in sewage, and smooth-bored** — though brittle, heavy and available only in short lengths.

**The materials for sewers, compared:**

| Material | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| **STONEWARE / vitrified clay** ← | **Excellent CHEMICAL resistance, smooth bore, durable indefinitely** ← | **BRITTLE, heavy, short lengths so many joints, small diameters only** ← |
| **RCC (reinforced concrete)** ← | **Strong, available in LARGE diameters, takes heavy external load** ← | **ATTACKED by sulphuric acid from sulphide — the crown corrosion problem — unless lined or made with sulphate-resisting cement** ← |
| **uPVC** ← | **Light, smooth, corrosion-proof, cheap, long lengths** ← | **Brittle at low temperature, UV-sensitive, deforms under load if not properly bedded** ← |
| **HDPE** ← | **Flexible, fusion-jointed, tolerant of ground movement** ← | **Needs careful bedding; more expensive** ← |
| **DUCTILE IRON** ← | **Very strong, takes heavy loads, long life** ← | **Corrodes internally in sewage unless lined; expensive** ← |
| **Brick** ← | **Historic large sewers, built in situ** ← | **Labour-intensive; the joints deteriorate** ← |
| **CAST IRON** | **For pressure mains and above-ground work** | **Corrodes** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW CONTAINS THE MOST IMPORTANT MATERIAL PROBLEM IN SEWERAGE AND IT IS WORTH SETTING OUT PROPERLY, since it destroys concrete sewers: CROWN CORROSION.**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Sewage in a slow or surcharged sewer goes ANAEROBIC** ← | **The dissolved oxygen is consumed** ← |
| **Sulphate-reducing bacteria in the slime layer produce HYDROGEN SULPHIDE** ← | **H₂S, which gives the characteristic rotten-egg smell** ← |
| **The H₂S escapes into the air space above the sewage** ← | ← |
| **On the moist CROWN of the sewer, aerobic Thiobacillus bacteria OXIDISE it to SULPHURIC ACID** ← | ← |
| **That acid attacks the cement in the concrete, converting it to gypsum** ← | **Which is soft and has no strength** ← |
| **The CROWN — not the invert — is progressively destroyed, and the sewer collapses** ← | **From the top down, which is why it is called crown corrosion** ← |

> **THE LOCATION OF THE DAMAGE IN THE LAST ROW IS THE COUNTER-INTUITIVE FEATURE AND IT IS THE POINT WORTH REMEMBERING: the sewer is destroyed ABOVE the water line, not below it.**

> **The invert, permanently submerged, is protected; the crown, moist and exposed to the gas, is attacked.**

> **So an inspection that looks at the invert finds nothing wrong, and the pipe fails by collapse of its top.**

> **And the whole mechanism requires TWO bacterial populations doing opposite things — one anaerobic in the sewage making sulphide, one aerobic on the crown making acid from it — which is why it occurs only in sewers with both a septic flow and a ventilated air space.**

**THE REMEDIES FOLLOW DIRECTLY FROM THE MECHANISM, WHICH IS WHY UNDERSTANDING IT MATTERS:**

| Remedy | Addresses |
|---|---|
| **Maintain SELF-CLEANSING velocity and avoid long detention** ← | **Prevents the sewage going septic in the first place — the root cause** ← |
| **VENTILATE the sewer well** ← | **Diluting and removing the H₂S before it can be oxidised on the crown** ← |
| **Avoid long RISING MAINS and surcharged reaches** ← | **Which are where sewage goes anaerobic** ← |
| **Use sulphate-resisting cement, or a PVC or epoxy LINING to the crown** ← | **Protecting the material rather than preventing the acid** ← |
| **Use vitrified clay or plastic pipe for small sewers** ← | **Immune to the acid entirely — which is this question's answer** ← |
| **Chemical dosing — lime, ferric salts or nitrate — in problem reaches** ← | **Suppressing sulphide formation** ← |

> **The first two rows are the preventive measures and they are much preferable to the last three, which are palliative: keeping the sewage fresh and the sewer ventilated deals with the cause, while lining the pipe merely resists the consequence.**

> **That distinction matters because the corrosive condition also produces the ODOUR nuisance and the safety hazard of H₂S in confined spaces — so preventing the sulphide addresses three problems at once, while a resistant pipe addresses only one.**

examTip.trick: **Chemical resistance and a smooth bore, but brittle, heavy and in short lengths** — hence small sewers only. Option (b) describes HDPE.
examTip.trap: **Crown corrosion destroys the sewer ABOVE the water line** — H₂S escapes to the air space and is oxidised to sulphuric acid on the moist crown. The submerged invert is fine.
examTip.mnemonic: **It needs TWO bacterial populations** — anaerobic in the sewage making sulphide, aerobic on the crown making acid. So keep the flow fresh and the sewer ventilated: cause, not consequence.

questions.stem: MANHOLES on a sewer are provided at every change of direction, gradient or diameter, and on straight reaches at intervals of about:
options: 10 to 15 m
30 to 45 m for small sewers
questions.solution:
**30 to 45 m for small sewers, increasing to 90 m or more for large ones that can be entered.**

**Where manholes are required:**

| Location | Reason |
|---|---|
| **At every CHANGE OF DIRECTION** ← | **A sewer is laid straight between manholes, so any bend needs one — the rodding and cleaning equipment cannot pass a bend** ← |
| **At every change of GRADIENT** ← | ← |
| **At every change of DIAMETER** ← | ← |
| **At every JUNCTION of two or more sewers** ← | ← |
| **At the HEAD of every sewer** ← | **For access and flushing** ← |
| **At intervals on straight reaches** ← | **30 to 45 m for pipes too small to enter, longer for large sewers** ← |

> **THE SPACING RULE IN THE LAST ROW IS GOVERNED BY THE CLEANING METHOD AND THAT IS THE KEY TO UNDERSTANDING IT: a small sewer is cleaned by rodding or jetting from a manhole, and the equipment has a limited reach.**

> **Traditional rodding reaches perhaps 30 m, so manholes at 30 to 45 m allow every point to be reached from one end or the other.**

> **A large sewer that a worker can enter is cleaned from within, so access points can be much further apart — the limit becoming ventilation and escape rather than reach.**

> **Modern high-pressure jetting reaches considerably further, so spacings have tended to increase where such equipment is available — which is a case of the maintenance TECHNOLOGY determining a design dimension.**

> **A town whose utility has only manual rodding equipment should not adopt a spacing suited to a jetting truck it does not own.**

**THE TYPES OF MANHOLE:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **SHALLOW manhole (inspection chamber)** ← | **Up to about 1 m deep; small, often at the head of a branch** ← |
| **NORMAL manhole** ← | **1 to 1.5 m deep, with a working chamber and a cover** ← |
| **DEEP manhole** ← | **Over 1.5 m; a working chamber with an access shaft above it, and step irons or a ladder** ← |
| **DROP manhole** ← | **Where an incoming sewer arrives much HIGHER than the outgoing one, the flow is dropped down a vertical shaft within or beside the manhole** ← |
| **JUNCTION or side-entrance manhole** | **Where sewers meet at an awkward angle or depth** ← |
| **FLUSHING manhole** | **At the head of a sewer, arranged to store water and release it as a flushing wave** ← |

> **THE DROP MANHOLE IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST IN A HILL TOWN AND ITS PURPOSE IS WORTH BEING CLEAR ABOUT: it takes up a large difference in level at one point, so that the sewer either side of it can be laid at a proper gradient.**

> **Without it, a sewer following steep ground would have to run at the ground's own slope, giving velocities far above the non-scouring limit and abrading its invert.**

> **So the drop manhole in sewerage plays exactly the part that the canal fall plays in irrigation and the break pressure tank plays in a water main: it concentrates a surplus of level at one designed structure so that the reaches between remain within their proper limits.**

> **Recognising those three as the same device in three subjects is worth doing, because the design consideration is identical in each — the ground falls faster than the conduit should, so the excess is taken up in steps.**

**A FEW DETAILS OF MANHOLE CONSTRUCTION THAT MATTER IN PRACTICE:**

| Detail | Note |
|---|---|
| **BENCHING — the floor is shaped to guide the flow smoothly from inlet to outlet** ← | **Sloped up to the sides so that solids are not left standing; a flat manhole floor collects deposits** ← |
| **The soffits (crowns) of the incoming and outgoing sewers are usually kept LEVEL** ← | **Rather than the inverts — so that a larger outgoing pipe does not cause a backwater** ← |
| **Covers must be sealed in flood-prone streets** ← | **Or storm water enters as INFLOW — the problem identified earlier** ← |
| **Step irons corrode away** ← | **And a worker's weight on a corroded step iron in a deep manhole is a genuine hazard** ← |
| **Every entry is a CONFINED SPACE entry** ← | **Requiring gas testing, ventilation, harness and a standby person — never a casual descent** ← |

> **The last row cannot be over-emphasised and it links to the sulphide discussion: a sewer manhole can contain hydrogen sulphide, methane, carbon dioxide and a deficiency of oxygen, in any combination.**

> **H₂S is particularly treacherous because it DEADENS the sense of smell at concentrations well below the lethal one — so a worker who notices the smell and then stops noticing it is in greater danger, not less.**

> **Deaths in sewers and manholes are depressingly regular in the region, and they very often involve a second person who entered to rescue the first — which is the confined space pattern noted under occupational safety, in its commonest single setting.**

examTip.trick: **30-45 m for small sewers, more for enterable ones** — the spacing is set by the CLEANING equipment's reach, plus manholes at every change of direction, gradient, diameter or junction.
examTip.trap: **A DROP manhole lets the sewer keep a proper gradient on steep ground** — the same device as a canal fall and a break pressure tank, concentrating surplus level at one point.
examTip.mnemonic: **Match soffits, not inverts**, so a larger outgoing pipe causes no backwater. And every manhole entry is a CONFINED SPACE entry — H₂S deadens the sense of smell before it kills.

questions.stem: An INVERTED SIPHON (depressed sewer) is used where a sewer must:
options: Be raised over an obstruction such as a bridge
Pass beneath an obstruction
Be flushed periodically by stored water
Discharge into a watercourse during storms
questions.solution:
**PASS BENEATH an obstruction — a stream, a subway or another pipeline** — the sewer dipping below it and running FULL under pressure, since gravity flow at the required gradient is impossible there.

**What it is and why it is troublesome:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **The sewer dips down, runs horizontally beneath the obstruction, and rises again** ← | ← |
| **In that reach it runs FULL and under pressure** ← | **So it is not, strictly, a siphon at all — the name is a misnomer of long standing** ← |
| **It has no free surface, so no ventilation and no self-cleansing action from a shallow fast flow** ← | ← |
| **Solids therefore tend to DEPOSIT in the low horizontal section** ← | **Which is the fundamental difficulty** ← |
| **And it cannot be rodded through in the ordinary way** ← | ← |

> **THE DEPOSITION PROBLEM IN THE FOURTH ROW IS WHAT MAKES THE DESIGN DIFFICULT AND IT IS ADDRESSED BY A CLEVER ARRANGEMENT WORTH KNOWING:**

| Provision | Note |
|---|---|
| **The siphon is built as TWO OR MORE PARALLEL BARRELS of different sizes** ← | **Not as a single large pipe** ← |
| **The SMALLEST barrel takes the dry weather flow alone** ← | **So the velocity in it is high enough to be self-cleansing even at low flow** ← |
| **As the flow increases, it spills over a weir in the inlet chamber into the SECOND barrel** ← | ← |
| **And at storm flow into the third** ← | ← |
| **So each barrel runs at a self-cleansing velocity when it runs at all** ← | **Which is the whole point of the arrangement** ← |

> **THE PRINCIPLE IN THE LAST ROW IS EXACTLY THAT OF THE ROTATIONAL CANAL OPERATION AND OF THE EGG-SHAPED SEWER, AND IT IS WORTH SEEING AS ONE IDEA: rather than run one large conduit slowly, run a small one properly and bring in others as needed.**

> **A single barrel sized for the storm flow would carry the dry weather flow at a hopelessly low velocity and would silt up solid.**

> **Dividing the duty between graded barrels means that whatever the flow, the water is moving fast enough to carry its solids — which is achieved purely by the inlet chamber's weir arrangement, with no moving parts and no operator.**

**THE OTHER PROVISIONS AN INVERTED SIPHON NEEDS:**

| Provision | Note |
|---|---|
| **INLET and OUTLET chambers, with penstocks or gates on each barrel** ← | **So any barrel can be isolated for cleaning while the others carry the flow** ← |
| **A means of CLEANING — usually a jetting or rodding access, or a facility to pass a 'pig'** ← | ← |
| **A means of DEWATERING the barrel being cleaned** ← | ← |
| **Barrels laid with a smooth profile and no sharp bends** ← | ← |
| **Adequate cover and protection where it passes beneath a stream** ← | **The stream's SCOUR must be considered — a siphon exposed by bed scour is vulnerable** ← |
| **Careful attention to the HEAD LOSS through it** ← | **Which must be available in the sewer's hydraulic profile, since the siphon consumes head rather than saving it** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE FAILURE MODE PARTICULAR TO A CROSSING BENEATH A HIMALAYAN STREAM AND IT DESERVES ATTENTION: the bed of such a stream can scour several metres in a single flood.**

> **A siphon laid a metre below the existing bed may be exposed, undermined and broken by one monsoon.**

> **So the founding depth must be below the ANTICIPATED SCOUR — computed as for a bridge foundation — and not merely below the present bed level, and the crossing is often protected with a concrete encasement or an apron.**

> **THE GENERAL PRACTICAL ADVICE ON INVERTED SIPHONS IS WORTH STATING AS A CLOSING POINT: avoid them if there is any alternative.**

> **They silt, they smell, they are difficult to clean, they consume head, they require a structure at each end, and they are a permanent maintenance liability.**

> **Where a small diversion of the alignment, a slightly deeper sewer, or a pumped crossing would avoid one, that is usually the better answer — and an alignment chosen to minimise the number of siphons is a better alignment even if it is longer.**

A stream, a subway or another pipeline — the sewer dipping below it and running FULL under pressure, since gravity flow at the required gradient is impossible there.

examTip.trick: **It dips BENEATH an obstruction and runs full under pressure** — not a siphon at all, despite the name. Option (a) is inverted.
examTip.trap: **Build it as TWO OR MORE graded barrels with weirs in the inlet chamber** — so the smallest carries the dry weather flow at a self-cleansing velocity. A single large barrel silts solid.
examTip.mnemonic: **Found it below the ANTICIPATED SCOUR, not the present bed** — a Himalayan stream can scour metres in one flood. And avoid siphons altogether where an alternative exists.

questions.stem: A sewer laid in a trench is bedded on granular material rather than directly on the trench bottom principally because the bedding:
options: Prevents groundwater from entering the sewer
Allows the sewer to be laid to a steeper gradient
Reduces the quantity of excavation required
Distributes the load over a wider arc of the pipe and provides uniform, continuous support
questions.solution:
**Because the bedding DISTRIBUTES the load over a wider arc of the pipe and provides UNIFORM, CONTINUOUS support** — so the pipe is not stressed by point contact on stones or by soft spots in the trench bottom.

**Why uniform support matters so much:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A pipe resting on a hard point carries its whole load at that point** ← | **A stone left in the trench bottom is a knife edge under a rigid pipe** ← |
| **A rigid pipe (clay, concrete) fails in BENDING or by cracking at such a point** ← | **Its strength depends entirely on being uniformly supported** ← |
| **A soft spot in the trench bottom leaves the pipe SPANNING between firmer points** ← | **Bending it as a beam, which it was never designed to be** ← |
| **Bedding replaces the variable trench bottom with a uniform, compactible layer** ← | **So the support is continuous and predictable** ← |
| **And the wider the arc of support, the LOWER the stress in the pipe wall** ← | **Which is the basis of the bedding CLASSES** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE QUANTITATIVE POINT AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE IT AFFECTS THE PIPE CLASS SPECIFIED:**

| Bedding class | Support | Load factor |
|---|---|---|
| **Class D — flat trench bottom, no bedding** ← | **Point or narrow support** ← | **1.1 — barely better than the worst case** ← |
| **Class C — shaped bedding, granular** | **Supported over about 90 degrees** | **1.5** ← |
| **Class B — granular bedding, well compacted around the lower part** ← | **Supported over about 120 to 180 degrees** ← | **1.9** ← |
| **Class A — concrete cradle or full surround** ← | **Supported over a wide arc and encased** ← | **2.2 to 3.4** ← |

> **THE LOAD FACTOR COLUMN MEANS THAT A PIPE ON CLASS B BEDDING CAN CARRY NEARLY TWICE THE EXTERNAL LOAD OF THE SAME PIPE ON A FLAT TRENCH BOTTOM, AND THAT IS AN IMPORTANT PRACTICAL LEVER: the pipe's strength can be effectively doubled by how it is laid rather than by buying a stronger pipe.**

> **Granular bedding is cheap, and a stronger class of pipe is not — so improving the bedding is usually the economical way to satisfy a heavy loading condition.**

> **Conversely a pipe of adequate class laid straight onto a rough trench bottom may fail under a load it was nominally strong enough for, and the failure will be attributed to the pipe rather than to the laying.**

**THE OTHER REQUIREMENTS OF SEWER LAYING, WHICH GO WITH THE BEDDING:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **The bedding must be brought up and COMPACTED around the lower half of the pipe** ← | **Merely placing the pipe on a layer of gravel achieves little — the material must be worked in under the haunches, which is the part most often skipped** ← |
| **The trench must be laid to the correct GRADIENT, checked with sight rails and a boning rod, or a laser** ← | **A sewer's gradient is the whole of its hydraulic design; a reversed fall between manholes is a permanent defect** ← |
| **The pipe must be laid UPHILL, socket facing upstream** ← | **So the spigot enters the socket in the direction of flow and the joint does not present a lip to the solids** ← |
| **Joints must be made properly, and TESTED before backfilling** ← | **After backfill nothing can be corrected** ← |
| **BACKFILL over the pipe must be placed in layers and compacted, but not by ramming directly on the pipe** ← | **A cushion of at least 300 mm before mechanical compaction passes over it** ← |
| **The trench must be kept DEWATERED while the pipe is laid and jointed** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW DESCRIBES THE SINGLE COMMONEST DEFICIENCY IN SEWER LAYING AND IT IS WORTH LOOKING FOR ON ANY SITE: the material under the pipe's HAUNCHES — the lower quadrants either side of the invert — must be worked in and compacted.**

> **A pipe simply lowered onto a bed of loose gravel bears on a narrow strip along its bottom, with voids to either side, and it has Class D support however good the material is.**

> **Achieving Class B requires someone to push and compact the bedding into those haunches with a tool, which is awkward, unrewarding and invisible once complete.**

> **So the specification's bedding class is achieved by a workman's diligence at a point where nobody will ever check, which is exactly the situation in which supervision matters most — and it is why sewer laying is inspected during the work rather than certified afterwards.**

examTip.trick: **Uniform continuous support over a wide arc** — a rigid pipe's strength depends on it, and a stone in the trench bottom is a knife edge.
examTip.trap: **Bedding class nearly DOUBLES the pipe's load capacity** (factor 1.1 for Class D against 1.9 for Class B) — improving the bedding is cheaper than buying a stronger pipe.
examTip.mnemonic: **Compact the bedding into the HAUNCHES** — a pipe lowered onto loose gravel has Class D support however good the gravel. And lay uphill, socket upstream.

questions.stem: A newly laid gravity sewer is tested for WATERTIGHTNESS before backfilling. The test is essential because leakage would:
options: Permit exfiltration of sewage into the ground
Reduce the sewer's structural strength
Cause the sewer to float in waterlogged ground
Increase the velocity in the sewer
questions.solution:
**Leakage would permit EXFILTRATION of sewage into the ground, contaminating groundwater and wells, and INFILTRATION of groundwater into the sewer**, wasting the capacity of the sewer and of the treatment works.

**The two directions of leakage and their separate consequences:**

| Direction | When | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **EXFILTRATION — sewage leaks OUT** ← | **When the sewer's water level is above the surrounding groundwater** ← | **Contaminates the soil and the groundwater; a serious hazard where shallow wells or springs are used nearby** ← |
| **INFILTRATION — groundwater leaks IN** ← | **When the water table is above the sewer** ← | **Dilutes the sewage, fills the sewer's capacity with clean water, and loads the treatment plant with flow it need never have received** ← |

> **BOTH DIRECTIONS ARE HARMFUL, WHICH IS WORTH NOTING BECAUSE THE TWO ARE SOMETIMES TREATED AS IF ONE CANCELLED THE OTHER: they occur at different times and places along the same sewer, and each does its own damage.**

> **A sewer above the water table exfiltrates; the same sewer downhill, below the water table, infiltrates.**

> **And in the monsoon, when the water table rises, a sewer that exfiltrated all summer begins to infiltrate — so the same defect produces contamination in one season and hydraulic overload in another.**

> **The exfiltration is the more serious in public health terms, particularly in a town where shallow dug wells and hand pumps are still used, since a leaking sewer and a shallow well in the same street is a direct and well-documented route for enteric disease.**

**THE TESTS, AND WHEN EACH IS USED:**

| Test | Method |
|---|---|
| **WATER test (hydrostatic)** ← | **The reach is plugged and filled with water to a head of about 1.5 m above the sewer's crown at the upper end; the LOSS over 30 minutes is measured and must not exceed a specified allowance** ← |
| **AIR test (low pressure)** ← | **The reach is plugged and pressurised with air to a small pressure (about 100 mm water gauge); the time for a specified PRESSURE DROP is measured** ← |
| **INFILTRATION test** ← | **On a completed sewer below the water table, the flow at the downstream manhole is measured with no upstream flow — anything arriving is infiltration** ← |
| **CCTV survey** ← | **Not a leakage test as such, but it locates defects, displaced joints, intruding connections and roots** ← |
| **MANDREL (ball) test** ← | **A ball or cylinder slightly smaller than the bore is drawn through, proving the pipe is not deformed and the line is true** ← |

> **THE AIR TEST IS FAVOURED IN PRACTICE FOR REASONS WORTH KNOWING, AND ALSO CARRIES A CAUTION:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is QUICK and needs no water** ← | **A great advantage where water is scarce or the reach is long** ← |
| **It is very SENSITIVE — it detects defects a water test would pass** ← | **Which is a virtue and occasionally a nuisance, since a damp pipe can fail it spuriously** ← |
| **But a FAILED air test does not prove the sewer will leak water** ← | **So a failure is usually followed by a water test to decide the matter** ← |
| **And the plugs must be RESTRAINED** ← | **A plug blown out of a pipe under even a low air pressure is a serious projectile hazard — air stores far more energy than water at the same pressure** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS A GENUINE SAFETY MATTER RATHER THAN A FORMALITY AND IT PARALLELS THE THRUST BLOCK WARNING: compressed air is a stored spring, and water is not.**

> **A water-filled pipe that loses its plug simply spills; an air-filled one launches the plug at speed, because the air expands as it escapes and continues to accelerate the plug.**

> **Fatalities have occurred from air-tested pipes, and the standard precautions are to restrain every plug mechanically, to keep everyone out of the line of the pipe ends, and never to exceed the specified test pressure.**

> **THE FUNDAMENTAL POINT ABOUT TESTING IS THE TIMING, AND IT IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN COMPROMISED BY PROGRAMME PRESSURE: the test must be done BEFORE backfilling.**

> **A defect found in an open trench is repaired in an hour; the same defect found after backfilling, road reinstatement and surfacing requires the whole to be broken out again.**

> **So there is a strong incentive to backfill quickly and test later or not at all — and a supervision regime that permits that has given up the only opportunity to obtain a sound sewer.**

> **A second test after backfilling is also worth doing, since the backfilling itself can damage joints — so best practice is to test twice, before and after, and the second test is the one that reflects the sewer as it will actually serve.**

examTip.trick: **Exfiltration contaminates groundwater; infiltration wastes sewer and treatment capacity.** Both harmful, in different seasons on the same sewer.
examTip.trap: **The air test is quick and very sensitive, but a failure does not prove a water leak** — follow it with a water test. And RESTRAIN the plugs: compressed air is a stored spring.
examTip.mnemonic: **Test BEFORE backfilling** — a defect in an open trench costs an hour, and the same defect under a reinstated road costs the whole excavation again. Better still, test twice.

questions.stem: Sewers are VENTILATED principally in order to:
options: Cool the sewage and slow its decomposition
Allow rainwater to enter the system
Remove the foul and explosive gases that accumulate
Increase the velocity of flow in the sewer
questions.solution:
**To remove the FOUL and EXPLOSIVE GASES that accumulate — hydrogen sulphide, methane and carbon dioxide — and to admit air**, so preventing crown corrosion, odour nuisance and the hazard of an explosive or asphyxiating atmosphere.

**The gases and what each does:**

| Gas | Hazard |
|---|---|
| **HYDROGEN SULPHIDE (H₂S)** ← | **TOXIC, and the cause of CROWN CORROSION; smells of rotten eggs at low concentration and DEADENS the sense of smell at higher ones — so the warning disappears as the danger rises** ← |
| **METHANE (CH₄)** ← | **EXPLOSIVE between about 5 and 15 per cent in air; odourless; lighter than air so it collects at the crown** ← |
| **CARBON DIOXIDE** ← | **ASPHYXIANT; heavier than air so it collects at the bottom of a manhole — exactly where a worker descends to** ← |
| **Oxygen DEFICIENCY** ← | **The commonest killer in confined spaces, and it gives no warning whatever** ← |
| **Ammonia, and various organic vapours** | **Irritant and unpleasant** ← |
| **PETROL and solvent vapours from illegal discharges** | **Explosive, and a real cause of sewer explosions** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS TOGETHER DESCRIBE WHY A MANHOLE IS SO DANGEROUS AND THE POINT DESERVES EMPHASIS: the hazardous atmosphere collects at the BOTTOM.**

> **Carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulphide are both heavier than air, so they pool in the base of a manhole while the air at the surface is perfectly breathable.**

> **A worker who leans in and detects nothing, then descends, meets the hazardous layer at chest and head height near the floor — and by then he is on a ladder in a shaft.**

> **This is why the atmosphere must be tested AT THE BOTTOM, by lowering the instrument, and not sniffed at the top; and why forced ventilation with a blower before and during entry is standard.**

**HOW SEWERS ARE VENTILATED:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **PERFORATED manhole covers** ← | **The simplest and commonest — but they also admit storm water as INFLOW, and they let the odour out at street level** ← |
| **VENTILATING SHAFTS (stink pipes) at intervals** ← | **A vertical pipe carried up above roof level, releasing the gases where they disperse harmlessly** ← |
| **The VENT PIPES of house drainage systems** ← | **Every property's soil vent pipe, carried above the eaves, ventilates the sewer through the house connection — collectively a very large ventilation provision** ← |
| **Mechanical extraction with odour treatment** ← | **At pumping stations and problem points, the extracted air being passed through a carbon or biological filter** ← |
| **Adequate air space above the flow** ← | **Which is why sewers are designed to run part full rather than full** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT AND THE LEAST APPRECIATED: the sewer system is ventilated principally through the houses connected to it.**

> **Every soil vent pipe is a chimney from the sewer to the open air above the roof, and there are thousands of them in a town.**

> **This is why the vent pipe must be carried to full height, must not be capped, and must not be omitted when a house is altered — and why a run of properties with defective or missing vents produces a sewer reach with poor ventilation, septic conditions and crown corrosion.**

> **It also explains the importance of the water seal in every trap: the trap is what keeps the sewer's atmosphere out of the house while the vent pipe lets it out above the roof.**

> **Lose the seal — by evaporation in an unused fitting, by siphonage, or by a badly designed system — and the sewer ventilates into the bathroom instead.**

> **THE FIFTH ROW CONNECTS BACK TO A DESIGN DECISION MADE EARLIER AND IT IS WORTH DRAWING THE LINK: a sewer designed to run FULL has no air space, cannot be ventilated, and becomes a pressure conduit.**

> **That is one of the reasons sewers are designed to run three-quarters to nine-tenths full at peak rather than exactly full — the remaining air space is a functional requirement and not merely a margin.**

> **A surcharged sewer loses its ventilation exactly when its flow is greatest and its contents most disturbed, which is why surcharge and odour complaints so often coincide.**

examTip.trick: **Remove H₂S, methane and CO₂ and admit air** — preventing crown corrosion, odour and an explosive or asphyxiating atmosphere.
examTip.trap: **CO₂ and H₂S are heavier than air and pool at the manhole BOTTOM** — the air at the top is fine. Test at the bottom by lowering the instrument, never by sniffing at the top.
examTip.mnemonic: **Houses ventilate the sewer** — every soil vent pipe is a chimney above the roof, and thousands of them do most of the work. So never cap or omit one.

questions.stem: The WATER SEAL in a trap of a house drainage system may be lost by SIPHONAGE. Self-siphonage differs from induced siphonage in that self-siphonage is caused by:
options: Evaporation of the seal during a long period of disuse
The discharge from the fitting's own outflow running full and drawing the seal out behind it
The wind blowing across the top of the vent pipe
Back pressure from a surcharged sewer forcing the seal upward
questions.solution:
**The DISCHARGE FROM THE FITTING'S OWN outflow running full and drawing the seal out behind it** — whereas induced siphonage is caused by the discharge from ANOTHER fitting on the same pipe.

**The ways a water seal can be lost, all of which must be designed against:**

| Mechanism | Cause |
|---|---|
| **SELF-siphonage** ← | **The fitting's own discharge fills its outlet pipe, forming a moving plug of water that creates a partial vacuum behind it and sucks the seal out — worst with a WASH BASIN, whose smooth flat bottom delivers a sudden full-bore surge** ← |
| **INDUCED siphonage** ← | **A discharge from ANOTHER fitting passes the branch connection and draws air from it, siphoning that trap** ← |
| **BACK PRESSURE (blow-out)** ← | **A surcharge or a compression wave below pushes the seal UP and out into the room** ← (option d) |
| **EVAPORATION** ← | **In a fitting unused for weeks — a floor drain in a spare bathroom is the classic case** ← (option a) |
| **CAPILLARY action** ← | **A thread, hair or rag hanging over the trap's weir slowly wicks the water out** ← |
| **WAVERING, from wind across the vent** ← | **Oscillation gradually reducing the seal** ← (option c) |
| **Momentum, from a sudden heavy discharge** | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW'S PARENTHETICAL POINT IS WORTH DWELLING ON BECAUSE IT EXPLAINS A FAMILIAR OBSERVATION: a wash basin is the fitting most prone to self-siphonage.**

> **A basin has a smooth, gently curved bottom and a single outlet, so when the plug is pulled the water leaves in one continuous accelerating rush that fills the waste pipe completely.**

> **A WC, by contrast, discharges a large volume through a large trap and its own outlet is never full for long; a bath empties slowly and its shallow gradient keeps the pipe part full; a sink usually contains scraps and its discharge is broken up.**

> **The basin's characteristic gurgle at the end of its discharge is precisely the sound of air being drawn back through a partly emptied seal, and if the pipework is poor the seal is lost altogether.**

**THE REMEDIES, WHICH ARE ALL ABOUT AIR:**

| Remedy | Note |
|---|---|
| **A VENT (anti-siphonage) pipe connected just downstream of the trap** ← | **Admitting air at that point so no vacuum can form — the classic and reliable answer** ← |
| **Limiting the LENGTH and GRADIENT of the branch waste** ← | **A short, gently graded branch does not run full, so no plug forms** ← |
| **Using a RESEALING trap** ← | **Which retains a reserve of water to restore the seal** ← |
| **An AIR ADMITTANCE VALVE** ← | **A one-way valve admitting air when the pressure falls and closing to prevent gas escaping — used where a vent pipe cannot be run** ← |
| **A deeper seal — 75 mm rather than 50 mm** ← | **More water to lose; required where the trap is not vented** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE MOST ECONOMICAL REMEDY AND IT IS WHY THE PLUMBING CODES SPECIFY BRANCH LENGTHS AND GRADIENTS SO PRECISELY: if the branch pipe never runs full, no siphon can form, and no vent is needed.**

> **A 32 mm basin waste of not more than about 1.7 m at a modest gradient will not run full; a longer or steeper one will.**

> **So the tables of maximum branch lengths in a plumbing code are not arbitrary — each is the length at which that pipe begins to prime, and observing them removes the need for individual vents throughout a small building.**

> **This is why a simple domestic installation can be built with no anti-siphonage pipework at all, while a tall building with long branches requires a full venting system.**

> **THE CONSEQUENCE OF LOSING A SEAL IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY AS A CLOSING POINT, SINCE IT IS THE REASON ALL THIS MATTERS: a trap without its seal is an open pipe from the sewer into the room.**

> **The sewer's atmosphere — hydrogen sulphide, methane, and whatever organisms it carries — then enters the building, and the trap has failed in precisely the duty it exists for.**

> **An empty floor drain in a rarely used bathroom is the commonest instance, and the remedy is as simple as pouring a jug of water down it occasionally — a piece of household maintenance whose reason is rarely explained and which is worth explaining.**

examTip.trick: **Self-siphonage: the fitting's OWN discharge. Induced: ANOTHER fitting's.** A wash basin is the worst offender — its smooth bottom gives one full-bore surge.
examTip.trap: **Options (a), (c) and (d) are all real seal-loss mechanisms** — evaporation, wavering and back pressure — but none is siphonage.
examTip.mnemonic: **If the branch never runs full, no siphon forms** — which is why plumbing codes specify maximum branch lengths and gradients, and why small houses need no vent pipes.

questions.stem: In a TWO-PIPE system of house drainage, as distinct from a one-pipe system:
options: Rainwater and sewage are carried in separate pipes
Hot and cold water are supplied through separate pipes
The drainage is carried in two pipes for redundancy in case one blocks
Soil wastes (from WCs and urinals) and waste wastes (from baths
questions.solution:
**SOIL wastes (from WCs and urinals) and WASTE wastes (from baths, basins and sinks) are carried in SEPARATE stacks**, the waste stack discharging through a trapped gully rather than directly into the drain.

**The systems of house drainage:**

| System | Arrangement |
|---|---|
| **TWO-PIPE (dual) system** ← | **Separate SOIL and WASTE stacks, each with its own vent stack — so up to FOUR vertical pipes** ← |
| **ONE-PIPE system** ← | **A SINGLE stack takes both soil and waste, with a separate VENT stack — two vertical pipes** ← |
