| **Glass, metal, textiles, rubber** | **A few per cent each** ← |
| **Inert — dust, ash, construction debris** | **The remainder** ← |
| **MOISTURE content** ← | **HIGH, 50 to 70 per cent, because of the organic fraction** ← |

> **THE FIRST AND LAST ROWS TOGETHER DETERMINE WHICH TECHNOLOGIES CAN WORK AND WHICH CANNOT, WHICH IS THE PRACTICAL POINT:**

> **A waste that is two-thirds organic and two-thirds water has a LOW CALORIFIC VALUE — so INCINERATION and waste-to-energy plants, which need a dry waste of high calorific value, perform badly and often need supplementary fuel, which is absurd.**

> **The same composition makes it ideal for COMPOSTING or ANAEROBIC DIGESTION, which want exactly a wet organic feedstock.**

> **So the appropriate technology follows directly from the composition, and importing an incinerator designed for a European waste stream — 30 per cent organic, dry, high in paper and plastic — into a Nepali town is a predictable failure.**

> **That failure has occurred often enough to be worth naming, and the composition analysis that would have predicted it is a cheap and simple study.**

**SEGREGATION AT SOURCE IS THE MEASURE THAT UNLOCKS EVERYTHING ELSE, AND IT DESERVES A CLOSING NOTE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Organic waste separated at the household is a clean feedstock for composting** ← | **And can be composted at the household or the neighbourhood, avoiding transport entirely** ← |
| **Mixed with the rest, it CONTAMINATES the recyclables** ← | **Wet paper and food-soiled plastic are worth far less or nothing** ← |
| **And the recyclables contaminate the compost** ← | **Glass fragments and plastic film make it unsaleable** ← |
| **So mixing destroys the value of BOTH fractions in a single act** ← | **And no amount of sorting afterwards fully recovers it** ← |
| **Segregation costs nothing but requires household participation** ← | **Which is a matter of communication and of consistent collection, not of technology** ← |

> **The fourth row is the argument that makes source segregation the first priority in any solid waste programme: mixing is an irreversible destruction of value that takes place in the household bin, before the municipality touches the waste at all.**

> **Everything the municipality can do afterwards is an attempt to undo it imperfectly and at cost — which is why the collection system's design and the public communication that accompanies it matter more than the processing plant at the end.**

With disposal as the last resort — because reducing the waste generated is more effective than dealing with it once it exists.

examTip.trick: **Reduce, reuse, recycle, recover, dispose** — in descending order of preference, following how much each expends.
examTip.trap: **Recycling is only the THIRD best** — it addresses waste already created and consumes collection, sorting and reprocessing energy. Reduction consumes none.
examTip.mnemonic: **60-70 % organic and 50-70 % moisture** — so composting and digestion suit, and incineration does not. Importing a European waste-to-energy design is a predictable failure.

questions.stem: A SANITARY LANDFILL differs from an open dump principally in that a sanitary landfill:
options: Is engineered
Receives only non-hazardous waste
Is located further from the town
Is operated by the municipality rather than privately
questions.solution:
**It is ENGINEERED — with a low-permeability LINER, a LEACHATE collection and treatment system, GAS management, DAILY COVER of the tipped waste, and a designed final capping and after-use.**

**The components of a sanitary landfill:**

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **A LINER of compacted clay, geomembrane, or both** ← | **Prevents leachate reaching the groundwater — the primary environmental protection** ← |
| **A LEACHATE collection layer and drainage pipes above the liner** ← | **Collects the leachate so it does not build up a head on the liner** ← |
| **LEACHATE treatment, or removal for treatment** ← | **Because collected leachate must still be dealt with** ← |
| **GAS collection wells and vents** ← | **Landfill gas is about half METHANE — explosive, and a potent greenhouse gas** ← |
| **DAILY COVER of soil over the tipped waste** ← | **Excludes flies, rodents, birds and windblown litter, and suppresses odour and fire** ← |
| **A final CAPPING of low permeability, with topsoil and vegetation** ← | **Keeping rainwater OUT, which is what limits leachate generation in the long term** ← |
| **Surface water DIVERSION around the site** ← | **So clean runoff does not enter the waste and become leachate** ← |
| **Groundwater MONITORING boreholes** ← | **Up-gradient and down-gradient, to detect any escape** ← |
| **A planned AFTER-USE and long-term aftercare** ← | **A landfill requires management for decades after it closes** ← |

> **THE SIXTH AND SEVENTH ROWS TOGETHER EXPRESS THE PRINCIPLE THAT GOVERNS LEACHATE MANAGEMENT AND IT IS WORTH STATING AS A RULE: keep the WATER OUT.**

> **Leachate is produced when water percolates through the waste, dissolving and carrying its contaminants.**

> **Every litre of rain that enters the waste becomes a litre of leachate that must be collected and treated for decades.**

> **So diverting surface water around the site, capping completed cells promptly, and shaping the surface to shed rather than pond are worth far more than a larger leachate treatment plant — they prevent the problem instead of processing it.**

> **In a monsoon climate this is decisive: an uncapped landfill in Nepal receives 1,500 mm of rain a year over its whole area, and the leachate volume that generates is unmanageable.**

> **Progressive capping — covering each cell as soon as it is complete rather than at the end of the site's life — is therefore not a refinement but the main leachate control measure available.**

**LEACHATE AND GAS, THE TWO PRODUCTS THAT MUST BE MANAGED:**

| Product | Character |
|---|---|
| **LEACHATE from a YOUNG landfill** ← | **Acidic, very high BOD (thousands of mg/l), high COD, high ammonia, readily biodegradable — treatable biologically** ← |
| **Leachate from an OLD landfill** ← | **Near neutral, much lower BOD but still high COD and very high AMMONIA — poorly biodegradable, so biological treatment works badly and physico-chemical methods are needed** ← |
| **LANDFILL GAS** ← | **About 50 to 60 per cent methane, 40 per cent CO₂, with traces of others** ← |
| **Methane's hazards** ← | **EXPLOSIVE at 5 to 15 per cent in air; it MIGRATES laterally through the ground and has accumulated in nearby buildings, with fatal results** ← |
| **And it is a greenhouse gas some 25 times more potent than CO₂** ← | **So collecting and burning it is worthwhile even when the energy is not used** ← |

> **THE CHANGE IN LEACHATE CHARACTER BETWEEN THE FIRST TWO ROWS IS A REAL DESIGN DIFFICULTY AND IT IS OFTEN MISSED: the treatment plant that suits a landfill's first ten years does not suit its next thirty.**

> **A biological plant sized for a young leachate finds itself, twenty years later, receiving a leachate it cannot treat — high in ammonia and refractory COD, low in the biodegradable carbon its process needs.**

> **So the leachate treatment provision must anticipate that transition, either by choosing a process that handles both or by planning for the plant to be changed — and a design based on a single leachate analysis taken in the site's first year will be wrong for most of the site's life.**

> **THE FOURTH ROW DESCRIBES A HAZARD THAT IS EASILY OVERLOOKED BECAUSE IT OCCURS OFF THE SITE: landfill gas does not simply rise from the surface.**

> **Methane migrates laterally through permeable strata and along service trenches, and it can accumulate in the basement or under the floor of a building tens or even hundreds of metres away.**

> **Explosions in buildings adjacent to landfills have killed people, and the source was not obvious to the occupants.**

> **This is why gas monitoring extends beyond the site boundary, why development is restricted within a distance of a landfill, and why a closed and grassed-over landfill that looks entirely harmless still requires monitoring and control for decades.**

examTip.trick: **Liner, leachate collection and treatment, gas management, daily cover, engineered capping and aftercare.** Engineering, not location or ownership.
examTip.trap: **Keep the WATER OUT** — every litre entering becomes leachate for decades. Progressive capping and surface water diversion beat a bigger treatment plant.
examTip.mnemonic: **Young leachate is biodegradable; old leachate is ammonia and refractory COD** — so the plant that suits year five fails by year twenty-five. And gas MIGRATES off site.

questions.stem: The severe winter AIR POLLUTION experienced in the Kathmandu valley is aggravated by a meteorological phenomenon in which:
options: Strong winds carry pollution in from surrounding districts
Heavy rainfall washes pollutants out of the atmosphere and into the air at ground level
A temperature inversion forms — a layer of warm air overlying cooler air near the ground
The valley's altitude reduces the oxygen available to disperse the pollutants
questions.solution:
**A TEMPERATURE INVERSION forms — a layer of warm air overlying cooler air near the ground — which prevents the polluted air rising** and disperses nothing, so emissions accumulate in the bowl of the valley.

**How an inversion works:**

| Condition | Note |
|---|---|
| **NORMALLY the air is COOLER with height** ← | **So air warmed at the ground is less dense than the air above it, RISES, and carries pollutants away — the atmosphere is unstable and mixes** ← |
| **In an INVERSION the air is WARMER with height** ← | **So air at the ground is DENSER than the air above and cannot rise** ← |
| **The atmosphere is then STABLE and does not mix vertically** ← | ← |
| **Emissions are trapped in a shallow layer near the ground** ← | **The 'mixing height' collapses from a kilometre or more to a few tens of metres** ← |
| **Concentrations rise steadily for as long as the inversion persists** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW EXPLAINS WHY THE EFFECT IS SO DRAMATIC RATHER THAN MARGINAL: the same quantity of emissions is diluted into a fraction of the air volume.**

> **If the mixing height falls from 1,000 m to 100 m, the same emissions produce ten times the concentration — and nothing about the emissions has changed at all.**

> **So the winter pollution episode is a DISPERSION event as much as an emission event, which has an important policy implication: the same emission controls that are adequate in summer are inadequate in winter, and an air quality standard that is met for nine months can be exceeded severely for three.**

**WHY KATHMANDU IS PARTICULARLY AFFECTED, WHICH IS WORTH SETTING OUT:**

| Factor | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is a BOWL, enclosed by hills on all sides** ← | **So there is no horizontal ventilation either — the pollution cannot blow away** ← |
| **Winter nights are clear and still** ← | **Ideal conditions for a radiation inversion to form: the ground radiates its heat to a clear sky, cools, and chills the air in contact with it** ← |
| **The inversion persists into the morning and may not break until midday** ← | **Covering the morning traffic and cooking peak** ← |
| **Brick kilns operate in the dry season** ← | **Precisely the season of worst dispersion** ← |
| **Vehicle numbers have grown rapidly, and much of the fleet is old** ← | ← |
| **Road dust and construction contribute heavily to particulate matter** ← | **An unpaved or broken road surface in a dry season is a continuous dust source** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS AN UNFORTUNATE COINCIDENCE OF TIMING AND IT IS WORTH NOTING AS A POLICY TARGET: brick production is necessarily a dry-season activity, and the dry season is exactly when the valley cannot disperse anything.**

> **So the largest point sources operate in the worst conditions, and improving kiln technology — from the traditional to the zigzag or vertical shaft designs — addresses the emissions at the season they matter most.**

> **That is a comparatively tractable intervention: the kilns are a limited number of identifiable sources, unlike the vehicle fleet.**

**THE POLLUTANTS AND THEIR EFFECTS, IN BRIEF:**

| Pollutant | Note |
|---|---|
| **PARTICULATE MATTER, PM₁₀ and PM₂.₅** ← | **The most damaging to health; PM₂.₅ penetrates deep into the lungs and enters the bloodstream** ← |
| **Sulphur dioxide** | **From coal and heavy fuel; respiratory irritant, and it forms acid deposition** ← |
| **Nitrogen oxides** | **From all combustion; respiratory effects, and a precursor of ozone** ← |
| **Carbon monoxide** | **From incomplete combustion; impairs oxygen transport** ← |
| **Ground-level OZONE** | **Formed photochemically from NOx and hydrocarbons in sunlight** ← |
| **INDOOR air pollution from cooking fires** ← | **Frequently WORSE than the outdoor exposure, and it falls disproportionately on women and young children** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW DESERVES ITS EMPHASIS BECAUSE IT IS THE LARGER PROBLEM IN MUCH OF THE COUNTRY AND IT ATTRACTS FAR LESS ATTENTION: a household cooking on a wood or dung fire in an unventilated room experiences particulate concentrations many times the worst outdoor pollution.**

> **The exposure is prolonged, daily, and concentrated on the person doing the cooking and the infant carried beside her.**

> **Improved cookstoves, chimneys, biogas and cleaner fuels address it directly, and they are cheap — so the intervention with the greatest health return per rupee in the country may be a chimney rather than anything to do with traffic.**

> **That is worth knowing because the visible problem and the largest problem are not the same, and attention naturally follows the visible one.**

examTip.trick: **Warm air over cool air stops vertical mixing** — the mixing height collapses and the same emissions produce many times the concentration.
examTip.trap: **It is a DISPERSION event as much as an emission event** — controls adequate in summer fail in winter, so an annual average conceals the problem entirely.
examTip.mnemonic: **Brick kilns run in the dry season, when the valley disperses nothing** — a limited number of identifiable sources, hence tractable. And INDOOR smoke may exceed all of it.

questions.stem: Noise is measured on the DECIBEL scale, which is LOGARITHMIC. It follows that when two identical noise sources each producing 60 dB operate together, the combined level is about:
options: 120 dB
63 dB
60 dB
90 dB
questions.solution:
**About 63 dB.**

**The reasoning:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The decibel is a LOGARITHMIC measure of sound POWER or PRESSURE** ← | **L = 10 log₁₀(P/P₀) for power** ← |
| **Two identical sources DOUBLE the sound POWER** ← | **Not the decibel figure** ← |
| **The increase is 10 log₁₀(2) = 3.01 dB** ← | ← |
| **So 60 dB + 60 dB = 63 dB** ← | **Not 120** ← |

> **THE RULE WORTH MEMORISING IS THAT DOUBLING THE SOURCES ADDS 3 dB, AND ITS CONSEQUENCES ARE WORTH FOLLOWING THROUGH BECAUSE THEY ARE COUNTER-INTUITIVE:**

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| **2 identical sources** | **+3 dB** ← |
| **4 sources** | **+6 dB** ← |
| **10 sources** ← | **+10 dB** ← |
| **100 sources** ← | **+20 dB** ← |
| **Adding a 50 dB source to a 60 dB source** ← | **+0.4 dB — essentially NOTHING** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE MOST USEFUL PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE AND IT DIRECTS ANY NOISE CONTROL EFFORT: a source 10 dB below the dominant one contributes almost nothing to the total.**

> **So silencing the quieter sources achieves nothing measurable while the loudest remains.**

> **Noise control must therefore attack the LOUDEST source first, and only when it has been brought down to the level of the next does the next become worth addressing.**

> **A programme that treats all the sources equally wastes most of its effort, and one that treats the easiest sources first — which is the natural temptation — may produce no perceptible improvement at all.**

> **The corresponding warning is that halving the number of noisy vehicles on a road reduces the noise by 3 dB, which is barely perceptible — so traffic noise cannot be solved by modest reductions in traffic.**

**THE PERCEPTUAL SCALE, WHICH GIVES THE NUMBERS MEANING:**

| Change | Perception |
|---|---|
| **1 dB** | **Imperceptible** ← |
| **3 dB** ← | **Just perceptible — and this is what DOUBLING the sources gives** ← |
| **5 dB** | **Clearly noticeable** ← |
| **10 dB** ← | **Perceived as roughly TWICE as loud — and it requires TEN times the sound power** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW CONTAINS THE FACT THAT MAKES NOISE SO DIFFICULT TO CONTROL AND IT IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY: to make something sound half as loud, its sound power must be reduced to a TENTH.**

> **A 90 per cent reduction in emitted energy buys a halving of perceived loudness.**

> **That is why noise problems are so intractable and why partial measures disappoint: a barrier that removes 3 dB is a genuine engineering achievement and the residents will barely notice it.**

**THE CONTROL MEASURES, IN THE ORDER THEY SHOULD BE CONSIDERED:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **At the SOURCE — quieter machines, silencers, maintenance, enclosure** ← | **Always the most effective, and the first to consider** ← |
| **Along the PATH — barriers, distance, screening, orientation of the building** ← | **A barrier must break the LINE OF SIGHT to work at all** ← |
| **At the RECEIVER — glazing, insulation, room layout, ear protection** ← | **The last resort, and it protects only inside** ← |
| **By TIME — restricting noisy operations to daytime** ← | **Often the cheapest and most acceptable measure of all** ← |

> **THIS SOURCE-PATH-RECEIVER ORDER IS THE SAME HIERARCHY AS THE OCCUPATIONAL SAFETY CONTROLS AND AS THE MITIGATION HIERARCHY, AND IT IS WORTH RECOGNISING AS ONE IDEA: deal with the problem at its origin, then in its transmission, and protect the individual only when neither is possible.**

> **The reason is the same in every case: a control at the source protects everyone automatically, and a control at the receiver protects only those who use it correctly.**

> **The fourth row is worth adding as a practical note, since it is the measure most often available in construction: restricting piling, blasting and heavy plant to daytime hours costs nothing in equipment and removes the complaint that matters most, which is sleep disturbance.**

examTip.trick: **Doubling the sources adds 3 dB** — 10 log₁₀(2). Decibels are logarithmic, so they never add arithmetically.
examTip.trap: **A source 10 dB below the dominant one adds 0.4 dB — nothing.** So attack the LOUDEST source first; treating the quiet ones achieves nothing measurable.
examTip.mnemonic: **10 dB is 'twice as loud' and needs a TENTH of the power** — so a 90 % energy reduction halves the perceived loudness. That is why noise is so intractable.

questions.stem: A PUBLIC HEARING is required as part of the EIA process principally in order to:
options: Satisfy a procedural requirement so that the report can be submitted
Explain the project to the community so that opposition is reduced
Allow the developer to demonstrate the project's benefits
Give the affected people an opportunity to raise concerns and provide local knowledge that the assessment may have missed
questions.solution:
**To give the AFFECTED PEOPLE an opportunity to raise concerns and provide LOCAL KNOWLEDGE that the assessment may have missed** — and to have those concerns recorded and answered before the decision is taken.

**What a public hearing is for, and what it is not for:**

| It IS for | It is NOT for |
|---|---|
| **Obtaining information the assessment team does not have** ← | **Persuading the community to accept a decision already made** ← (option b) |
| **Identifying who is actually affected, and how** ← | **Marketing the project's benefits** ← (option c) |
| **Testing the assessment's findings against local experience** ← | **Discharging a procedural box** ← (option a) |
| **Recording concerns so that they must be ANSWERED** ← | ← |
| **Establishing a relationship before construction begins** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IN THE 'IS FOR' COLUMN IS THE SUBSTANTIVE JUSTIFICATION AND IT IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN FORGOTTEN: the community holds information the assessment cannot otherwise obtain.**

> **They know the history of the site over decades, not the fortnight the survey team spent there.**

> **They know where the water comes from, which slope moved in 1993, where the landslide debris reached, which fields flood, who uses the forest and on what terms, and what happened the last time somebody built something there.**

> **A consultant's baseline study cannot discover most of that, and the hearing is the mechanism by which it enters the assessment.**

> **So a hearing treated as a presentation, in which the developer speaks and the community listens, has inverted the purpose — the information is supposed to flow the other way.**

**WHAT MAKES A HEARING GENUINE RATHER THAN NOMINAL:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Adequate NOTICE, in the local language, by means people actually see** ← | **A notice in a national newspaper is not notice to a village** ← |
| **The information made available BEFOREHAND, in a form people can use** ← | **A 400-page English report is not disclosure; a summary in Nepali is** ← |
| **Held at a place and TIME people can attend** ← | **Not in the district headquarters on a working morning** ← |
| **Conducted so that people can actually SPEAK** ← | **Which requires the officials to listen more than they talk, and requires the socially quieter groups — women, the landless, lower castes — to have a genuine opportunity** ← |
| **A RECORD kept of what was said** ← | ← |
| **And a documented RESPONSE to each substantive point** ← | **Whether accepted, and if not, why** ← |
| **Held BEFORE the decision, with the decision genuinely open** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE HARDEST TO ACHIEVE AND THE MOST OFTEN MISSING, AND IT MATTERS BECAUSE OF WHO IS AFFECTED: a public meeting is dominated by those accustomed to speaking in public meetings.**

> **The people most affected by a project — those without land title, those who use common resources, women whose water collection route is disrupted — are frequently the least likely to speak in a formal gathering with officials present.**

> **So a hearing that is procedurally correct can systematically miss the concerns of the most affected, and a competent process supplements it with separate smaller discussions with those groups.**

> **That is more work and it produces information the formal hearing would not, which is precisely the point.**

> **THE SIXTH ROW IS WHAT DISTINGUISHES CONSULTATION FROM A FORMALITY AND IT IS WORTH INSISTING ON: every substantive point raised should be answered in writing in the final report.**

> **Not necessarily agreed to — many points cannot be accommodated — but recorded, considered, and answered with a reason.**

> **A community whose concerns are recorded and reasonably refused has been consulted; one whose concerns are recorded and ignored has not, and it will know the difference.**

> **And the practical consequence of the difference appears later: unanswered concerns become obstruction during construction, and the cost of dealing with them then, with plant standing idle, exceeds by a wide margin the cost of answering them at the hearing.**

examTip.trick: **To OBTAIN local knowledge and record concerns before the decision** — the information is supposed to flow toward the assessment, not away from it.
examTip.trap: **A hearing run as a presentation has inverted the purpose.** So has one held after the decision is effectively made — there is then nothing the concerns can change.
examTip.mnemonic: **A formally correct hearing can miss the most affected** — the landless, the users of common land, the women. Supplement it with separate smaller discussions.

questions.stem: ENVIRONMENTAL AUDITING, as required after a project has been implemented, is carried out in order to:
options: Check whether the predicted impacts actually occurred
Calculate the project's financial return
Prepare the environmental impact assessment report
Determine whether an EIA was required in the first place
questions.solution:
**To CHECK whether the predicted impacts actually occurred, whether the mitigation measures were implemented and whether they worked** — so that compliance can be enforced and future assessments improved.

**The three questions an audit answers:**

| Question | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Were the mitigation measures actually IMPLEMENTED?** ← | **COMPLIANCE — the enforcement function** ← |
| **Did the predicted impacts actually OCCUR, and to the predicted degree?** ← | **PREDICTION ACCURACY — the learning function** ← |
| **Did the measures WORK?** ← | **EFFECTIVENESS — which informs what is recommended next time** ← |

> **THE SECOND AND THIRD FUNCTIONS ARE THE ONES MOST OFTEN NEGLECTED AND THEY ARE THE ONES WITH THE GREATER LONG-TERM VALUE, which is worth arguing:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Environmental assessment PREDICTS, and prediction is difficult** ← | ← |
| **Yet the predictions are almost never CHECKED against what happened** ← | ← |
| **So the discipline has little systematic feedback on how accurate it is** ← | **Which is an extraordinary state of affairs for a predictive activity** ← |
| **Auditing supplies that feedback** ← | **Telling practitioners which predictions were reliable, which were consistently wrong, and in which direction** ← |
| **Without it, the same errors are repeated indefinitely** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW DESERVES TO BE STATED AS BLUNTLY AS IT DESERVES: a profession that makes predictions and never checks them cannot improve.**

> **An engineer designing a beam has the beam's behaviour to learn from; a hydrologist has the next flood; a geotechnical engineer has the settlement records.**

> **An environmental assessor predicts that a mitigation measure will hold the turbidity below a stated value, and in the overwhelming majority of cases nobody ever finds out whether it did.**

> **Auditing is the mechanism that would close that loop, and where it is done systematically it has shown that certain classes of prediction are reliable and others are not — which is knowledge the discipline needs and largely lacks.**

**THE PRACTICAL DIFFICULTIES OF AUDITING, WHICH EXPLAIN WHY IT IS SO SELDOM DONE WELL:**

| Difficulty | Note |
|---|---|
| **It requires the BASELINE to have been properly established** ← | **Without which nothing can be compared** ← |
| **It requires monitoring to have been CARRIED OUT and RECORDED** ← | **Which requires the EMP's monitoring plan to have been funded and enforced** ← |
| **The predictions must have been stated in a TESTABLE form** ← | **'Some increase in turbidity is expected' cannot be audited; 'turbidity will not exceed 50 NTU at the village intake' can** ← |
| **Nobody's interest is served by an unflattering audit** ← | **Neither the developer's, nor the consultant's, nor the approving authority's** ← |
| **And by the time it is due, the project team has dispersed** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ONE AN ASSESSOR CAN ACT ON DIRECTLY AND IT IS A DISCIPLINE WORTH ADOPTING: write predictions that can be proved wrong.**

> **A vague prediction is unfalsifiable and therefore useless for learning, for monitoring and for enforcement — and it is also, conveniently, unaccountable.**

> **A specific one — a number, a place, a time — can be checked, and stating it commits the assessor to a claim.**

> **The willingness to make falsifiable predictions is what distinguishes an assessment that is doing technical work from one that is producing text, and it is visible on the page.**

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE INSTITUTIONAL PROBLEM AND IT HAS THE OBVIOUS IMPLICATION: auditing must be done by someone INDEPENDENT of those whose work it examines.**

> **A self-audit by the developer records what the developer wishes to record.**

> **The audit function therefore belongs with the regulator or with an independent party reporting to it, and its findings should be public — because the disciplining effect of an audit comes largely from the prospect of its being read.**

> **Where auditing is left to the proponent and never published, it becomes a further document in a file, and the loop it exists to close stays open.**

examTip.trick: **Were the measures implemented, did the predicted impacts occur, and did the measures work?** Compliance, accuracy and effectiveness.
examTip.trap: **The learning function matters most and is most neglected** — a predictive discipline that never checks its predictions cannot improve, which is an extraordinary position.
examTip.mnemonic: **Write predictions that can be proved WRONG** — a number, a place, a time. Vague predictions are unauditable, unenforceable and conveniently unaccountable.

questions.stem: The 'POLLUTER PAYS' PRINCIPLE, one of the foundations of environmental regulation, holds that:
options: A polluter should be fined an amount equal to the profit made from polluting
Pollution is acceptable provided a fee is paid for it
The cost of preventing pollution and of remedying the damage it causes should be borne by the party responsible
The government should pay to clean up pollution and recover the cost through general taxation
questions.solution:
**The COST of preventing pollution and of remedying the damage it causes should be borne by the PARTY RESPONSIBLE** — rather than by the public, by the victims, or by the state — so that the cost is INTERNALISED and reflected in the price of the activity.

**Why internalising the cost matters, which is the economic substance of the principle:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **An untreated discharge imposes real costs — on health, on downstream users, on fisheries, on the treatment of water abstracted below** ← | ← |
| **Those costs are EXTERNALITIES: real, but borne by someone other than the person who caused them** ← | ← |
| **So the polluting activity appears CHEAPER than it is, and more of it occurs than would if its true cost were paid** ← | ← |
| **Making the polluter pay INTERNALISES the cost** ← | **The price of the product then includes the cost of dealing with its waste** ← |
| **And the polluter then has a direct incentive to REDUCE the pollution** ← | **Because doing so reduces his own cost, not somebody else's** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE PRINCIPLE'S REAL POWER AND IT IS WORTH APPRECIATING: it aligns the polluter's interest with the public's.**

> **Where the cost falls elsewhere, the polluter's interest is to pollute; where it falls on him, his interest is to find the cheapest way to reduce it — and he is far better placed than any regulator to know what that is.**

> **So the principle harnesses the polluter's own knowledge and ingenuity rather than requiring the regulator to specify the solution.**

> **That is a more efficient arrangement than prescriptive regulation wherever the outcome can be measured, which is why economic instruments — charges, tradeable permits, deposit schemes — sit alongside direct regulation in most modern systems.**

**THE COMMON MISREADING IN OPTION (b) DESERVES A DIRECT ANSWER, SINCE IT IS WIDESPREAD:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The principle is NOT 'pay and pollute'** ← | **It does not license pollution on payment of a fee** ← |
| **It operates ALONGSIDE standards, not instead of them** ← | **Discharge limits still apply, and exceeding them is an offence rather than a priced option** ← |
| **Within the permitted range, the principle allocates the COST of compliance and of any residual damage** ← | ← |
| **It also covers the cost of PREVENTION, not merely of damage** ← | **The treatment plant is the polluter's cost, not the public's** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE ESSENTIAL QUALIFICATION AND IT ANSWERS THE OBJECTION THAT THE PRINCIPLE LETS THE RICH POLLUTE FREELY: standards set the limit, and the principle determines who bears the cost of staying within it.**

> **A discharge above the standard is not permitted at any price.**

**THE RELATED PRINCIPLES, WHICH ARE USUALLY STATED TOGETHER AND ARE WORTH DISTINGUISHING:**

| Principle | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **POLLUTER PAYS** ← | **The responsible party bears the cost — this question** ← |
| **PRECAUTIONARY principle** ← | **Where an activity threatens SERIOUS or IRREVERSIBLE harm, a LACK OF FULL SCIENTIFIC CERTAINTY is not a reason to postpone preventive measures** ← |
| **PREVENTION is better than cure** ← | **Preventing pollution costs less than remedying it — the same reasoning as the mitigation hierarchy** ← |
| **SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT** ← | **Meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs — the Brundtland formulation** ← |
| **INTER-GENERATIONAL equity** ← | **The present generation holds the environment in trust for those who follow** ← |
| **PUBLIC PARTICIPATION and access to information** ← | **Those affected have a right to know and to be heard** ← |

> **THE PRECAUTIONARY PRINCIPLE IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN MISSTATED AND ITS PRECISE FORM MATTERS: it does not say that an activity must be proved harmless before it may proceed.**

> **It says that where the threatened harm is SERIOUS or IRREVERSIBLE, scientific uncertainty shall not be used as a REASON FOR POSTPONING cost-effective preventive measures.**

> **The qualifications carry the weight: the harm must be serious or irreversible, and the measures must be cost-effective.**

> **So it is a rule about who bears the burden of uncertainty in a particular class of case, not a general prohibition on anything unproven — and stating it in the stronger form makes it easy to dismiss, which does the principle no service.**

> **The IRREVERSIBILITY qualification is the heart of it: a harm that can be undone if the prediction proves wrong is one where waiting for evidence is reasonable, and a harm that cannot is one where waiting means the decision has been made by default.**

examTip.trick: **The responsible party bears the cost of prevention AND of remedy** — so the cost is internalised into the price of the activity.
examTip.trap: **It is NOT 'pay and pollute'** — standards still set the limit, and the principle allocates the cost of complying with them. Exceeding a limit is an offence, not a priced option.
examTip.mnemonic: **Precautionary principle, precisely: where harm is SERIOUS or IRREVERSIBLE, uncertainty is no reason to postpone COST-EFFECTIVE prevention.** The qualifications carry the weight.

questions.stem: For a project in Nepal requiring an EIA, the report is submitted through the concerned ministry and the APPROVAL is granted by:
options: The local municipality or rural municipality
The ministry responsible for the environment
The Department of Roads in every case
The project proponent's own board
questions.solution:
**The MINISTRY responsible for the ENVIRONMENT, whereas an IEE report is approved by the concerned SECTORAL ministry.**

**The division of approving authority:**

| Level of study | Approved by |
|---|---|
| **BES — Brief Environmental Study** ← | **The concerned body, at the level prescribed in the Rules** ← |
| **IEE** ← | **The CONCERNED (sectoral) ministry — the ministry responsible for that type of project** ← |
| **EIA** ← | **The ministry responsible for the ENVIRONMENT** ← |

> **THE REASON FOR THE DIFFERENT AUTHORITY AT THE TWO LEVELS IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING RATHER THAN MEMORISING, AND IT CONCERNS INDEPENDENCE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A sectoral ministry both PROMOTES its sector and, for an IEE, approves its environmental study** ← | **The Ministry responsible for roads wants roads built** ← |
| **That is a conflict of interest, accepted for smaller projects in the interest of speed** ← | ← |
| **For a project large enough to require an EIA, the approval is moved to a ministry with NO stake in the project proceeding** ← | ← |
| **So the significance of the project determines how independent its scrutiny is** ← | **Which is a reasonable allocation of a limited regulatory capacity** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IDENTIFIES A TENSION PRESENT IN EVERY ENVIRONMENTAL REGULATORY SYSTEM AND IT IS WORTH BEING ABLE TO NAME: the body that wants the project built should not be the body that decides whether its environmental study is adequate.**

> **Separating those roles is the whole reason environment ministries and independent regulators exist, and the degree of separation is a fair measure of how seriously a system takes the function.**

**THE PROPONENT'S OBLIGATIONS, WHICH THE APPROVAL CARRIES WITH IT:**

| Obligation | Note |
|---|---|
| **The project must be implemented IN ACCORDANCE with the approved report and its EMP** ← | **The approval is conditional on that** ← |
| **The mitigation measures in the EMP must be carried out** ← | ← |
| **MONITORING must be undertaken and reported** ← | ← |
| **Any material CHANGE to the project requires the assessment to be revisited** ← | **A project approved on one design and built to another has not been approved** ← |
| **The concerned body may INSPECT, and may direct corrective action** ← | ← |
| **Non-compliance attracts penalties and, in principle, suspension of the work** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE OBLIGATION MOST OFTEN BREACHED WITHOUT ANYONE NOTICING AND IT IS WORTH FLAGGING: projects change between assessment and construction.**

> **An alignment is shifted to avoid a land dispute, a quarry is opened somewhere other than where the report assumed, a spoil disposal site is changed because the planned one proved unavailable, the capacity is increased because the demand forecast changed.**

> **Each of those may be reasonable and each invalidates part of the assessment on which the approval rested.**

> **Spoil disposal in particular is the change that most often causes real environmental damage in Nepali hill road and hydropower projects — the report shows designated tipping sites, and the contractor, finding them inconvenient, side-casts the spoil over the hillside into the river below.**

> **That single departure can cause more damage than everything the assessment considered, and it happens after the approval, outside anyone's view, as an operational decision by a contractor who never read the report.**

> **Which is why the EMP's measures must appear in the CONTRACT, as argued earlier, and why supervision of spoil disposal is worth more than most of the monitoring that is actually carried out.**

**AND THE INSTITUTIONS INVOLVED, IN OUTLINE:**

| Body | Role |
|---|---|
| **The PROPONENT** ← | **Prepares the report, implements the EMP, monitors and reports** ← |
| **The CONCERNED (sectoral) ministry** ← | **Receives the report, approves an IEE, forwards an EIA with its opinion** ← |
| **The ministry responsible for the ENVIRONMENT** ← | **Approves an EIA, may inspect and enforce** ← |
| **LOCAL government** ← | **Consulted, hosts the public hearing and the notices, and has its own role in local-level projects under the federal structure** ← |
| **The affected PUBLIC** ← | **Consulted, and entitled to information** ← |

> **The fourth row has grown in importance under Nepal's federal structure, and it is worth noting that responsibilities for environmental management are now shared between the federal, provincial and local levels — so the applicable authority for a particular project depends on which level of government is responsible for that class of project, and the position continues to develop.**

examTip.trick: **EIA to the ENVIRONMENT ministry; IEE to the concerned SECTORAL ministry.** The larger the project, the more independent the scrutiny.
examTip.trap: **A sectoral ministry both promotes its sector and approves its own IEEs** — an accepted conflict for smaller projects, removed for those needing an EIA.
examTip.mnemonic: **Projects CHANGE after approval, and SPOIL DISPOSAL is the change that does most damage** — side-cast over the hillside by a contractor who never read the report.

questions.stem: Among the effects of a changing climate that bear most directly on civil engineering practice in Nepal, the most significant for the DESIGN of drainage and hydraulic structures is that:
options: Average annual temperatures are rising
Glaciers are retreating in the high Himalaya
Average annual rainfall totals are changing slowly
Rainfall is becoming more intense and more variable
questions.solution:
**RAINFALL is becoming more INTENSE and more variable** — so that the intensity-duration-frequency relationships on which drainage design depends are no longer STATIONARY, and a structure designed to a historic return period may face that event far more often.

**Why the loss of stationarity matters so much:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **All conventional hydrological design assumes STATIONARITY** ← | **That the statistics of the past describe the future — so a 50-year flood computed from 40 years of record will remain a 50-year flood** ← |
| **Every frequency analysis, every IDF curve and every design storm rests on that assumption** ← | ← |
| **A changing climate breaks it** ← | **The distribution itself is shifting, so the past record is no longer a sample of the future** ← |
| **A culvert designed for a historic 1-in-25-year storm may now face it every 10 or 15 years** ← | **Without anything about the culvert having changed** ← |
| **And the design method offers no way to allow for this from the record alone** ← | **Since the record is precisely what has stopped being representative** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE GENUINE METHODOLOGICAL DIFFICULTY AND IT SHOULD BE STATED HONESTLY RATHER THAN GLOSSED OVER: the standard tools assume the very thing that is no longer true.**

> **Extending the record does not help, because the older data is drawn from a different climate.**

> **The practical responses available are to apply a deliberate uplift factor to the design rainfall, to design to a longer return period than the standard requires, to favour designs that fail SAFELY when exceeded, and to build in the capacity to be enlarged later.**

> **None of those is theoretically satisfying and all of them are better than proceeding as though nothing had changed.**

**THE PRACTICAL DESIGN RESPONSES, WHICH ARE WORTH KNOWING AS A SET:**

| Response | Note |
|---|---|
| **Apply an ALLOWANCE to the design rainfall intensity** ← | **Many jurisdictions now specify an uplift of 10 to 40 per cent on peak rainfall for the structure's design life** ← |
| **Design for GRACEFUL failure** ← | **A culvert that overtops onto a properly protected road embankment survives; one that washes the embankment away does not — and the difference is a scour apron and a designed overflow path** ← |
| **Provide for future ENLARGEMENT** ← | **Headwalls and abutments set so a second barrel can be added; land reserved beside a drain** ← |
| **Favour measures that are ROBUST to uncertainty** ← | **Catchment management, retention, and green infrastructure degrade gracefully, while a fixed-capacity pipe does not** ← |
| **Review the design life** ← | **A structure with a 100-year life faces far more change than one with a 25-year life, and warrants a larger allowance** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE MOST VALUABLE AND THE LEAST COSTLY OF THESE AND IT DESERVES EMPHASIS: designing for what happens when the capacity IS exceeded costs very little and changes the consequence completely.**

> **Every drainage structure will be exceeded eventually, climate change or not — the return period says so.**

> **The question is whether the exceedance causes an inconvenience or a catastrophe, and that is settled by whether an overflow route was designed, whether the embankment is protected, and whether the failure is progressive or sudden.**

> **A designer who cannot know the future intensity can still ensure that being wrong is survivable, and that is the appropriate engineering response to an uncertainty that cannot be resolved.**

**THE OTHER EFFECTS IN THE OPTIONS ARE REAL AND EACH MATTERS ELSEWHERE, WHICH IS WORTH ACKNOWLEDGING:**

| Effect | Where it matters most |
|---|---|
| **Glacier RETREAT** ← | **Long-term dry-season river flows, and the GROWTH of glacial lakes and hence GLOF risk — a hydropower and a hazard issue** ← |
| **Rising TEMPERATURE** ← | **Water demand, crop water requirements, pavement design temperatures, and the range of vector-borne disease moving up in altitude** ← |
| **Changing annual TOTALS** ← | **Water resource availability and irrigation planning** ← |
| **Increasing INTENSITY and variability** ← | **DRAINAGE and hydraulic structure design — this question, and the most immediate for ordinary practice** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW CONNECTS BACK TO THE GLOF QUESTION AND IS WORTH DRAWING OUT: glacier retreat is not only a long-term water resource issue but an immediate HAZARD issue, because the retreating glaciers are creating and enlarging the very lakes whose moraine dams may fail.**

> **So the hazard is growing rather than static, and a GLOF risk assessment based on a lake inventory ten years old understates the present position.**

> **The second row's last item is also worth noting because it is often missed in an engineering context: the altitude limit of malaria and dengue transmission is rising as temperatures rise, so valleys that were historically free of them are no longer — which affects the design of water storage and drainage in exactly the ways discussed under rainwater tanks and road gullies.**

examTip.trick: **Design rainfall statistics are no longer STATIONARY** — a historic 1-in-25-year storm may now recur every 10 or 15 years, with nothing about the structure having changed.
examTip.trap: **Extending the record does not help** — the older data comes from a different climate. That is the methodological difficulty, and it has no clean solution.
examTip.mnemonic: **Design for GRACEFUL failure** — every structure is exceeded eventually. An overflow route and a scour apron cost little and change a catastrophe into an inconvenience.
